and so conditions c) and $\mathrm { d }$ ) follow from Proposition 12.5.12 items 1(a) and 1(b).

Corollary 12.5.14. Let $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ be a pair of non-negative integers and let $( G , b )$ be a non-degenerate symmetric torsion group. There exists a non-degenerate odd lattice $L$ of rank $r$ , signature $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ and with discriminant form $( G , b )$ if $r \_ { \geq }$ $\ell ( G ) + 3$ .

Historical and Bibliographical Notes. The existence of lattices with given discriminant quadratic form was first shown by C.T.C. Wall in [245]. In Section 12.1 we have given his proof, of which the crucial ingredient, the euclidean algorithm and its consequences, was already discussed in Section 4.3.

Uniqueness up to stable equivalence dates back to A. Durfee's thesis [56], which we have closely followed. The concept of "index mod 8" is due to V. Nikulin [171] who attributes its calculation to C.T.C. Wall. Our version as given in Section 12.3 is inspired by the calculations used to prove Theorem 8.14 in the book [99] by F. Hirzebruch, W. Neumann and S. Koh.

The insight that the classical existence results Theorems 12.4.1 and 12.4.2 can be reformulated in terms of the discriminant form (cf. Theorems 12.4.4, 12.5.13) is due to V. Nikulin and has been elaborated in his article [171]. It also contains the characterization of the genus in the case of odd lattices which is stated here as Theorem 12.5.9.

# The Spin Group

# Introduction

The spin group of a quadratic vector space $( V , q )$ over a field $k$ is defined by means of its Clifford algebra ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ . As a vector space this is just the exterior algebra $\Lambda ( V )$ and it contains $V$ . The algebra structure comes from $q$ . For us its importance lies in the action of the algebra conjugation. Firstly, conjugation with a non-isotropic vector $u \in V$ preserves $V$ and, secondly, in $V$ this gives the hyperplane reflection $\sigma _ { u }$ up to a sign. This property for $u$ can be extended to a "large" subgroup of ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ . To do this properly, one makes use of a canonical splitting of ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ into even and odd elements. The even elements form a subalgebra, the even Clifford algebra. The conjugation with $u$ receives a sign according to whether $u$ is odd or even. The Clifford group consists of the invertible elements $u$ of the Clifford algebra which have the property that twisted conjugation with $u$ preserves $V$ .

The classical Hamilton quaternions form the even Clifford algebra for the standard inner product on $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ , as we shall see in Example 13.1.3.2; the non-zero quaternions give the special Clifford group as shown in Example 13.2.1.1. In Example 13.1.3.2 we show that, surprizingly, the classification of real Clifford algebras is equivalent to the classification of symmetric forms on $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 }$ -vector spaces having an at most 1-dimensional radical. So the Arf invariant reappears here. Remarkably, the Arf invariant also comes up in $\ S$ 13.1.B where the center of the Clifford algebra is calculated.

In the remainder of the chapter the field $k$ has characteristic different from 2. In Section 13.2 some essential properties of the Clifford group are established. These are used to make sense of the spinor norm, a certain $k ^ { \times }$ valued function on $\operatorname { C l i f } ( q )$ which is introduced in Section 13.3. Now one makes use of two observations: any element in the Clifford group is an algebra product of non-isotropic vectors in $V$ and secondly, the Clifford algebra acts on $V$ through a twisted adjoint action which for $u \in V$ is given by the reflection $\sigma _ { u }$ . Combining the two, one defines the spinor norm of a product of such reflections as the spinor norm of the corresponding $u$ The Cartan-Dieudonné theorem implies that in this way we can define the spinor norm for any isometry. Since the decomposition of an isometry into reflections is not unique, this is ambiguous. To take this into account, we do not take $k$ as the value group of this spinor norm, but $\mathsf { D } ( k ) = k ^ { \times } / ( k ^ { \times } ) ^ { 2 }$ . This version of the spinor norm shall play an essential role in establishing the classification of indefinite lattices given in Chapter 14.1 In the final Section 13.4 we define all of the preceding concepts in the setting of lattices.

# 13.1 The Clifford Algebra

In this section $k$ is a feld of any characterisic $V$ a $k$ -vector space and $q$ a (possibly degenerate) quadratic form on $V$ .

13.1.A Basic properties. Recall that the exterior algebra $\Lambda ( V )$ is the quotient of the tensor algebra $T ( V )$ by the two-sided ideal generated by the tensors $x \otimes x$ , $x \in$ $V$ . This is a $k$ vector space of dimension $2 ^ { \dim V }$ . In the presence of a quadratic form we consider another (non-commutative) unital $k$ -algebra, the Clifford algebra ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ of $( V , q )$ , which might be viewed as a deformation of $\Lambda ( V )$ in that the generating relations $x \otimes x = 0$ have been replaced by

$$
x \otimes x = q ( x ) \cdot { \bf 1 } , \quad x \in V ,
$$

where we denote the unit by $\mathbf { 1 }$ in ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ and the product with a dot. One finds back $\Lambda ( V )$ in case $q = 0$ and in that sense ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ is a deformation of the exterior algebra and so both vector spaces have the same dimension. This is elaborated below resulting in Lemma 13.1.2.

The Clifford algebra ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ contains $V$ (see below). The defining rule (13.1) implies first of all that non-isotropic vectors $x \in V$ are invertible within ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ with two-sided inverse $q ( x ) ^ { - 1 } x$ . Secondly, using the algebra rules, the commutation rule for two vectors $x , y \in V$ is completely determined by (13.1):

$$
\begin{array} { c } { { b _ { q } ( x , y ) \cdot { \bf 1 } = q ( x + y ) \cdot { \bf 1 } - q ( x ) \cdot { \bf 1 } - q ( y ) \cdot { \bf 1 } } } \\ { { { } ~ = ( x + y ) \cdot ( x + y ) - x \cdot x - y \cdot y } } \\ { { { } ~ = x \cdot y + y \cdot x . } } \end{array}
$$

It follows in particular that $x \cdot y + y \cdot x = 0$ whenever $x$ and $y$ are orthogonal. Surprisingly, using this commutation rule, conjugation within ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ by a non-isotropic $u \in V$ preserves $V$ and induces in $V$ the reflection $\sigma _ { u }$ up to sign:2

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { u \cdot x \cdot u ^ { - 1 } = ( u \cdot x + x \cdot u ) u ^ { - 1 } - x , \quad x \in V } \\ { \ } \\ { \ } \\ { \qquad = b _ { q } ( x , u ) u ^ { - 1 } - x , } \\ { \ } \\ { \ } & { = b _ { q } ( x , u ) q ( u ) ^ { - 1 } u - x } \\ { \ } & { = - \sigma _ { u } ( x ) . } \end{array}
$$

If the characteristic is different from 2, the Cartan-Dieudonné theorem 7.2.4 then implies that all orthogonal transformations up to sign extend to the algebra ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ as conjugations. This shows the relevance of this algebra. Its formal definition is as follows:

Definition 13.1.1. The Clifford algebra ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ is defined as the quotient of the tensor algebra $T ( V )$ on $V$ by the two-sided ideal $I ( q )$ generated by $x \otimes x - q ( x ) \cdot { \bf 1 }$ , $x \in V$ , and with multiplication induced by the multiplication in $T ( V )$ . We denote the multiplication in the Clifford algebra by a dot.

The natural composition

$$
\iota : V \to T ( V ) \to T ( V ) / I ( q ) = \mathsf { C } ( q )
$$

is a map of $k$ -vector spaces for which $\iota ( x ) \cdot \iota ( x ) = q ( x ) \cdot { \bf 1 }$ . One can show that $\iota$ is injective. We refer to [137, Ch. I.1] for a proof. To simplify notation we shall identify $V$ with its image $\iota ( V )$ .

Alternatively, we may use the Bourbakist definition of this algebra which is as follows: the Clifford algebra on $q$ is a pair $( \mathsf C ( q ) , \iota )$ of a $k$ -algebra ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ with unit 1 together with a $k$ -linear map $\iota : V \to \mathsf C ( q )$ for which $\iota ( x ) \cdot \iota ( x ) = q ( x ) \cdot { \bf 1 }$ and which satisfies the following universality property: any $k$ -linear map $u : V \to A$ to a $k$ -algebra $A$ such that $u ( x ) \cdot u ( x ) = q ( x ) \cdot 1$ extends to ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ . For the statement and proof that the preceding construction implies universality, see [137, Ch. I, Prop 1.1].

The grading on $T ( V )$ does not descend to ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ since the ideal $I ( q )$ is not homogeneous. However, it is generated in even degrees only, which implies that ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ gets a $\mathbb { Z } / 2 \mathbb { Z }$ -grading, that is

$$
\mathsf C ( q ) = \mathsf C ^ { 0 } ( q ) \oplus \mathsf C ^ { 1 } ( q ) , \quad \mathsf C ^ { i } ( q ) \cdot \mathsf C ^ { j } ( q ) \subset \mathsf C ^ { i + j } ( q ) ,
$$

where the indices are taken modulo 2. In particular ${ \mathsf { C } } ^ { 0 } ( q )$ is a subalgebra, the even Clifford algebra. The universality property for the Clifford algebra applied to $u = - \iota$ shows for example that there exists an involution $\alpha$ restricting to -id on $V \subset \mathsf { C } ^ { \mathrm { 1 } } ( q )$ . It satisfies

$$
\alpha : \mathsf { C } ( q ) \to \mathsf { C } ( q ) , \quad \left\{ \begin{array} { r l } { \alpha | _ { \mathsf { C } ^ { 0 } ( q ) } } & { = \mathrm { ~ i d } , } \\ { \alpha | _ { \mathsf { C } ^ { 1 } ( q ) } } & { = - \mathrm { i d } . } \end{array} \right.
$$

This gives the Bourbakist definition of the even and odd Clifford algebra as eigenspaces of $\alpha$ .

We claimed above that ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ is a deformation of the exterior algebra $\Lambda ( V )$ . This can be made more precise. The tensor-degree defines an obvious filtration $F ^ { \bullet }$ on $T ( V )$ which descends to ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ . It preserves the algebra structure in the sense that $F ^ { i } \cdot F ^ { j } \subset F ^ { i + j }$ and the associated grading gives ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ the structure of a graded algebra. The graded algebra $\Lambda V$ is canonically isomorphic to this graded algebra through the map which sends $v _ { 1 } \wedge \dots \wedge v _ { k }$ to the class of $v _ { 1 } \cdots v _ { k }$ . This map is clearly surjective and one can show by induction on the degree that it is also an injective map. See e.g. [137, Ch 1.1, Prop. 1.2].

This shows:

Lemma 13.1.2. There is a canonical vector space isomorphism $\Lambda ( V ) { \stackrel { \cong } { \to } } \mathsf C ( q )$ . In particular, dim C(q) = 2dim V.

Examples 13.1.3. 1. Hamiltonian quaternions revisited. Consider the standard diagonal form $x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } + x _ { 3 } ^ { 2 }$ on $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ . Its Clifford algebra has as a vector space basis $\{ 1 , e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } , e _ { 3 } , i = e _ { 2 } e _ { 3 } , j = e _ { 3 } e _ { 1 } , k = e _ { 2 } e _ { 1 } , e _ { 1 } e _ { 2 } e _ { 3 } \}$ , where $\{ e _ { 1 } , e _ { 2 } , e _ { 3 } \}$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ . Since for $i , j = 1 , 2 , 3$ we have $e _ { i } e _ { j } = - e _ { j } e _ { i }$ for $i \neq j$ , and $e _ { i } ^ { 2 } = 1$ , it follows that $\pmb { i } \cdot \pmb { j } = e _ { 2 } e _ { 3 } e _ { 3 } e _ { 1 } = e _ { 2 } e _ { 1 } = \pmb { k }$ and similarly for the cyclic permutations of $i , j , k$ . Moreover, $\pmb { i } ^ { 2 } = \pmb { j } ^ { 2 } = \pmb { k } ^ { 2 } = - 1$ . So the vector space with basis $\{ 1 , \pmb { i } , \pmb { j } , \pmb { k } \}$ generates the algebra of the Hamilton quaternions $\mathbb { H }$ which we already encountered in $\ S$ 5.4.A. This is the even Clifford algebra for the dot product form on $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ . As a special case of the second example below we shall see that $\mathbb { H }$ also figures as the full Clifford algebra of the form $- x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } - x _ { 2 } ^ { 2 }$ on $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ .

Recall also that we explained in Section 5.4 how to associate a ternary quadratic form to any quaternion algebra $\begin{array} { r } { D = \left( \frac { a , b } { k } \right) } \end{array}$ , namely the norm form restricted to the subspace ${ \cal D } ^ { ( 0 ) }$ of the quaternions of trace $0$ . For the Hamilton quaternions this is the dot product form on $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ where $\mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ is identified with the real space with basis $\{ \dot { \pmb { i } } , \dot { \pmb { j } } , \pmb { k } \}$ , the so-called pure quaternions. In general the even Clifford algebra of the norm form on ${ \cal D } ^ { ( 0 ) }$ is precisely $D$ .

2. Real Clifford algebras (cf. [68, 179]) By Sylvester's law 8.1.3 nondegenerate real forms are classified by their signature $( r , s )$ with representing diagonal quadratic forms $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { r } x _ { i } ^ { 2 } - \sum _ { i = r + 1 } ^ { n } x _ { i } ^ { 2 }$ b $n = r + s$ The corresponding Clifford algebra ${ \mathsf C } _ { r , s }$ is then generated by the standard basis $\{ \pmb { e } _ { 1 } , \ldots , \pmb { e } _ { r + s } \}$ subject to the relations

$$
\begin{array} { r } { e _ { i } ^ { 2 } = \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { 1 } & { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } i \leq r } \\ { - 1 } & { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } i > r } \end{array} \right. \quad \mathrm { a n d } \quad e _ { i } \cdot e _ { j } + e _ { i } \cdot e _ { j } = 0 \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } i \neq j . } \end{array}
$$

For example, ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { 0 , 0 } = \mathbb { R }$ , $\mathrm { C } _ { 1 , 0 } = \mathbb { R } \oplus \mathbb { R }$ , while ${ \mathsf C } _ { 0 , 1 } = \mathbb C$ . We shall now show that the isomorphism class of the Clifford algebra of a real quadratic form does not determine the signature. To do so we make basic use of quadratic forms over $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 }$ as suggested by the signs that appear in the above relations. We start by considering the group ring $\mathbb { R } [ G ]$ , $G = \Pi ^ { n } C _ { 2 }$ . where $C _ { 2 }$ is the cyclic group of order 2. Viewing $C _ { 2 }$ as the field $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 }$ and switching to additive notation and identifying groupelements of $G$ with vectors $\pmb { x } \in \mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n }$ , this group ring becomes the real vector space $V : = \oplus _ { x \in G } \mathbb { R } \cdot e _ { x }$ with algebra structure induced by the additive group structure, i.e., the product $^ *$ is given by $e _ { x } * e _ { y } = e _ { x + y }$ . As vector spaces $V$ and ${ \mathsf C } _ { r , s }$ are isomorphic: identify $e _ { x } \in \ V$ with the element $\pmb { e } _ { i _ { 1 } } \cdot \cdot \cdot \pmb { e } _ { i _ { k } } \in \mathbb { C } _ { r , s }$ where $_ x$ has $i$ -t coordinate 1 precisely if $i \in \{ i _ { 1 } , \ldots , i _ { k } \}$ . In particular, if $\{ e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { n } \}$ is the standard basis of $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 }$ ,

$$
e _ { e _ { k } } { \mathrm { ~ c o r r e s p o n d s ~ t o ~ } } e _ { k } .
$$

The possibly non-commutative Clifford algebra ${ \mathsf C } _ { r , s }$ comes from the twisted group action

$$
e _ { x } \cdot e _ { y } = ( - 1 ) ^ { \beta ^ { r , s } ( x , y ) } e _ { x } * e _ { y } ,
$$

where $\beta ^ { r , s }$ is the $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 }$ -valued (in general non-symmetric) bilinear form on $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n }$ , which in coordinates with respect to the standard basis $\{ e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { n } \}$ is given by $x A ^ { r , s } { \bf y } ^ { \scriptscriptstyle 1 }$ ,

where $A$ is the upper-triangular matrix

$$
A ^ { r , s } = \left( \begin{array} { l l l l } { 0 } & { 1 } & { \cdots } & { 1 } \\ { \vdots } & { 0 } & { \ddots } & { \vdots } \\ { \vdots } & { \ldots } & { \ddots } & { 1 } \\ { 0 } & { \cdots } & { \ldots } & { 0 } \end{array} \right) + \left( \begin{array} { l } { 0 _ { r } } \\ { \phantom { - } } \\ { 0 _ { s \times r } } \end{array} \right| \left( \begin{array} { l } { 0 _ { r \times s } } \\ { \phantom { - } } \\ { \phantom { - } } \\ { 0 _ { s \times r } } \end{array} \right)

By the correspondence (13.4) the relations $( - 1 ) ^ { A _ { i j } ^ { r s } } = - 1$ for $j > i$ and $( - 1 ) ^ { A _ { i j } ^ { r s } } = 1$ for $j < i$ imply that the desired anti-commutation relations hold, while $( - 1 ) ^ { A _ { i i } ^ { r s } } = \mathbf { 1 }$ for $i \leq r$ and $( - 1 ) ^ { A _ { i i } ^ { r s } } = - { \bf 1 }$ for $i > r$ , proving the remaining two relations.

Observe that as in equation (1.1) in Chapter 1, a bilinear form defines a unique quadratic form on $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n }$ . Conversely, given a basis for a $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 }$ -vector space, a quadratic form $q$ determines an upper-triangular bilinear form $\beta$ which can be used to define a twisted product (13.5). The resulting associative algebra is denoted $C _ { \mathbb { R } } [ \mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n } , q ]$ . This algebra has a special structure: either the generators $\mathbf { \boldsymbol { e } } _ { i }$ and $e _ { j }$ for $i \neq j$ anticommute (namely if $\beta _ { i j } = 1$ for $i < j$ since then $\pmb { e } _ { i } \cdot \pmb { e } _ { j } = - \pmb { e } _ { i } * \pmb { e } _ { j }$ and $\pmb { e } _ { j } \cdot \pmb { e } _ { i } = \pmb { e } _ { i } * \pmb { e } _ { j }$ ), or they commute (if $\beta _ { i j } = 0$ for $i < j$ , since then $\pmb { e } _ { i } \cdot \pmb { e } _ { j } = \pmb { e } _ { j } \cdot \pmb { e } _ { i } = \pmb { e } _ { i } * \pmb { e } _ { j }$ ). It follows that isometric forms $q$ give isomorphic algebras.

So the classification of the real Clifford algebras follows from the classification of the quadratic forms on the vector spaces $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { n }$ as given in Example 8.2.7. The nondegenerate forms live on even-dimensional spaces and come in two types depending on the Arf invariant. The ones with zero Arf invariant are the form $q _ { 0 } = \mathbb { Q } ^ { m } U$ , $n = 2 m$ , the ones with Arf invariant 1 are of the form $q _ { 1 } = \Phi ^ { m - 1 } U \odot \Phi ^ { 2 } \langle 1 \rangle$ , $n = 2 m$ . On odd dimensional spaces, say of dimension $n = 2 m + 1$ , one has three types with $\mathrm { d i m } \operatorname { r a d } ( q ) \leq 1$ , namely $q _ { 0 } ^ { \prime } = \Phi ^ { m } U \circledast 0$ , $q _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } = \oplus ^ { m - 1 } U \oplus \oplus ^ { 2 } \langle 1 \rangle \oplus 0$ and $q _ { 2 } = \Phi ^ { m } U \odot$ [1]. We shall show that these types indeed give all the real Clifford algebras ${ \mathsf C } _ { r , s }$ .

This poses no problem for $\mathsf { C } _ { \mathbb { R } } \left[ \mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { 2 } , q _ { i } \right]$ , $i \in \{ 0 , 1 \}$ : these are the 4-dimensional Clifford algebras $\mathrm { C _ { 2 , 0 } , C _ { 0 , 2 } }$ with generators $\mathbf { \boldsymbol { e } } _ { 1 } , \mathbf { \boldsymbol { e } } _ { 2 }$ subject to

# 13.2 The Clifford Group

In this section $V$ is a vector space over a field $k$ of characteristic $\neq 2$ and $q : V \to k$ is a non-degenerate quadratic form, i.e. $( V , q )$ is a quadratic inner product space.

The Clifford group, to be defined below, is a subgroup of the group $C ( q ) ^ { \times }$ of the invertible elements of the Clifford algebra ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ of $q$ . Examples of invertible elements are the non-isotropic vectors $u \in V$ , whose inverses are, we recall, given by $q ( u ) ^ { - 1 } u$ . In that case, $\mathrm { A d } _ { u }$ , conjugation by $u$ within the Clifford algebra, preserves $V$ and $- \operatorname { A d } _ { u } | V = \sigma _ { u }$ by equation (13.2). It is convenient for our purposes to extend $- \operatorname { A d }$ , which leads to the twisted adjoint

$$
\widetilde { \mathrm { A d } } : \mathsf { C } ( q ) ^ { \times } \longrightarrow \mathrm { A u t } ( \mathsf { C } ( q ) ) , \quad \widetilde { \mathrm { A d } } _ { u } \boldsymbol { x } = \boldsymbol { \alpha } ( u ) \cdot \boldsymbol { x } \cdot \boldsymbol { u } ^ { - 1 } ,
$$

where $\alpha$ is the involution (13.3). In other words, if $u \in \mathsf { C } ^ { \mathrm { 0 } } ( q )$ , this is the usual adjoint, but for $u \in C ^ { 1 } ( q )$ this is minus the adjoint. The Clifford group consists of $a l l$ invertible elements of the Clifford algebra whose twisted adjoint action preserves $V$ :

$$
\operatorname { C l i f } ( q ) : = \{ u \in \mathbb { C } ( q ) ^ { \times } | \widetilde { \operatorname { A d } } _ { u } ( V ) \subset V \} .
$$

 $\operatorname { C l i f } ( q )$ contains $k ^ { \times }$ and is indeed a group. For instance, if $u \in \operatorname { C l i f } ( q )$ then $u ^ { - 1 } \in \mathrm { C l i f } ( q )$. To see this, observe that $v \in V$ can be written in the form $v = \alpha ( u ) \cdot v ^ { \prime } \cdot u ^ { - 1 }$, since $\widetilde { \mathrm { A d } _ { u } }$ is an automorphism, and then $\alpha ( u ^ { - 1 } ) \cdot v \cdot u =$ $\alpha ( u ^ { - 1 } ) \alpha ( u ) \cdot v ^ { \prime } \cdot u ^ { - 1 } \cdot u = v ^ { \prime } \in V$.

The special Clifford group is given by $\mathsf { C l i f } ^ { \mathsf { U } } ( q ) : = \mathsf { C l i f } ( q ) \cap \mathsf { C } ^ { \mathsf { 0 } } ( q )$ .

Example 13.1.3.2). Proposition 13.2.2. The kernel of the homomorphism $\operatorname { C l i f } ( q ) \to \operatorname { A u t } ( V )$ given by $u \mapsto \widetilde { \mathrm { A d } } _ { u } \vert V$ is equal to $k ^ { \times } \cdot { \bf 1 }$ .

There is a second fundamental involution on ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ induced by the order reversal map $x _ { 1 } \otimes \cdot \cdot \cdot \otimes x _ { r } \mapsto x _ { r } \otimes \cdot \cdot \cdot \otimes x _ { 1 }$ on $T ( V )$. Since this map preserves the ideal $I ( V )$, it descends to an involution on the Clifford algebra, the canonical involution, denoted by $u \mapsto u ^ { * }$. This is in fact an anti-involution with respect to the product in the sense that $( u \cdot v ) ^ { * } = v ^ { * } \cdot u ^ { * }$ and $( u ^ { * } ) ^ { * } = u$, which is immediate from the definitions. $u ^ { * } = u$ whenever $u \in V$. Moreover, since the canonical involution respects the $\mathbb { Z } / 2 \mathbb { Z }$ grading, $\alpha ( u ^ { * } ) \ : = \ : \alpha ( u ) ^ { * }$. In other words, the two fundamental involutions commute. We shall use two more properties:

# 13.3 The Spin Group and Spinor Norm

In this section $( V , q )$ is a quadratic inner product space over $k$ , $\operatorname { c h a r } ( k ) \neq 2$ .

For vectors $v \in V \subset \mathsf { C } ( q )$ we have $v \cdot v \ = \ q ( v )$ which we may rewrite as $v \cdot \alpha ( v ^ { * } ) = - q ( v )$ . Although Example 13.2.4 shows that for $u \in \mathsf { C } ( q )$ the product $u \cdot u ^ { * }$ need not belong to $k$ , we shall show that the product does belong to $k$ if $u \in \mathrm { C l i f } ^ { 0 } ( q )$ . In fact, we show that the spinor norm

$$
\begin{array} { r } { \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u ) : = u \cdot \alpha ( u ^ { * } ) , \quad u \in \mathrm { C l i f } ( q ) , } \end{array}
$$

belongs to $k ^ { \times }$ and so the spinor norm, by Lemma 13.2.3 a priori only $\operatorname { C l i f } ( q )$ - valued, is a $k$ -valued function and which extends the quadratic form $q$ (restricted to non-isotropic vectors):

Proposition 13.3.1. The spinor norm is a homomorphism from $\operatorname { C l i f } ( q )$ to $k ^ { \times }$ .

Proof. We follow the arguments in [137, Ch. 1.2]. Let us first show that for $u \in \operatorname { C l i f } ( q )$ , $\mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u ) \in k ^ { \times }$ .

By definition, $\alpha ( u ) \cdot v \cdot u ^ { - 1 } \in V$ whenever $v \in V$ . It suffices to show that the twisted adjoint of $\mathrm { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u )$ induces the identity in $V$ since then the result follows from Proposition 13.2.2. Let us elaborate this. Since $u \in \operatorname { C l i f } ( q )$ implies $u ^ { * } \in \operatorname { C l i f } ( q )$ (see Lemma 13.2.3), the element $\alpha ( u ^ { * } ) \cdot v \cdot ( u ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 }$ is in $V$ . Applying the homomorphism $\alpha$ then yields that $u ^ { * } \cdot v \cdot \alpha ( u ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \in V$ . Since the canonical involution is the identity on $V$ , we then find that

$$
\boldsymbol { u } ^ { * } \cdot \boldsymbol { v } \cdot \boldsymbol { \alpha } ( \boldsymbol { u } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } = ( \boldsymbol { u } ^ { * } \cdot \boldsymbol { v } \cdot \boldsymbol { \alpha } ( \boldsymbol { u } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } ) ^ { * } = \boldsymbol { \alpha } ( \boldsymbol { u } ^ { - 1 } ) \cdot \boldsymbol { v } \cdot \boldsymbol { u } .
$$

On the other hand, setting $w = \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u ) = u \cdot \alpha ( u ^ { * } )$ , we find

$$
\widetilde { \mathrm { A d } } _ { w } \boldsymbol { v } = \boldsymbol { \alpha } ( \boldsymbol { w } ) \cdot \boldsymbol { v } \cdot \boldsymbol { w } ^ { - 1 } = \boldsymbol { \alpha } ( \boldsymbol { u } ) \cdot \boldsymbol { u } ^ { * } \cdot \boldsymbol { v } \cdot \boldsymbol { \alpha } ( \boldsymbol { u } ^ { * } ) ^ { - 1 } \cdot \boldsymbol { u } ^ { - 1 } \overset { ( 1 3 . 1 0 ) } { = } \boldsymbol { v } .
$$

This completes the proof that the twisted adjoint of $\mathrm { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u )$ induces the identity in $V$

To check that the spinor norm is a group homomorphism, $u v \cdot$ $\alpha ( ( u v ) ^ { * } ) = u v \cdot \alpha ( v ^ { * } u ^ { * } ) = u \cdot ( v \cdot \alpha ( v ^ { * } ) ) \cdot \alpha ( u ^ { * } ) = ( u \cdot \alpha ( u ^ { * } ) ) \cdot ( v \cdot \alpha ( v ^ { * } ) )$,since the middle term $\boldsymbol { v } \cdot \boldsymbol { \alpha } ( \boldsymbol { v } ^ { * } )$ belongs to $k$ and hence commutes with all elements in the Clifford algebra.

Remark 13.3.2. For non-isotropic vectors $v \in V$ , $\mathrm { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( v ) = - q ( v )$ .

Corollary 13.3.3. 1. For $u \in \operatorname { C l i f } ( q )$ the induced map $\widetilde { \mathrm { A d } _ { u } }$ on $V$ is an orthogonal transformation, and if $u \in \mathrm { C l i f } ^ { 0 } ( q )$ , it is a rotation.

2. $u \in \operatorname { C l i f } ( q )$ can be written as a product $u = v _ { 1 } \cdot \cdot \cdot v _ { r }$ with non-isotropic $v _ { j } \in V$ , $j = 1 , \dotsc , r$ . Consequently

$$
\mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u ) = u \cdot \alpha ( u ^ { * } ) = ( - 1 ) ^ { r } q ( v _ { 1 } ) \cdot \cdot \cdot q ( v _ { r } ) \in k ^ { \times } .
$$

If $u \in \mathrm { C l i f } ^ { 0 } ( q )$ , then $r$ can be taken even.

3. Ad induces isomorphisms $\mathsf { C l i f } ( q ) / k ^ { \times } \overset { \simeq } { \to } \mathsf { O } ( q )$ and $\mathrm { C l i f } ^ { 0 } ( q ) / k ^ { \times } \overset { \simeq } { \to } \mathrm { S O } ( q ) .$

Proof. 1. We first prove that the $k$ -linear automorphism $\widetilde { \mathrm { A d } _ { u } } | _ { V }$ is an isometry on non-isotropic vectors. First we show that this map indeed preserves non-isotropic vectors $v \in V$ . If $u \in \operatorname { C l i f } ( q )$ , then $\widetilde { \mathrm { A d } _ { u } }$ , being an automorphism of ${ \mathsf { C } } ( q )$ , preserves invertible elements so that $w = \widetilde { \mathrm { A d } } _ { u } ( v ) \in V$ is invertible in the Clifford algebra. Hence $q ( w ) ~ = ~ - w \cdot w \neq 0$ (see Remark 13.3.2). We use this in the following computation:

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { q ( \widetilde { \mathrm { A d } } _ { u } v ) = - \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( \widetilde { \mathrm { A d } } _ { u } v ) } \\ & { \qquad = - \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( \alpha ( u ) \cdot v \cdot u ^ { - 1 } ) } \\ & { \qquad = - \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( \alpha ( u ) ) \cdot \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( v ) \cdot \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u ^ { - 1 } ) } \\ & { \qquad = - \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u ) \cdot - q ( v ) \cdot \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u ^ { - 1 } ) } \\ & { \qquad = q ( v ) \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u ) \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u ^ { - 1 } ) = q ( v ) \mathrm { ~ } ( \mathrm { s i n c e ~ } q ( v ) \in k ) . } \end{array}
$$

We also used that $\mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( \alpha ( u ) ) \ = \ \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u )$ . This is the case since $\alpha ( u )$ $\alpha ( \alpha ( u ) ^ { * } ) = \alpha ( u \cdot ( \alpha ( u ) ^ { * } ) ) = \alpha \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u ) = \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ( u )$ .

Since the inverse $\widetilde { \mathrm { A d } } _ { u ^ { - 1 } } | _ { V }$ of the map $\widetilde { \mathrm { A d } _ { u } } | _ { V }$ also preserves non-isotropic vectors, both must send isotropic vectors to isotropic vectors, completing the proof of 1.

2. By the Cartan-Dieudonné theorem all orthogonal transformations of $V$ are products of reflections in non-isotropic vectors, say $\widetilde { \mathrm { A d } _ { u } } | _ { V } ~ = ~ \sigma _ { v _ { 1 } } \circ \cdot \cdot \cdot \circ _ { \sigma _ { v _ { r } } }$ ._On the other hand, for the restrictions to $V$ we have $\widetilde { \mathrm { A d } } _ { v _ { r } } = - \sigma _ { v _ { r } }$ , and so $\widetilde { \mathrm { A d } _ { u } } \ =$ $( - 1 ) ^ { r } \widetilde { \mathrm { A d } } _ { v _ { 1 } } \circ \cdot \cdot \cdot \widetilde { \mathrm { A d } } _ { v _ { r } } = ( - 1 ) ^ { r } \widetilde { \mathrm { A d } } _ { v _ { 1 } } . . . v _ { r }$ . Hence by Proposition 13.2.2, $u$ and $v _ { 1 } \cdots v _ { r }$ differ by a multiplicative non-zero constant in $k$ which we use to adjust $v _ { 1 }$ . So every orthogonal transformation comes from twisted conjugation with elements of the Clifford algebra and the rotations from conjugation with elements in the even Clifford algebra.

Assertion 3 follows directly from these considerations.

We next define the $( \mathrm { s } ) \mathrm { p i n }$ roups as the owg k $\mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { { s p i n } } }$ .

Definition 13.3.4. The (s)pin group is the group

$$
\begin{array} { r c l } { { \mathsf { P i n } ( q ) } } & { { = } } & { { \mathrm { k e r } \left( \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathsf { s p i n } } : \mathsf { C l i f } ( q ) \to k ^ { \times } \right) , \mathrm { ~ r e s p e c t i v e l y , } } } \\ { { \mathsf { S p i n } ( q ) } } & { { = } } & { { \mathrm { k e r } \left( \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathsf { s p i n } } : \mathsf { C l i f } ^ { 0 } ( q ) \to k ^ { \times } \right) . } } \end{array}

Since $\mathsf { N } m _ { \mathrm { s p i n } }$ restricted to $k ^ { \times }$ is given by squaring, the spinor norm does not descend directly to the orthogonal group ${ \mathsf { O } } ( q ) = { \mathsf { C l i f } } ( q ) / k ^ { \times }$ . Theorem 13.3.5. The (s)pin group maps in a 2-to-1 fashion onto a normal subgroup of the appropriate orthogonal group:

$$

The image of the spinor norm on the rotation group is a subgroup of $\mathsf { D } ( k )$ which might be a proper subgroup as shown in Remark 13.3.6.1 below. We introduce a shorthand notation for this group:

$$
\mathsf { S } _ { V } = \mathrm { I m } ( \mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } : \mathsf { S O } ( q ) \to \mathsf { D } ( k ) ) .
