Historical and Bibliographical Notes. For Sections 14.114.4 on spinor equivalence in relation to genus equivalence and equivalence we have largely followed Chapters 10 and 11 in J. Cassels's book [36] as well as Kapittel VIII in M. Kneser's book [122].

As indicated in Remark 14.5.4, surjectivity of the reduction homomorphism $r _ { L }$ r failure thereof has been extensively studied in Ch. VIII of the preprint [156] by R. Miranda and D. Morrison. We only elaborate a simple case ensuring surjectivity.

The applications to $p$ -elementary lattices are based on V. Nikulin's approach in [169].

# Lattice Embeddings

# Introduction

In Subsection 1.7.C of Chapter 1 we showed that overlattices of a non-degenerate lattice correspond bijectively to isotropic submodules of its discriminant form and that an isometry between two non-degenerate lattices extend to isometries between overlattices if it induces a homomorphism between the corresponding isotropic submodules. This chapter is devoted to overlattices of the orthogonal sum of two non-degenerate lattices $S \oplus T$ . In Section 15.1 we show that overlattices of $S \textsuperscript { \textregistered T }$ exist in which $S$ and $T$ embed primitively if a certain glueing criterion on the discriminant forms of $S$ and $T$ holds. The question whether $S$ can be primitively embedded in a given lattice $L$ is harder to decide using these techniques, since we then should first find a candidate for $T$ . For unimodular lattices $L$ this problem is solved in Section 15.2, and, with the help of these results, in Section 15.3 for non-unimodular lattices. Here we use most of the techniques and results obtained in previous chapters. In $\ S$ 15.2.C we apply the results of Section 15.2 to lattice involutions.

# 15.1 Primitive Embeddings of Lattices

Recall from Subsection 1.7.C that an overlattice of a non-degenerate symmetric or quadratic lattice $N$ is an integral lattice $L$ containing $N$ as a finite index sublattice. Here we consider overlattices $L$ of lattices of the form $N = S \oplus T$ with $S$ and $T$ proper sublattices. The inclusions $L \subset L ^ { * } \subset N ^ { * }$ induce in this case inclusions $L / ( S \oplus T ) \subset L ^ { * } / ( S \oplus T ) \subset S ^ { * } / S \oplus T ^ { * } / T = \mathrm { d g } _ { S } \oplus \mathrm { d g } _ { T }$ such that $L / ( S \oplus T )$ is an isotropic subspace of $\mathsf { d g } _ { S } \mathbb { O } \mathsf { d g } _ { T }$ . We require also that $S$ and $T$ embed primitively in the overlattice $L$ . By Remark 1.3.2 this is equivalent to $S = T ^ { \perp }$ and $T = S ^ { \perp }$ .

We aim to reverse the construction, i.e., given non-degenerate lattices $S$ and $T$ , find a criterion allowing to construct an overlattice $L$ of $S \oplus T$ in which $S$ and $T$ embed primitively such that $T = S ^ { \perp }$ and $S = T ^ { \perp }$ . Before we do this, we first show that the compositions of the inclusion $L / ( S \oplus T ) \hookrightarrow \mathrm { d g } _ { S } \oplus \mathrm { d g } _ { T }$ with the projections on the first, respectively the second summand of the right-hand side are injective. It suffices to verify this for the composition $p : L / ( S \oplus T ) \to \deg _ { T }$ . To see this, let $\bar { x } \in L / ( S \oplus T )$ , $x \in L$ , be in the kernel of $p$ . Writing $x$ as $x _ { 1 } + x _ { 2 }$ with $x _ { 1 } \in S ^ { * }$ and $x _ { 2 } \in T ^ { * }$ , then $p ( { \bar { x } } ) = 0$ just means that $x _ { 2 } \in T$ . Then $x - x _ { 2 } = x _ { 1 } \in S ^ { * } \cap L = \ S$ . So $x \in S \textcircled { \perp } T$ . In other words, we have shown that the image of $L / ( S { \textcircled { \perp } } T )$ in $\mathsf { d g } _ { S } \mathbb { O } \mathsf { d g } _ { T }$ is the "graph" $\bot$ of an injective homomorphism $\psi _ { S , T } : \mathsf { H } _ { S } \hookrightarrow \mathsf { d g } _ { T }$ where $\mathsf { H } _ { S } \subset \mathsf { d g } _ { S }$ is the first embedded copy of $L / ( S \mathbb { Q } T )$ . This is summarized in the commutative diagram

$$
\int \limits _ { \log s } ^ { \infty } \int \limits _ { \ H _ { s } } ^ { \infty } e ^ { \int \limits _ { \log } ^ { \infty } \phi d g _ { T } } \sum \limits _ { p  \infty } ^ { \infty } d g _ { T } .
$$

f $L$ is unimodular, using (1.8), Lemma 1.3.1 shows that $\vert \deg _ { S } \vert = \vert \deg _ { T } \vert = \lbrack L : S \oplus T \rbrack$ Since also $[ L : S \oplus T ] = | \mathsf { H } _ { S } |$ , we conclude that $\mathsf { H } _ { S } = \mathsf { d } \mathrm { g } _ { S }$ and that $\psi _ { S , T }$ maps ${ \mathsf { d g } } _ { S }$ isomorphically onto ${ \mathsf { d g } } _ { T }$ .

Returning to the general setting, recall from Proposition 1.7.4 that the form on $L$ becomes zero on the quotient $L / ( S \mathbb { Q } T )$ which means that the graph of $\psi _ { S , T }$ is an isotropic subgroup of $\mathsf { d g } _ { S } \mathbb { O } \mathsf { d g } _ { T }$ . Phrasing this differently, one has:

Proposition 15.1.1. Let L be a non-degenerate symmetric (respectively quadratic) lattice, $S$ a primitive non-degenerate sublattice and $T = S ^ { \perp }$ . With the notation of diagram (15.1), the following equivalent properties hold:

1. on $\mathsf { H } _ { S } \subset \mathsf { d g } _ { S }$ the glueing criterion $b _ { T } ^ { \# } ( \psi _ { S , T } - , \psi _ { S , T } - ) + b _ { S } ^ { \# } ( - , - ) = 0$ , respectively $q _ { T } ^ { \# } \ L { \circ } \psi _ { S , T } + q _ { S } ^ { \# } = 0$ holds;

2. up to a sign the embedding $\psi _ { S , T }$ is an isometry of torsion forms;

3. $\mathsf { H } : = g r a p h$ of $\psi _ { S , T } \subset \mathrm { d g } _ { S } \oplus \mathrm { d g } _ { T }$ is an isotropic subspace.

If L is unimodular, then $\mathsf { H } _ { S } = \mathsf { d } \mathrm { g } _ { S }$ , $\psi _ { S , T }$ is an isomorphism and the glueing condition becomes $b _ { S } ^ { \# } \simeq - b _ { T } ^ { \# }$ (respectively $q _ { S } ^ { \# } \simeq - q _ { T } ^ { \# } ,$ .

Example 15.1.2. An example illustrating Proposition 15.1.1 is the following. Let $L = U \mathbb { \ Q } U$ be the sum of two copies of the hyperbolic plane $U$, the first one with the usual basis $e, f$ (so $b ( e, e ) = b ( f, f ) = b ( e, f ) - 1 = 0,$ and the second one with similar basis $e ^ { \prime }, f ^ { \prime }$. Take $S$ to be the span of $e + f, e ^ { \prime } + f ^ { \prime }$ in $L$, and let $T$ be the span of $e - f, e ^ { \prime } - f ^ { \prime }$ in $L$. Then $L$ is an even unimodular overlattice of $S \textsuperscript { \textregistered T }$. The discriminant groups of $S$ and $T$ are $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { d } \mathrm { g } _ { S } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } S / S = \langle u = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( e + f ) + S, u ^ { \prime } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( e ^ { \prime } + f ^ { \prime } ) + S \rangle } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { d } \mathrm { g } _ { T } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } T / T = \langle v = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( e - f ) + T, v ^ { \prime } = \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( e ^ { \prime } - f ^ { \prime } ) + T \rangle } \end{array}$. The image of $L / ( S \mathbb { Q } T )$ in $\mathsf { d g } _ { S } \oplus \mathsf { d g } _ { T }$ equals $\left\{ 0, ( u, v ), ( u ^ { \prime }, v ^ { \prime } ), ( u + u ^ { \prime }, v + v ^ { \prime } ) \right\}$, which is the graph of the isomorphism $\psi _ { S, T } : \mathrm { d g } _ { S } \mathrm { d g } _ { T }$ determined by $\psi _ { S, T } ( u ) = v$ and $\psi _ { S, T } ( u ^ { \prime } ) = v ^ { \prime }$. $\begin{array} { r } { b _ { S } ^ { \# } ( u, u ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } + \mathbb { Z } = - b _ { T } ^ { \# } ( v, v ) } \end{array}$, etc. Also, for the associated quadratic form $\begin{array} { r } { q ( x ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } b ( x, x ) } \end{array}$ we have $\begin{array} { r } { q _ { S } ^ { \# } ( u ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \cdot \frac { 1 } { 2 } + \mathbb { Z } = \frac { 1 } { 4 } + \mathbb { Z } } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { q _ { T } ^ { \# } ( v ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } \cdot - \frac { 1 } { 2 } + \mathbb { Z } = - \frac { 1 } { 4 } + \mathbb { Z } } \end{array}$, etc.

Now we are ready to reverse the construction starting with two lattices $S$ and $T$ .

Proposition 15.1.3. Let $S$ and $T$ be non-degenerate symmetric (respectively quadratic) lattices, $\mathsf { H } _ { S } \subset \mathsf { d g } _ { S }$ a subgroup, and $\psi _ { S , T } : { \mathsf { H } } _ { S } \hookrightarrow { \mathsf { d g } } _ { T }$ an injective homomorphism. Suppose that the glueing criterion of Proposition (15.1.1) holds. Then, setting $N : = S \textcircled { \perp } T$ , we have

1. The lattice $L = \{ y \in N ^ { * } \mid y$ mod $N \in \mathsf { H }$ }, where $\mathsf { H }$ is the graph of $\psi _ { S , T }$ , is $a$ symmetric (respectively quadratic) overlattice of $N$ satisfying $[ L : N ] = | \mathsf { H } _ { S } |$ ;

2. S and $T$ embed primitively in $L$ and $T = S ^ { \perp }$ , $S = T ^ { \perp }$ ;

3. If $\mathsf { H } _ { S } = \mathsf { d } \mathrm { g } _ { S }$ and $\psi _ { S , T }$ is an isomorphism, then $L$ is unimodular.

Proof. Item 1 is implied by Proposition 1.7.4. The equality $[ L : N ] = | \mathsf { H } _ { S } |$ follows from the isomorphism $L / ( S \oplus T ) \simeq \mathsf { H } _ { S }$ . Moreover, if $\mathsf { H } _ { S } = \mathsf { d g } _ { S }$ and $\psi _ { S , T }$ is an isomorphism, then $[ L : N ] = | \deg _ { S } | = | \operatorname { d i s c } ( S ) | = | \deg _ { T } | = | \operatorname { d i s c } ( T ) |$ , and Lemma 1.3.1 implies that $L$ is unimodular, proving item 3.

2. The assumptions imply that the composition of the embedding $L / ( S \oplus T ) \stackrel { \simeq } { \to }$ $\mathsf { H } \subset \mathsf { d g } _ { S } \oplus \mathsf { d g } _ { T }$ with the projection onto either one of the summands of $\mathsf { d g } _ { S } \mathbb { O } \mathsf { d g } _ { T }$ is injective. We claim that this implies that $S$ and $T$ are primitive in $L$ . If for instance $S$ were not primitive in $L$ , there would exist a vector $x \in L$ , $x \notin S$ , such that $n x \in S$ for some integer $n > 1$ . Since then $x \in S ^ { * }$ , this would give a non-zero element in the kernel of the composition $L / ( S \oplus T ) \hookrightarrow \mathrm { d g } _ { S } \oplus \mathrm { d g } _ { T } \to \mathrm { d g } _ { T }$ . As before, by Remark 1.3.2, then $S = T ^ { \perp }$ .

Surprisingly, if $S$ embeds primitively in an even lattice $L$ which is unique in its genus, also any lattice in the genus of $S$ can be embedded primitively in $L$ :

Corollary 15.1.4. Let $L$ be a non-degenerate even lattice with one isometry class in its genus and suppose that the non-degenerate lattice $S$ embeds primitively in $L$ . Then any lattice $S ^ { \prime }$ in the same genus as $S$ embeds primitively in $L$ .

Proof. Let $T$ be the orthogonal complement of $S$ in $L$ and $N = S { \textcircled { \perp } } T$ . The subgroup $\mathsf { H } = L / N$ of ${ \mathsf { d g } } _ { N }$ is then isotropic with respect to the discriminant quadratic form. By Lemma 1.9.4 the discriminant quadratic form of $S$ only depends on the genus of $S$ and so $N$ and $N ^ { \prime } = S ^ { \prime } \oplus T$ have isometric discriminant quadratic forms (with an isometry respecting the summands). Therefore, the isotropic graph $\mathsf { H }$ of $\psi _ { S , T }$ (as in Proposition 15.1.3) can be transported to a graph $\psi _ { S ^ { \prime } , T }$ , which is isotropic in $\mathsf { d g } _ { S ^ { \prime } } \mathbb { O } \mathsf { d g } _ { T }$ . So by Proposition 1.7.4.3 it determines a unique even overlattice $L ^ { \prime }$ of $N ^ { \prime }$ . Moreover, by Proposition 1.7.4.2 the discriminant form of $L ^ { \prime }$ is the same as that of $L$ . Lastly, $L$ and $L ^ { \prime }$ have the same signature  as this is the case for $N ^ { \prime }$ and $N$ . This shows that $L$ and $L ^ { \prime }$ have the same genus invariants and so they are in the same genus (cf. Theorem 11.3.1). Hence, by assumption, $L$ and $L ^ { \prime }$ are isometric and so $S ^ { \prime }$ also embeds primitively in $L$ . □

Example 15.1.5. Here is an example of two non-isometric lattices in the same genus that embed in the same even unimodular lattice. The lattices $E _ { 8 } \ @ E _ { 8 }$ and $\Gamma _ { 1 6 }$ are in the same genus, but are not isometric (see Examples 1.5.1 and 11.3.2). The indefinite unimodular lattices $\{ \Phi ^ { k } U \ @ E _ { 8 } \ @ E _ { 8 }$ and $\mathbb { \oplus } ^ { k } U \mathbb { \oplus } \Gamma _ { 1 6 }$, $k = 1, 2, \ldots$, however, are both even and have the same signature, and so are isometric by Theorem 2.4.1. Corollary 15.1.4 applies in this case, but is not needed.

Application: Extending isometries to overlattices. In Subsection 1.7.C we discussed the problem of extending a lattice isometry $N  N ^ { \prime }$ to an isometry between overlattices $L \to L ^ { \prime }$ . Applying this in the situation of overlattices of an orthogonal direct sum $N = S \oplus T$ , Proposition 15.1.3 gives a second extension criterion:

Proposition 15.1.6 (Extending isometries, II). Let $S , S ^ { \prime } , T , T ^ { \prime }$ be non-degenerate quadratic lattices related by isometries $\sigma : S \stackrel { \sim } { \to } S ^ { \prime }$ and $\tau : T \stackrel { \sim } {  } T ^ { \prime }$ . Suppose $L$ , $L ^ { \prime }$ are quadratic overlattices of $S \oplus T$ , $S ^ { \prime } \mathcal { \text O T } ^ { \prime }$ , respectively. Assume that $S$ and $T$ are primitively embedded in $L$ , and similarly for $S ^ { \prime }$ and $T ^ { \prime }$ .

Then the isometry $\lambda = \sigma \oplus \tau$ extends to an isometry $L \stackrel { \sim } {  } L ^ { \prime }$ if and only if (the map induced by) $\lambda$ sends the subgroup $L / ( S \mathbb { Q } T )$ of $\mathsf { d g } _ { S } \mathbb { O } \mathsf { d g } _ { T }$ to the subgroup $L ^ { \prime } / ( S ^ { \prime } \mathbb { \oplus } T ^ { \prime } )$ of $\mathsf { d g } _ { S ^ { \prime } } \mathbb { O } \mathsf { d g } _ { T ^ { \prime } }$ . In other words, using the notation of diagram (15.1), $\lambda$ extends if and only if there is a commutative diagram

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { \mathrm { d } \mathrm { g } _ { S } \longleftrightarrow } & { { } \longleftrightarrow \mathsf { H } _ { S } \longleftrightarrow \quad \quad \psi _ { S , T } \quad \quad \mathrm { ~ } \mathsf { \Gamma } \lambda } \\ { r _ { S , S ^ { \prime } } ( \sigma ) \underset { \mathrm { d } \mathrm { g } _ { S ^ { \prime } } \longleftrightarrow } { \downarrow } } & { { } \underset { H _ { S ^ { \prime } } \longleftrightarrow } { \downarrow } \underbrace { \vphantom { \sqrt { \Gamma _ { T , T ^ { \prime } } ( \tau ) } } \mathrm { d } r _ { T , T ^ { \prime } } ( \tau ) } } & { { } \mathrm { ~ } \forall r _ { T , T ^ { \prime } } ( \tau ) } \end{array}
$$

where $r _ { S , S ^ { \prime } } ( \sigma )$ and $r _ { T , T ^ { \prime } } ( \tau )$ are induced by $\sigma$ and $\tau$ , respectively. In particular, if $L$ (and hence $L ^ { \prime }$ ) is unimodular, using Propositions 15.1.1, 15.1.3, this reduces to the glueing criterion exhibited by the commutative diagram

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { \mathrm { d g } _ { S } \cfrac { \simeq } { \psi _ { S , T } } } & { \to \mathrm { d g } _ { T } } \\ { r _ { S , S ^ { \prime } } ( \sigma ) \sqrt { \qquad } } & { \sqrt { r _ { T , T ^ { \prime } } ( \tau ) } } \\ { \mathrm { d g } _ { S ^ { \prime } } \cfrac { \simeq } { \psi _ { S ^ { \prime } , T ^ { \prime } } } } & { \to \mathrm { d g } _ { T ^ { \prime } } } \end{array}
$$

The preceding result for embeddings in the same lattice $L = L ^ { \prime }$ is a version of Witt's theorem 7.2.8 and as in that case we speak of equivalent embeddings:

Theorem 15.1.7 (Witt's extension theorem for lattices). 1. Let $L$ be a nondegenerate even lattice and let $i , i ^ { \prime } : S \hookrightarrow L$ be two primitive embeddings. Then these embeddings are equivalent if and only if an isometry $T = i ( S ) ^ { \perp } \stackrel { \sim } { \to } T ^ { \prime } = i ^ { \prime } ( S ) ^ { \perp }$ exists inducing a commutative diagram like (15.2).

2. Suppose in addition that $L$ is unimodular, then two primitive embeddings of S in $L$ with isometric orthogonal complements are equivalent if the reduction homomorphism $r _ { T } : { \cal O } ( T ) \to { \cal O } ( q _ { T } ^ { \# } )$ is surjective, where $T$ is the orthogonal complement of an embedded copy of $S$ .

roof. The first assertion follows directly from Proposition 15.1.6.

2 Identify $S$ with the image under the first embedding, let $S ^ { \prime }$ be the image of the second embedding. This yields the isometry $\sigma : S  S ^ { \prime }$ which relates the embeddings. Setting $T = S ^ { \perp }$ , $T ^ { \prime } = S ^ { \prime \bot }$ , one seeks an isometry $\tau : T \stackrel { \sim } {  } T ^ { \prime }$ such that $\sigma \oplus \tau$ extends to an isometry of $L$ . Since $L$ is unimodular $\psi _ { S , T }$ and $\psi _ { S ^ { \prime } , T ^ { \prime } }$ are isomorphisms by Proposition 15.1.1, hence so is $\bar { \tau } : = \psi _ { S ^ { \prime } , T ^ { \prime } } \circ r _ { S , S ^ { \prime } } ( \sigma ) \circ \psi _ { S , T } ^ { - 1 } : \mathsf { d g } _ { T } \ : \stackrel { \sim } {  } \ :$ $\mathsf { d g } _ { T ^ { \prime } }$ . It is even an isometry since $\psi _ { S , T }$ and $\psi _ { S ^ { \prime } , T ^ { \prime } }$ reverse signs of the discriminant forms and $r _ { S , S ^ { \prime } } ( \sigma )$ is an isometry. Since $T$ and $T ^ { \prime }$ are isometric, the assumption that the reduction homomorphism $r _ { T }$ is surjective implies that the isometry $\bar { \tau } : { \mathsf { d g } } _ { T } \to$ $\mathsf { d g } _ { T ^ { \prime } }$ lifts to an isometry $\tau : T \stackrel { \sim } {  } T ^ { \prime }$ . By construction the resulting diagram (15.3) is commutative and then $\sigma \oplus \tau$ extends.

The weakness of the above result is twofold. First, if $S$ is a given lattice we would like to know if it embeds primitively in $L$ . Secondly, we are using properties of $T$ , the orthogonal complement of $S$ . In the next section we arrive at a more manageable condition in the case of unimodular lattices. In Section 15.3 we treat the general case.

# 15.2 Primitive Embeddings into Unimodular Quadratic Lattices

In this section we assume that $( L , q )$ is a unimodular quadratic lattice.

15.2.A Existence of Embeddings. Suppose now that we are given a nondegenerate quadratic lattice $S$ which we want to embed primitively in a unimodular quadratic lattice $L$ . In order to apply the preceding results, we need to find all in any cae have candidate orthogonal complements $q _ { T } ^ { \# } \simeq - q _ { S } ^ { \# }$ $T$ in $L$ . By Propositions 15.1.1, 15.1.3 we should a lattice $T$ is completely determined if, in addition, we know the signature $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ of the resulting overlattice. In other words, to be able to embed $S$ primitively in some unimodular lattice of signature $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ there should exist a lattice $T$ with genus invariant $\mathsf { g } ( T ) = ( r _ { + } - s _ { + } , r _ { - } - s _ { - } , [ - q _ { S } ^ { \# } ] )$ . There is however an additional condition since the signature of an even unimodular lattice is divisible by 8 (cf. Corollary 2.4.3). This leads to the following criterion:

Proposition 15.2.1 ([171, Theorem 1.12.2 & Cor. 1.12.3]). Let $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ be a pair of non-negative integers for which $r _ { + } - r _ { - } \equiv 0$ mod 8 and let $S$ be a non-degenerate even lattice of signature $( s _ { + } , s _ { - } )$ with $s _ { + } \leq r _ { + }$ and $s _ { - } \leq r _ { - }$ , discriminant group ${ \mathsf { d g } } _ { S }$ and discriminant quadratic form $q ^ { \# }$ . Suppose that, moreover, $( r _ { + } + r _ { - } ) - \mathrm { r a n k } ( S ) \geq$ $\ell ( \mathrm { d g } _ { S } )$ . Then the following conditions are equivalent.

1. S can be primitively embedded in some even unimodular lattice $L$ of signature $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ $L$ is unique up to isometry in case $r _ { + } > 0$ and $r _ { - } > 0$ );

2. A (non-degenerate) even lattice $T$ of signature $( r _ { + } - s _ { + } , r _ { - } - s _ { - } )$ with discriminant quadratic form $- q ^ { \# }$ exists;

3. A (non-degenerate) even lattice $T ^ { \prime }$ of signature $( r _ { - } - s _ { - } , r _ { + } - s _ { + } )$ with discriminant quadratic form $q ^ { \# }$ exists;

4. The equality2 $\mathrm { d i s c } ( L _ { q _ { p } ^ { \# } } ) ~ = ~ ( - 1 ) ^ { r _ { - } - s _ { - } } | \ : \mathrm { d g } _ { S } \ : |$ in $\mathsf { D } ( \mathbb { Z } _ { p } )$ holds in the following cases:

• for any prime $p \neq 2$ for which $\mathrm { d g } _ { S _ { p } }$ , the $p$ -primary part of ${ \mathsf { d g } } _ { S }$ , has length equal to $( r _ { + } + r _ { - } ) - \mathrm { r a n k } ( S )$ ;   
for $p = 2$ in case $\ell ( \mathrm { d } \mathrm { g } _ { S _ { 2 } } ) = ( r _ { + } + r _ { - } ) - \mathrm { r a n k } ( S )$ and $\mathsf { d g } _ { S _ { 2 } }$ does not split off a cyclic order 2 module.

In particular, all of these these conditions are satisfied if $( r _ { + } + r _ { - } ) \mathrm { - r a n k } ( S ) > \ell ( \mathrm { d g } _ { S } )$

Proof. From the discussion so far 1) implies 2), while item 3 is equivalent to item 2 (just reverse the sign of the form). To show that 2) implies 1), first observe that, assuming 2), there exists an isomorphism from ${ \mathsf { d g } } _ { S }$ onto ${ \mathsf { d g } } _ { T }$ such that the glueing condition holds for the quadratic forms. Then Proposition 15.1.3 implies that there exists an even overlattice $L$ of $S \oplus T$ such that $[ L : S \oplus T ] = | \deg _ { S } | = | \operatorname { d i s c } ( S ) | =$ $| \operatorname { d i s c } ( T ) |$ . By Lemma 1.3.1 this implies that $L$ is unimodular as required.

Item 4 is the existence criterion of Theorem 12.4.4 applied to $T ^ { \prime }$ . The penultimate assertion follows from Corollary 12.4.6 since the stated condition implies the existence of an even lattice $T ^ { \prime }$ as in item 3. The seemingly missing condition on the signature modulo 8 is automatic since $r _ { + } - r _ { - } \ \equiv \ 0 \bmod \ 8 .$ so that $\tau _ { 8 } ( q ^ { \# } ) \equiv s _ { + } - s _ { - } \equiv r _ { - } - s _ { - } - ( r _ { + } - s _ { + } ) \equiv \tau ( T ^ { \prime } )$ mod 8.

Since even indefinite unimodular lattices are determined up to isometry by their signature as demonstrated in Chapter 2, the lattice $L$ in item 1 is unique if $r _ { + } > 0$ and $r _ { - } > 0$ .

Remark 15.2.2. If $S$ is definite, the preceding embedding result is less interesting since the uniqueness of $L$ need not hold. For instance $E _ { 8 }$ embeds trivially in $E _ { 8 } \ @ E _ { 8 }$ but does not embed in $\Gamma _ { 1 6 }$ .

We apply the preceding results to show embeddability for a large class of lattices.

Theorem 15.2.3 (Universal Embeddability). Let $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ be a pair of non-negative integers for which $r _ { + } { - } r _ { - } \equiv 0$ mod 8 and let $( s _ { + } , s _ { - } )$ be a pair of non-negative integers with $s _ { + } \leq r _ { + }$ and $s _ { - } \leq r _ { - }$ .

Then every even non-degenerate lattice $S$ of signature $( s _ { + } , s _ { - } )$ satisfing $r _ { + } + r _ { - } -$ $\operatorname { r a n k } ( S ) \geq \ell ( \mathsf { d g } _ { S } )$ can be primitively embedded in some even unimodular lattice $L$ of signature $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ if

$$
s _ { + } + s _ { - } \leq \frac 1 2 \mathrm { r a n k } ( L ) .
$$

In case $r _ { + } > 0$ and $r _ { - } > 0$ , the unimodular lattice $L$ is unique up to isometry.

Proof. Assume we have an even non-degenerate lattice $S$ of signature $( s _ { + } , s _ { - } )$ with discriminant form $q ^ { \# }$ for which (15.4) holds. We want to show that $S$ embeds in some (non-specified) unimodular even lattice $L$ of signature $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ . Again, by Theorem 12.4.4.2 we have $\operatorname { r a n k } ( S ) = s _ { + } + s _ { - } \geq \ell ( \deg _ { S } )$ and hence, using the assumption (15.4),

$$
\operatorname { r a n k } ( L ) - \operatorname { r a n k } ( S ) \geq \operatorname { r a n k } ( S ) \geq \ell ( \deg _ { S } ) .
$$

If one of these inequalities is strict, $S$ can be embedded primitively in such a lattice $L$ as follows from Proposition 15.2.1. It remains to consider the situation where one has equality everywhere, that is,

$$
\operatorname { r a n k } ( S ) = { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \operatorname { r a n k } ( L ) = \ell ( \deg _ { S } ) .
$$

To show that $S$ embeds in $L$ , by Proposition 15.2.1.3 it suffices to show that a lattice $T ^ { \prime }$ with signature $( r _ { - } - s _ { - } , r _ { + } - s _ { + } )$ and quadratic torsion group $G = \deg _ { S } , q ^ { \# } )$ exists. We want to apply the existence criterion of Theorem 12.4.4.

•First of all, condition (1) on the signature holds since $( r _ { - } - r _ { + } ) - ( s _ { - } - s _ { + } ) \equiv$ ${ s _ { + } - s _ { - } }$ mod $8 \equiv \tau _ { 8 } ( q ^ { \# } )$ mod 8 (since $q ^ { \# }$ is the discriminant form of $S$ ).   
• Equality (15.5) implies that $\operatorname { r a n k } ( L ) - \operatorname { r a n k } ( S ) = \operatorname { r a n k } ( S ) \geq \ell ( G _ { p } )$ for all primes $p$ so that condition 2 holds. The verification of the remaining condition is more involved. First observe that equality (15.5) yields

$$
\begin{array} { c } { { r _ { + } - s _ { + } = r _ { + } - \left( s _ { + } + s _ { - } \right) + s _ { - } } } \\ { { { } } } \\ { { = r _ { + } - \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( r _ { + } + r _ { - } ) + s _ { - } } } \\ { { { } } } \\ { { = \displaystyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } ( r _ { + } - r _ { - } ) + s _ { - } , } } \end{array}
$$

and since by assumption $r _ { + } - r _ { - }$ is divisible by 8, we have $r _ { + } - s _ { + } \equiv s _ { - }$ (mod 2) and so

$$
( - 1 ) ^ { s _ { - } } = ( - 1 ) ^ { r _ { + } - s _ { + } } .
$$

Let $p$ be a prime for which $\ell ( G ) = \ell ( G _ { p } )$ . Then (15.5) gives $\operatorname { r a n k } ( S ) = \ell ( G _ { p } )$ . We invoke item 3 of Theorem 12.4.4 applied to $S$ and $G$ , and use (15.6) which leads to the equality

$$
( - 1 ) ^ { r _ { + } - s _ { + } } \cdot | G | = \mathrm { d i s c } ( L _ { q _ { p } ^ { \# } } ) \mathrm { i n } \ \mathsf { D } ( \mathbb { Z } _ { p } ) ,
$$

which is valid for odd $p$ and for $p = 2$ if no cyclic summand of order two splits off from $G _ { 2 }$ . Hence, also the remaining condition for the existence of $T ^ { \prime }$ is satisfied, and so in the case where (15.5) holds $S$ can also be embedded.

We tie this in with the embedding criterion we found in Section 1.8 and its generalization, Proposition 6.3.12. Recall that it states that any even lattice $S$ of rank $s$ can be embedded in $\textcircled{1} ^ { s } U$ with $S ^ { \perp } \simeq S ( - 1 )$ . This can be used to embed $S$ in an arbitrary even unimodular lattice $L$ whose Witt-index is at least s. Indeed, by the classification theorem 2.4.1 an indefinite even unimodular lattice is isometric to an orthogonal sum of say $t$ hyperbolic planes and a number of copies of $E _ { 8 }$ or $E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ . The number $t$ is the Witt index. So, clearly, $S$ embeds in such a lattice which leads to rephrase the result as follows:

Lemma 15.2.4. An even lattice $S$ can be embedded in an indefinite even unimodular lattice $L$ if the Witt index of $L$ is $\geq$ rank(S). In particular, $S$ embeds in $\mathbb { Q } ^ { s } U$ , $s = \mathrm { r a n k } ( S )$ , with $S ^ { \perp } \simeq S ( - 1 )$ .

We see that in case $S$ is non-degenerate Theorem 15.2.3 states that $S$ can be primitively embedded in $L = \oplus ^ { a } U \oplus \oplus ^ { b } E _ { 8 } ( \pm 1 )$ if ${ \mathrm { r a n k } } ( S ) \leq { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } { \mathrm { r a n k } } ( L ) = a + 4 b$ , while Lemma 15.2.4 just provides the condition $\operatorname { r a n k } ( S ) \leq a$ .

Example 15.2.5. We discuss under what condition an even non-degenerate lattice $T$ of rank $a + e$ with $e > 0$ can be embedded in the hyperbolic lattice ${ \mathbb { O } } ^ { a } U$ . Clearly, if $e$ copies of $U$ can be split off, say ${ \cal T } = \oplus ^ { \epsilon } U \oplus { \cal S } ^ { \prime }$ , then the lattice $S ^ { \prime }$ which has rank $a { - } e \mathrm { ~ - ~ } \mathrm { c a n }$ be primitively embedded in $\mathbb { O } ^ { a - e } U$ and hence $T$ embeds primitively in $\textcircled { \scriptsize { \perp } } ^ { a } U$ .

We claim that the converse holds. To see this, let the signature of $T$ be $( k , a +$ $e - k )$ . Assume that $T$ embeds primitively in $\mathbb { Q } ^ { a } U$ . Then $a \geq a + e - k$ so that $k \geq e$ and $S : = T ^ { \perp }$ has signature $( a - k , k - e )$ and index $a + e - 2 k$ . The lattice ${ \mathbb { O } } ^ { e } U { \mathbb { O } } S ( - 1 )$ has index $2 k - a - e$ and rank $a + e$ $T$ $q _ { S } ^ { \# } = - q _ { T } ^ { \# }$ it hs also the ${ \mathbb { O } } ^ { e } U { \mathbb { O } } S ( - 1 )$ $T$ by Theorem 11.3.1. Since $\ell ( \mathbf { d g } _ { T } ) = \ell ( \mathbf { d g } _ { S } ) \leq \mathrm { r a n k } ( T ) - 2 e$ , Corollary 14.4.3 implies that $T$ and ${ \oplus ^ { e } U \oplus S ( - 1 ) }$ are isometric. So we conclude that indeed $T$ embeds primitively in ${ \mathbb { O } } ^ { a } U$ if and only if $\mathbb { Q } ^ { e } U$ is an orthogonal direct summand of $T$ .

15.2.B Uniqueness of Embeddings. While up to now we only invoked Nikulin's existence results 12.4.4, we can say more using Nikulin's theorems about uniqueness of the isometry class in a genus as we now explain. More precisely, we shall use Corollary 14.4.3 stating that a non-degenerate indefinite quadratic lattice $S$ is unique in its genus if $\ell ( \mathrm { d g } _ { S } ) \leq \mathrm { r a n k } ( S ) - 2$ , and Theorem 14.5.5 which asserts that under this condition the reduction map $r _ { S } : { \cal O } ( S )  { \cal O } ( q _ { S } ^ { \# } )$ is surjective. Proposition 15.2.1 can be paraphrased by saying that $S$ embeds primitively in an indefinite unimodular quadratic lattice $L$ with $T = S ^ { \perp }$ if $\ell ( \mathrm { d g } _ { S } ) < \mathrm { r a n k } ( T )$ . Replacing this condition with $\ell ( \mathrm { d g } _ { S } ) \le \mathrm { r a n k } ( T ) - 2$ the just stated results imply the following:

Theorem 15.2.6. Let $L$ be an indefinite even unimodular lattice and $( S , q )$ a nondegenerate quadratic lattice with $\ell ( \mathbf { d g } _ { S } ) \leq \mathrm { r a n k } ( L ) - \mathrm { r a n k } ( S ) - 2$ . Let $L$ and $S$ have signature $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ , $( s _ { + } , s _ { - } )$ , respectively, and assume that $r _ { + } > s _ { + }$ , $r _ { - } > s _ { - }$ . Then

1. the orthogonal complement of a primitively embedded $S \hookrightarrow L$ has genus invariant $( r _ { + } - s _ { + } , r _ { - } - s _ { - } , - [ q _ { S } ^ { \# } ] )$ ;

2. S admits a primitive embedding in $L$ and such primitive embeddings are unique up to equivalence, i.e., ${ \sf O } ( L )$ acts transitively on primitive embeddings of $S$ in $L$ .

Proof. Let ${ \bf g } ( S ) = ( s _ { + } , s _ { - } , q _ { S } ^ { \# } )$ . As observed just before the statement of this theorem, Proposition 15.2.1 shows that there exists an isometry class of a lattice $T$ with genus invariant $\mathsf { g } ( T ) = ( r _ { + } - s _ { + } , r _ { - } - s _ { - } , [ - q _ { S } ^ { \# } ] )$ . Theorem 14.5.5 shows that the reduction map $r _ { T } : { \cal O } ( T )  { \cal O } ( q _ { T } ^ { \# } )$ is surjective. Hence Theorem 15.1.7 implies unicity of the embedding $S \hookrightarrow L$ . Moreover, since $S ^ { \bot }$ has the same genus invariant as $T$ , the two are isometric.

Since $\ell ( \mathrm { d g } _ { S } ) \leq \mathrm { r a n k } ( S )$ , Theorem 15.2.6 implies:

Corollary 15.2.7. Let $L$ be an indefinite even unimodular lattice of $r a n k \geq 4$ , and signature $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ . A non-degenerate even lattice $S$ of signature $( s _ { + } , s _ { - } )$ , $( s _ { \pm } \leq r _ { \pm } )$ , admits a primitive embedding in $L$ which is unique up to equivalence if $\operatorname { r a n k } ( S ) \leq$ ${ \scriptstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \mathrm { r a n k } ( L ) - 1$

Examples 15.2.8. 1 . Let $L = \Lambda _ { { \sf K } 3 } = U \oplus U \oplus U \oplus E _ { 8 } ( - 1 ) \oplus E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ , the K3-lattice. Then any non-degenerate even lattice of rank $\leq 2$ can be embedded uniquely as a primitive lattice in $\Lambda _ { \mathsf { K 3 } }$ . This holds more generally for any non-degenerate even lattice of rank $r \leq 1 0$ which has signature $( 0 , r )$ , $( 1 , r - 1 )$ or $( 2 , r - 2 )$ . For the same reason, if $L = U ^ { \oplus a } \oplus E _ { 8 } ( - 1 ) ^ { \oplus b }$ , then any non-degenerate lattice of rank $\leq a - 1$ or of rank $r \leq a + 4 b - 1$ and signature $( s , r - s )$ , $s \leq a - 1$ can be embedded uniquely in $L$ as a primitive lattice.

2. Again $L = { \Lambda } _ { \mathsf { K 3 } }$ but now $S = A _ { k _ { 1 } } ( - 1 ) \oplus A _ { k _ { 2 } } ( - 1 ) \oplus \dots \oplus A _ { k _ { \ell } } ( - 1 )$ . If $\textstyle \sum k _ { j } \leq 1 0$ conditions 1 and 2 hold.

15.2.C Applications. We first give an application to the group of isometries of a unimodular lattice $L$ that preserve a given sublattice $S$ .

Proposition 15.2.9. Let $L$ be a quadratic unimodular lattice, $S \subset L$ a primitive non-degenerate sublattice, $T = S ^ { \perp }$ and $\sigma \in \operatorname { O } ^ { \# } ( S )$ .

The isometry $\sigma$ idT of $S @ T$ extends to an isometry $e _ { S } ( \sigma )$ of $L$ . The assignment $\sigma \mapsto e _ { S } ( \sigma )$ defines an injective homomorphism $e _ { S } : { 0 } ^ { \# } ( S ) \to { 0 } ( L )$ with image contained in the subgroup ${ \mathsf { O } } ^ { \# } ( L ) _ { S }$ of the stabilizer ${ \sf O } ( L ) _ { S }$ of $S$ in ${ \sf O } \left( L \right)$ given by

$$
{ \sf O } ^ { \# } ( L ) _ { S } : = \{ \gamma \in { \sf O } ( L ) _ { S } \ | \ r _ { S } ( \gamma ) = r _ { T } ( \gamma ) \} .
$$

In other words, there is an exact sequence

$$
1 \to 0 ^ { \# } ( S ) \stackrel { e _ { S } } { \longrightarrow } 0 ^ { \# } ( L ) _ { S } \stackrel { \rho _ { T } } { \longrightarrow } 0 ( T ) ,
$$

where $\rho _ { T }$ is the restriction map. If the reduction map $r _ { S } : { \cal O } ( S )  { \cal O } ( q _ { S } ^ { \# } )$ is surjective, then also $\rho _ { T }$ is surjective.

Proof. If $\sigma \in { \mathsf { O } } ^ { \# } ( S )$ , then ${ \boldsymbol { \sigma } } \oplus \operatorname { i d } _ { T }$ induces the identity on $\mathsf { d g } _ { S } \mathbb { O } \mathsf { d g } _ { T }$ and hence preserves its subspace $L / S { \textcircled { \perp } } T$ and so it extends to $L$ by Proposition 15.1.6. Clearly this gives an injective homomorphism $e _ { S }$ and $e _ { S } ( \sigma )$ preserves $S$ . Since $e _ { S } ( \sigma )$ is the identity on $T$ , we have $\rho _ { T ^ { \circ } } e _ { S } ( \sigma ) = \operatorname { i d } _ { T }$ .

The kernel of the map $\rho _ { T }$ consists of isometries inducing the identity on $T$ . These isometries act trivially on ${ \mathrm { d g } _ { T } \simeq \mathrm { d g } _ { S } }$ and so their restrictions to $S$ by definition belong to ${ \sf O } ^ { \# } ( S )$ . Finally, if $r _ { S }$ is surjective, then for any $\psi \in \mathsf { O } ( T )$ , some $\varphi \in \operatorname { O } ( S )$ exists with $r _ { S } ( \varphi ) = r _ { T } ( \psi )$ since $0 ( q _ { s } ^ { \# } ) \simeq 0 ( q _ { T } ^ { \# } )$ . So, by the glueing condition (Proposition 15.1.6), $\varphi \oplus \psi$ extends as an isometry of $L$ which by construction preserves $S$ and $T$ and by construction belongs to ${ \mathsf { O } } ^ { \# } ( L ) _ { S }$ . □

Next, we give an application to lattice involutions, making use of the invariant lattice.

Proposition 15.2.10 (Comparing lattice involutions). Let $L$ and $L ^ { \prime }$ be isometric indefinite quadratic unimodular lattices admitting lattice involutions $i$ , respectively $i ^ { \prime }$ . Suppose that

the corresponding invariant lattices $S , S ^ { \prime }$ are isometric, • $T = S ^ { \perp } , T ^ { \prime } = S ^ { \prime \perp }$ are indefinite and have rank $\geq 4$ hen there is an isometry $\lambda : L \ { \stackrel { \simeq } { \to } } \ L ^ { \prime }$ intertwining $i$ and $i ^ { \prime }$ , that is, there is a commutative diagram

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } { L \longrightarrow } & { { } } & { \simeq \qquad \times L ^ { \prime } } \\ { i \Bigg \downarrow \Bigg \downarrow } & { { } } & { i ^ { \prime } \Bigg \downarrow } \\ { L \longrightarrow } & { { } } & { \simeq \qquad \times L ^ { \prime } . } \end{array}
$$

Proof. Since $S$ and $S ^ { \prime }$ are invariant lattices, they are also non-degenerate (see Example 1.7.3), and then so are $T$ and $T ^ { \prime }$ . By the same example these four lattices are 2-elementary. Also the lattices $T$ and $T ^ { \prime }$ are isometric since first of all they $q _ { T } ^ { \# } \cong$ $q _ { S } ^ { \# } ( - 1 ) \cong q _ { S ^ { \prime } } ^ { \# } ( - 1 ) \cong q _ { T ^ { \prime } } ^ { \# } )$ , and, secondly, by Corollary 14.6., 2-elementary lattices of rank $\geq 4$ in the same genus are isometric.

Let $\sigma : S  S ^ { \prime }$ be an isometry. We will construct an isometry $\tau : T  T ^ { \prime }$ such that $\sigma \oplus \tau$ extends to a global isometry $\lambda : L \to L ^ { \prime }$ . Since $\lambda$ commutes with $i$ and $i ^ { \prime }$ on the finite index sublattice $S \textsuperscript { \textregistered T }$ , it does so on $L$ . By Proposition 15.1.6 the desired isometry $\tau$ should satisfy $r _ { T , T ^ { \prime } } ( \tau ) = \psi _ { S , T ^ { \circ } } r _ { S , S ^ { \prime } } ( \sigma ) \circ \psi _ { S , T } ^ { - 1 }$ . The right-hand side is an isometry (see the proof of Theorem 15.1.7) and if the reduction map $r _ { T } : { \cal O } ( T )  { \cal O } ( q _ { T } ^ { \# } )$ is surjective, then as in loc. cit. an isometry $\tau$ as desired exists.

To show that $r _ { T }$ is surjective,, using the notation of Lemma 14.6.1 and observing that $T$ is 2-elementary, we can write ${ \cal T } _ { 2 } = { \cal T } ^ { ( 0 ) } \oplus { \cal T } ^ { ( 1 ) } ( 2 )$, where $T ^ { ( 0 ) }$ and $T ^ { ( 1 ) }$ are unimodular. Since $\mathrm { r a n k } ( T ) \geq 4$ at least one of the two summands has rank $\geq 2$ and surjectivity of $r _ { T }$ follows from Theorem 14.5.5.

This then implies that all primitive embeddings of $T$ in $L$ are equivalent and in particular that

Now giving a primitive embedding $s \hookrightarrow M$ is equivalent to giving a primitive embedding $S \oplus T \hookrightarrow L$ . Here $i : S \hookrightarrow M$ and $i ^ { \prime } : S \hookrightarrow M$ are considered as isomorphic if they are related by an isometry of $L$ .

Embeddings $S \hookrightarrow M$ can thus be obtained in two stages. To ensure that $S \textsuperscript { \textregistered T }$ is primitively embedded in $M \oplus T$ we shall consider the primitive closure $V ^ { \prime }$ of $S \textsuperscript { \textregistered T }$ in $M \oplus T$ and then embed $V ^ { \prime }$ primitively in $L$. To capture $V ^ { \prime }$ we shall list all overlattices $V$ of $S \textsuperscript { \textregistered T }$ such that $S$ and $T$ are primitively embedded in $V$ up to isometries of $T$. Next, we shall list the primitive embeddings of such a $V$ in $L$ up to isometries of $V$ and $L$. some of those $V$ may not be embeddable in $L$. To ensure this we use the supplementary assumptions.

By Proposition 15.1.3 an overlattice $V$ of $S \textsuperscript { \textregistered T }$ is determined by a subgroup $H _ { S } \subset \mathrm { d g } _ { S }$ and an injection $\psi : H _ { S } \hookrightarrow \mathrm { d g } _ { T }$ satisfying the glueing condition. Because of (15.8), ${ \mathsf { d g } } _ { T } \ \simeq \ { \mathsf { d g } } _ { M }$ with opposite forms and so we consider the graph $\Gamma _ { \psi } \subset$ $\mathsf { d g } _ { S } \mathbb { O } \mathsf { d g } _ { T }$ of $\psi$ as a subgroup of $\mathsf { d g } _ { S } \mathbb { O } \mathsf { d g } _ { T }$ equipped with the form $q _ { s } ^ { \# } \Phi - q _ { M } ^ { \# }$ .In fact, this subgroup is isotropic and Proposition 1.7.4 tells us that $\kappa ^ { \psi } = \Gamma _ { \psi } ^ { \perp } / \Gamma _ { \psi }$ is the discriminant quadratic form of the overlattice $V$ .

Next, we by Proposition 15.2.1 the lattice $V$ embeds primitively in $L$ if and only if a lattice with genus-invariant $( m _ { + } - s _ { + }, m _ { - } - s _ { - }, [ - q _ { V } ^ { \# } ] )$ exists. By assumption, one has an isometry $\gamma _ { K } ^ { \psi } : q _ { K } ^ { \# } \ \tilde { } \ - \Gamma _ { \psi } ^ { \bot } / \Gamma _ { \psi } = - \kappa ^ { \psi }$ and so $K$ has the required genus invariant. Consequently, a primitive embedding $j : V \hookrightarrow L$ exists and under this embedding $V ^ { \perp }$ and $K$ are isometric. $$

and so by Proposition 15.1.6 the lattice $V$ uniquely embeds in $L$ up to isometries of $L$ . Next, we compare two primitive embeddings. Clearly, if two primitive embeddings of $S$ in $M$ are equivalent, the comparison conditions hold. Remark 15.3.2. 1. The case $H _ { S } = 0$ is allowed and serves for instance to cover unimodular lattices $M$ . Similarly, if $M = L \oplus M ^ { \prime }$ , where $L$ is unimodular and $S$ embeds primitively in $L$ , then $H _ { S } = 0$ .

Proof. # 15.4 On Embeddings into Odd Unimodular Lattices

Let $S$ be a non-degenerate symmetric lattice of signature $( s _ { + } , s _ { - } )$ . We want to investigate whether $S$ can be primitively embedded in some odd unimodular lattice $L$ , say of signature $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ . As in the even case, a necessary condition is $s _ { \pm } \leq r _ { \pm }$ . We consider two cases:

Case 1: $S$ or $T = S ^ { \perp }$ is odd, where $S$ is assumed to be primitively embedded in some odd unimodular lattice $L$ . For the sake of the argument, we assume that $S$ is odd and search for conditions that $T$ be odd, respectively even. Taking into account that, by Proposition 15.1.1, $b _ { s } ^ { \# } \simeq - b _ { T } ^ { \# }$ , one sees that the following analog of Proposition 15.2.1 holds (with analogous proof, but now also invoking Corollary 12.5.14):

Proposition 15.4.1. Let $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ be a pair of non-negative integers and let $S$ be a non-degenerate odd lattice of signature $( s _ { + } , s _ { - } )$ with $s _ { + } ~ \leq ~ r _ { + }$ and $s _ { - } ~ \leq ~ r _ { - }$ and discriminant bilinear form $b ^ { \# }$ . Proposition 15.4.2. Either $r _ { + } - r _ { - } \not \equiv 0$ mod 8, or else, ${ \mathsf { O } } ( q ^ { \# } )$ is properly included in ${ \mathsf { O } } ( b ^ { \# } )$ and a (non-degenerate) even lattice $T$ of signature $( r _ { + } - s _ { + } , r _ { - } - s _ { - } )$ with discriminant form $- b ^ { \# }$ exists;

Examples 15.4.3. 1. $L = \textcircled { 9 } ^ { a + b } \langle 1 \rangle \textcircled { \textmd { 1 } } \textcircled { 9 } ^ { b + c } \langle - 1 \rangle$ , where $a , b , c \ > \ 0$ and let ${ \boldsymbol { S } } \ =$ ${ \mathbb { O } } ^ { a } \langle 1 \rangle \oplus { \mathbb { O } } ^ { b } \langle A _ { 1 } ( - 2 ) \rangle$ . Then $\operatorname { r a n k } ( L ) - \operatorname { r a n k } ( S ) = b + c = \ell ( \deg _ { S } ) + c$ and so, if $c \geq 3$ $S$ can be primitively embedded in $L$ with $S ^ { \bot }$ odd or even.

2. Let $L = \oplus ^ { a + b } \langle 1 \rangle \oplus \oplus ^ { b + c } \langle - 1 \rangle$ , $a , b , c > 0$ with $a \equiv c$ mod 8. Let $S$ be an even unimodular lattice of signature $( a , c )$ . Then $S$ cannot be embedded in $L$ with even orthogonal complement, but if $a \mathrm { ~ + ~ } c \mathrm { ~ \geq ~ 3 ~ }$ the lattice $S$ can be embedded in $L$ with $S ^ { \perp } = \oplus ^ { b } \langle 1 \rangle \oplus \oplus ^ { b } \langle - 1 \rangle$ . If instead $S ~ = ~ \oplus ^ { b } U ( 2 )$ , then $b _ { s } ^ { \# } \simeq \oplus ^ { b } u _ { 1 }$ is isometric to a symplectic form $b _ { q }$ on an $\mathbb { F } _ { 2 }$ vector space of rank $2 b$ and hence ${ \mathrm { O } } ( q )$ is strictly contained in ${ \mathrm { O } } ( b _ { q } )$ . Recall that using Theorem 14.5.5, the existence criterion Corollary 12.4.6 for even lattices yields Theorem 15.2.6, which is a version of Witt's extension theorem for embeddings in even unimodular lattices. Similarly, using the above existence criterion for odd lattices one deduces a version of Witt's theorem for embeddings of odd or even lattices $S$ in indefinite odd unimodular lattices. We only state the version for $S$ odd, leaving the even case to the reader:

Theorem 15.4.4. Let $L$ be an indefinite odd unimodular lattice and $S$ a nondegenerate odd lattice with $\ell ( { \mathrm { d g } } _ { S } ) \leq \mathrm { r a n k } ( L ) - \mathrm { r a n k } ( S ) - 3$ . Then $S$ admits $a$ primitive embedding into $L$ and such primitive embeddings are unique up to equivalence, i.e., $\mathrm { O } ( L )$ acts transitively on primitive embeddings of $S$ in $L$ . Furthermore, for each primitive embedding of $S$ with $T = S ^ { \perp }$ odd, respectively even, $T$ has genus invariant $( r _ { + } - s _ { + } , r _ { - } - s _ { - } , [ - b _ { S } ^ { \# } ] )$ , respectively $( r _ { + } - s _ { + } , r _ { - } - s _ { - } , [ - q _ { S } ^ { \# } ] )$ , where $( r _ { + } , r _ { - } )$ , $( s _ { + } , s _ { - } )$ are the signatures of $L$ and $S$ , respectively.

Historical and Bibliographical Notes. The material of this chapter is largely based on V. Nikulin's results from [171]. The embedding results are generalizations of much older results of C.T.C. Wall [244] and of D.G. James [109].

# The Structure of Orthogonal Groups I, Vector spaces

# Introduction

The first three sections of this chapter are devoted to isometries of vector spaces. In Section 16.1 sign structures are considered in relation to the spinor norm. In Section 16.2 special attention is given to characteristic 2 where a proper definition of a rotation is given with the help of the Dickson invariant. We determine the size of the orthogonal groups over finite fields in Section 16.3 along the lines of [122, $\ S$ 13].

In Section 16.4 we give an application of the Arf invariant to the classical subject of theta characteristics. These have been widely studied in relation to theta functions. We give a very short synopsis of this vast subject. We discuss also the connection with the 28 bitangents of a plane quartic curve.

# 16.1 Vector Space Isometries and Sign Structures

Next, in the case of indefinite forms, we shall give an alternative way to describe the above subgroups using $q ^ { \pm }$ -orientations, also called sign structures. To define these, recall that all maximal subspaces of $V$ on which $q > 0$ or $q < 0$ have the same dimension, say $n _ { + } > 0$ , respectively $n _ { - } > 0$ (Sylvester's law, Corollary 8.1.3). The relevant Grassmann variety

$$

To see this, remark that $G ( V )$ is homogeneous under the Lie group $G = { \mathsf { O } } ( V , q ) \simeq { \mathsf { O } } ( n _ { + } , n _ { - } )$ with isotropy group (isomorphic to) $\mathrm { O } ( n _ { + } ) \times$ $\mathrm { O } ( n _ { - } )$ . This manifold is connected since by Proposition 13.3.7 the group ${ \mathrm { O } } ( n _ { + } , n _ { - } )$ has four components each containing one of the four components of ${ \mathsf { O } } ( n _ { + } ) { \times } { \mathsf { O } } ( n _ { - } )$ . We use this to explain the notions of a $q ^ { + }$ and $q ^ { - }$ -orientation. Recall that an orientation of a vector space $W$ is an equivalence class of ordered bases of $W$ where two ordered bases define the same orientation if and only if they are related by a linear transformation with positive determinant. A vector space of dimension $> 0$ has two orientations. Choosing an orientation for a maximal subspace on which $q > 0$ induces an orientation on all such subspaces since $G ( V )$ is connected. A choice of such a coherent system of orientations is called a $q ^ { + }$ -orientation. Switching to the second description for the Grassmann variety $G ( V )$ , one obtains the definition of a $q ^ { - }$ -orientation.

Let us consider the special case of a hyperbolic vector space whose definition we recall. Suppose $V$ has a basis $\{ e _ { 0 } , e _ { 1 } , \ldots , e _ { n } \}$ such that the polarization of the quadratic form is given by

$$
x \cdot y = x _ { 0 } y _ { 0 } - \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } x _ { i } y _ { i } , \quad x = \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { n } x _ { i } e _ { i } , y = \sum _ { i = 0 } ^ { n } y _ { i } e _ { i } .
$$

We call $V$ with this inner product a hyperbolic vector space.

Lemma 16.1.3. Let $V$ be a hyperbolic vector space. The "light cone" $\{ x \in V \mid$ $x \cdot x > 0 \}$ is a disjoint union ${ \mathsf { C } } _ { V } \cup { \mathsf { - C } } _ { V }$ of two convex cones where $C _ { V }$ is contained in the half space $x _ { 0 } > 0$ . For points $x , y$ in the light cone we have:

$$
x \cdot y > 0 \iff x , y \in \mathsf C _ { V } \ o r \ x , y \in - \mathsf C _ { V } .
$$

If $x \neq 0$ and $x \in { \overline { { C _ { V } } } }$ , $y \in { \mathsf { C } } _ { V }$ , then we still have $x \cdot y > 0$ .

Then combine this with the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } x _ { i } y _ { i } \ \leq \ \sqrt { x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + x _ { n } ^ { 2 } } \cdot \sqrt { y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + y _ { n } ^ { 2 } } } \end{array}$ .If $x \neq 0$ and $x \in \overline { { C _ { V } } }$ , then $0 < x _ { 0 } = { \sqrt { x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + x _ { n } ^ { 2 } } }$ . From $y _ { 0 } > { \sqrt { y _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + y _ { n } ^ { 2 } } }$ we then infer $x \cdot y > 0$ in this case as well.

Using the equivalence (16.2), convexity of $C _ { V }$ follows from a straightforward computation involving $( t x + ( 1 - t ) y ) ) \cdot ( t x + ( 1 - t ) y ) )$ and $t x _ { 0 } + ( 1 - t ) y _ { 0 } > 0$ , $0 \leq t \leq 1$ .

Observe that positive lines, i.e., lines on which the form is positive definite, are exactly those lines that, apart from the origin, belong to the light cone. Hence the subgroup of the Lorentz group $\operatorname { O } ( 1 , n )$ preserving the components of the light cone is the subgroup preserving a fixed orientation of such lines, that is the subgroup of isometries with Nmspin :

$$
{ \mathsf { O } } ^ { - } ( V ) = \{ g \in { \mathsf { O } } ( V ) \mid g ( \mathsf { C } _ { V } ) \subset \mathsf { C } _ { V } \} .
$$

\Xi _ { s E } - \Xi _ { E } = p ( s ) = \sum _ { 1 \leq i , j \leq n } a _ { j } a _ { i j } c _ { i j } + \sum _ { 1 \leq i , j \leq n } a _ { j + n } b _ { i j } d _ { i j } + \sum _ { 1 \leq i , j \leq n } b _ { i j } c _ { i j } .
$$

This motivates the following definition.

Definition 16.2.1. Let $s$ be a symplectic transformation whose matrix with respect to $\pmb { { \cal E } }$ is given by

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { \left( \begin{array} { l l } { ( a _ { i j } ) _ { 1 \leq i , j \leq n } } & { ( c _ { i j } ) _ { 1 \leq i , j \leq n } } \\ { ( b _ { i j } ) _ { 1 \leq i , j \leq n } } & { ( d _ { i j } ) _ { 1 \leq i , j \leq n } } \end{array} \right) \in \mathsf { S p } ( n ) . } \end{array}
$$

Then the Dickson invariant of the triple $( q , s , \pmb { { E } } )$ is the element in the field $k$ given by

$$
D ( q , s , E ) = z _ { s E } - z _ { E } = p ( s ) = \sum _ { 1 \leq i , j \leq n } a _ { j } a _ { i j } c _ { i j } + \sum _ { 1 \leq i , j \leq n } a _ { j + n } b _ { i j } d _ { i j } + \sum _ { 1 \leq i , j \leq n } b _ { i j } c _ { i j } .
$$

Observe that (16.7) implies

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \wp ( D ( q , s , { \pmb { E } } ) ) = \wp ( p ( s ) ) = z _ { s { \pmb { E } } } ^ { 2 } + z _ { s { \pmb { E } } } - z _ { { \pmb { E } } } ^ { 2 } - z _ { { \pmb { E } } } } \\ & { \qquad \equiv \operatorname * { a r f } ( q ^ { ( s ) } ) - \operatorname * { a r f } ( q ) , \quad q ^ { ( s ) } ( x ) : = q ( s x ) , } \end{array}
$$

which gives another proof that the Arf invariant is independent of the choice of a symplectic basis. Moreover, since $\wp ( p ( s ) ) = 0$ if and only if $p ( s ) = 0$ or $p ( s ) = 1$ , applying this when $\boldsymbol { q } ^ { ( s ) } = \boldsymbol { q }$ , we obtain:

Corollary 16.2.2. An isometry of the quadratic form $q$ has Dickson invariant 0 or 1.

Example 16.2.3. Let $\varepsilon = t _ { u , a }$ be a transvection where $u = \textstyle \sum u _ { i } e _ { i }$ . Comparing with (8.5) we find

$$
D ( q , \varepsilon , \mathbf { E } ) = a \cdot \bigg [ q ( u ) + ( a q ( u ) + 1 ) \cdot \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } { u _ { i } u _ { i + n } } \bigg ] .
$$

Of course this can also be found by direct calculation. Observe that $\varepsilon$ preserves the quadratic form $q$ if and only if $q ( u ) = a ^ { - 1 }$ , and if so, its Dickson invariant equals 1. Such transvections are the orthogonal reflections.

We cannot expect the Dickson invariant to be additive on the entire symplectic group. In fact, writing as before $q ^ { ( s ) }$ for the quadratic form $x \mapsto q ( s x )$ , we have

$$
D ( q , t \circ s , { \cal E } ) = D ( q , s , { \cal E } ) + D ( q ^ { ( s ) } , t , s { \cal E } ) .
$$

To see this, we use the transformation law (16.7) for $t \circ s$ which gives $z _ { t s ( E ) } + z _ { E } =$ $D ( q , t \circ s , \pmb { E } )$ , but since $D ( q , t , s E ) = \pmb { z } _ { t s ( E ) } + \pmb { z } _ { s E }$ , one gets

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { D ( q , s , { \cal E } ) + D ( q ^ { ( s ) } , t , s { \cal E } ) = z _ { s { \cal E } } + z _ { { \cal E } } + z _ { t s ( { \cal E } ) } + z _ { s { \cal E } } } } \\ { ~ } \\ { { ~ = z _ { \cal E } + z _ { t s ( { \cal E } ) } } } \\ { { ~ = D ( q , t \circ s , { \cal E } ) . } } \end{array}
$$

Suppose now that $s$ is $q$ orthogonal. Then $q ^ { ( s ) } = q$ . The matrix of $t$ with respect to the basis $s E$ is the same as the matrix of $s ^ { - 1 } t s$ with respect to $\pmb { { \cal E } }$ and so $D ( q ^ { ( s ) } , t , s E ) = D ( q , s ^ { - 1 } t s , E )$ . So, if we replace $t$ with $s t s ^ { - 1 }$ in the formula (16.8), we obtain

$$
D ( q , s \circ t , \pmb { E } ) = D ( q , s , \pmb { E } ) + D ( q , t , \pmb { E } ) .
$$

So on transformations that preserve $q$ the Dickson invariant gives an additive homomorphism ${ \mathsf { O } } ( q ) \to \{ 0 , 1 \} = \mathbb { F } _ { 2 }$ . The kernel of this homomorphism then is a subgroup of ${ \mathrm { O } } ( q )$ of index 2, by definition the subgroup of rotations:

Definition 16.2.4. Let $( V , q )$ be a quadratic space over a field of characteristic 2. A rotation is an orthogonal transformation with Dickson invariant 0.

Examples 16.2.5. 1. Since an orthogonal transvection is just a reflection and has Dickson invariant 1, an even product of reflections is a rotation.

2. Consider the hyperbolic plane $U$ . We have seen in Example 6.5.5.2 that the only isometries are $i _ { a }$ and $j _ { b }$ . These have Dickson invariant 0, respectively 1. Since $j _ { 1 ^ { \circ } } j _ { b } = i _ { b }$ , a rotation is a product of two reflections.

3. As we observed before (cf. Remark 7.2.6), almost all quadratic spaces have the property that orthogonal transformations are products of reflections and for those spaces rotations are even products of reflections. This leads to an alternative interpretation of the Dickson invariant $D ( q , s , \pmb { { E } } )$ for orthogonal transformations $s$ , namely $D ( q , s , { \cal E } ) = \dim ( \operatorname { I m } ( s - \operatorname { i d } ) )$ mod 2 (see [223, p. 160]). Indeed, the Dickson invariant being a homomorphism, it suffices to observe that a reflection hyperplane in a (non-degenerate) symplectic space has odd dimension.

The exceptional quadratic space is $N \odot N$ where $N = \mathbb { F } _ { 2 } ^ { 2 }$ with quadratic form $x ^ { 2 } + x y + y ^ { 2 }$ . The isometry $s$ exchanging the two copies of $N$ is not a product of two reflections. Its Dickson invariant is $0$ but here again $\mathrm { d i m } ( \mathrm { I m } ( s - \mathrm { i d } ) )$ is even, so the above interpretation of the Dickson invariant is uniformly valid. 4. Let $k = \mathbb { F } _ { 2 }$ and $K = k ( \xi )$ the unique separable quadratic extension of $k$ . Then $\xi ^ { 2 } + \xi + 1 = 0$ and the norm form $\mathsf { N } _ { K / k }$ is the quadratic form $x ^ { 2 } + x y + y ^ { 2 }$ on $k ^ { 2 }$ . As we saw in $\ S$ 6.3.B, example 6, multiplication with a norm 1 element $a + b \xi$ in $K$ gives an ioery with m $M _ { a , b } = \left( \begin{array} { c c } { { a } } & { { b } } \\ { { b } } & { { a + b } } \end{array} \right)$ and the Dickson invariant equals $a b + b ( a + b ) + b ^ { 2 } = 0$ . Hence this is a rotation. We also saw that all other orthogonal transformations have matrix $M _ { a , b } ^ { \prime } = { \binom { a } { b } } \quad { \begin{array} { l } { a + b } \\ { a } \end{array} }$ and those have Dickson invariant equal to $a b + a ( a + b ) + b ( a + b ) = a ^ { 2 } + a b + b ^ { 2 } = 1$ . So half the orthogonal $M _ { a , b } ^ { \prime } \circ M _ { 1 , 0 } ^ { \prime } = M _ { a , b }$ also in this example all rotations are products of two reflections.

The calculation of $s ( V )$ is performed by induction. So suppose $V = U \mathbb { \textcircled { \div } } W$ with $\dim W = n$ . Let $\{ e , f \}$ be the standard basis of $U$ and write an isotropic vector in $V$ as $x \cdot e + y \cdot f + w$ , $w \in W$ . We have the following possibilities:

• $q _ { W } ( w ) = 0 , x y = 0$ which gives $2 q - 1$ possibilities with $w \ne 0$ leading to $( 2 q - 1 ) s ( W )$ possible vectors, and $2 q - 2$ in the case that $w = 0$ ; • $q _ { W } ( w ) \neq 0$ and $x y = q _ { W } ( w )$ . This gives $( q ^ { n } - s ( W ) - 1 ) ( q - 1 )$ possibilities since $x \in \mathbb { F } _ { q } ^ { \times }$ together with each of the $( q ^ { n } - 1 ) - s ( W )$ possible vectors $w$ determine $y$ .

This sums up to give $s ( U \oplus W ) = q \cdot s ( W ) + ( q ^ { n } + 1 ) ( q - 1 )$ . From this one finds $s ( U ^ { \\\mathbb { Q } m } )$ by induction. Applying it to type II we find for $m = 1$ the stated number $( q ^ { 2 } + 1 ) ( q - 1 )$ , and then for arbitrary $m$ it follows by induction. For type III the proof proceeds in the same way with induction starting from $m = 1$ with $q ^ { 2 } - 1$ .

The value of $s ( V )$ also gives the value $s _ { \alpha } ( V )$ , $\alpha \in k ^ { \times }$ , the number of vectors $x$ in $V$ with $q ( x ) = \alpha$ . In the cases I, $\mathrm { I I }$ , and in case III for characteristic 2, this follows since then $V ( \alpha ) \simeq V$ if $\alpha \neq 0$ . This is easily verified for $U$ and hence for $\mathbb { Q } ^ { m } U$ using the bijective map $x e + y f \mapsto x e + y \alpha f$ ; for the surjective norm map $N _ { K / k } : K ^ { * } \to k ^ { * }$ use that the cosets of the kernel have equal size; for $[ a ]$ in characteristic 2 use that $\alpha$ is a square in $k$ . It follows that $s _ { 1 } ( V ) = s _ { \alpha } ( V )$ for all $\alpha \neq 0$ . Hence, if $n = \dim V$ , we have

$$
s _ { \alpha } ( V ) = \frac { q ^ { n } - s _ { 0 } ( V ) } { q - 1 } = \frac { q ^ { n } - 1 - s ( V ) } { q - 1 } , \quad \alpha \neq 0 .

For case III, characteristic $p \neq 2$ , this is slightly more involved since the result depends on whether $a ^ { - 1 } \alpha$ is a square or a non-square. The square case is as before, but for the non-square case the calculation is a bit different. See [122, §13] for details.

We next calculate $\operatorname { O } ( V )$ for the various types, again using the method of splitting off a hyperbolic plane. By Remark 7.2.9.2 the Witt extension theorem holds for isotropic vectors and so $\operatorname { O } ( V )$ acts transitively on these. Suppose as before that $V = U \odot W$ with $\dim W = n$ and $\{ e , f \}$ the standard basis of $U$ . It follows that

$$
| \mathsf { O } ( V ) | = s ( V ) \cdot | \mathsf { O } _ { e } ( V ) | .
$$

Decompose $\gamma \in \mathsf { O } _ { e } ( V )$ according to $U \not \odot W$ (here we also use the polar form):

$$
\gamma = \left( \begin{array} { c c } { 1 } & { - q ( \pmb { w } ) } \\ { 0 } & { 1 } \\ { 0 } & { \pmb { w } } \end{array} \right) , \quad \pmb { w } \in W , \phi \in \mathrm { O } ( W ) .

Hence $| \mathsf { O } _ { e } ( V ) | = q ^ { n } \cdot | \mathsf { O } ( W ) |$ . To start the induction we have to calculate the number of elements in $\mathrm { O } ( W )$ for $W = \mathsf { N } _ { K / k }$ and for $[ a ]$ . For the norm form we do this separately for even and odd characteristics using the remarks in $\ S \ 6 . 3 . \mathrm { B }$ , example 4, respectively Examples 16.2.5.

Case 1: $p$ odd. The rotations correspond precisely to the elements of norm 1. There are exactly $( q ^ { 2 } - 1 ) / ( q - 1 ) = q + 1$ of those and so $| \mathsf { O } ( \mathsf { N } _ { K / k } ) | = 2 ( q + 1 )$ .

Case 2: $p = 2$ . Here rotations have Dickson invariant 0 and form a subgroup of index 2 in the group of all orthogonal transformations and so the same result holds.
