Concluding argument. The conditions on $L$ imply that $\dim _ { \mathbb { F } _ { 2 } } L / 2 L \geq 6$ and $\mathrm { d i m } _ { \mathbb { F } _ { 3 } } L / 3 L \ge 5$ so that the exceptions in Step 1 do not occur and thus

$$
\begin{array} { r c l } { { \mathsf { W } ^ { + } ( L ) \cap \mathsf { S O } ( L ) = \displaystyle \bigcap _ { p } \mathsf { W } ^ { + } ( L _ { p } ) \cap \mathsf { S O } ^ { + } ( L ) \mathrm { ~ ( S t e p ~ 3 ) ~ } } } \\ { { } } & { { = \displaystyle \bigcap _ { p } \mathsf { O } ^ { \# } ( L _ { p } ) \cap \mathsf { S O } ^ { + } ( L ) \mathrm { ~ ( S t e p ~ 1 ) ~ } } } \\ { { } } & { { = \mathsf { O } ^ { \# } ( L ) \cap \mathsf { S O } ^ { + } ( L ) . } } \end{array}
$$

This result equally applies to ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( L )$ :

Corollary 17.2.12. Under the same conditions on $( L , q )$ , one has $\mathsf { W } ^ { \epsilon } ( L ) = \mathsf { O } ^ { \epsilon , \# } ( L )$

Proof. By the (proof of) Theorem 17.2.11, the group $\mathsf { W } ^ { + } ( L ) \cap \mathsf { S O } ( L )$ is generated by products $u = \sigma _ { x } \sigma _ { y }$ of two reflections in roots $x , y$ with $q ( x ) = q ( y ) = 1$ (and so $\mathsf { N m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } u = 1$ ). Since $\mathsf { W } ^ { + } ( L ) = \mathsf { W } ^ { + } ( L ) \cap \mathsf { S O } ( L ) \cup \sigma _ { x } \cdot [ \mathsf { W } ^ { + } ( L ) \cap \mathsf { S O } ( L ) ]$ , one has $\mathsf { W } ^ { + } ( L ) = \mathsf { O } ^ { + , \# } ( L )$ . Replace $L$ with $L ( - 1 )$ . The assumptions hold equally well for the lattice $L ( - 1 )$ . The same argument with the $( - )$ -spinor norm gives the result for $\epsilon = - 1$ .

Remark 17.2.13. The condition on the signature is necessary as we see from Theorem 17.2.9 which demonstrates that the Weyl group in a Lorentzian lattice is rarely of finite index in the full orthogonal group. See also Theorem 17.3.7 below.

# 17.3 Eichler-Siegel Transformations

17.3.A Basic properties. Before considering lattices, we first consider rational inner product spaces $( V , b )$ , where $^ { b }$ is the polar form of a quadratic form $q$ .

Definition 17.3.1. Given a pair of vectors $\{ f , y \}$ in $V$ where $f$ is isotropic and $b ( f , y ) = 0$ , the Eichler-Siegel transformation with respect to $\{ f , y \}$ is given by

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } {  { \psi _ { f , y } : V \longrightarrow V \longrightarrow V } } \\ & { } & { x \longmapsto x + b ( x , y ) f - b ( x , f ) y - b ( x , f ) q ( y ) f . } \end{array}
$$

The linear map $\psi _ { f , y }$ is an isometry (by direct computation) with inverse $\psi _ { f , - y }$ (see Lemma 17.3.3). If $y$ and $f$ are linearly dependent, then $\psi _ { f , y }$ is simply the identity.

Lemma 17.3.2. Assume that $q ( y ) \neq 0$ . Then the Eichler-Siegel transformation $\psi _ { f , y }$ is the unique isometry of $V$ which satisfies

$$
\psi _ { f , y } z = z + b ( z , y ) f \quad \forall z \in \mathbb { R } f ^ { \perp } .
$$

In particular, $\psi _ { f , y } f = f$ .

Proof. Since $^ { b }$ is non-degenerate $\dim V \geq 3$ , and so there exists a vector $g$ with $b ( f , g ) = 1$ and $b ( g , y ) = 0$ . The vectors $f , g , y$ span a three-dimensional space $W$ , and $g$ and $f ^ { \bot }$ span $V$ . Let $\psi : V \to V$ be an isometry which acts on $f ^ { \bot }$ in the same way as $\psi _ { f , y }$ . Then we need to verify that $\psi ( g ) = \psi _ { f , y } ( g ) = g - q ( y ) f - y$ . Since $W ^ { \bot } \subset f ^ { \bot }$ and $\psi _ { f , y } | _ { W ^ { \perp } } = \mathrm { i d }$ , we have $\psi | _ { W ^ { \bot } } = \mathrm { i d }$ and so $\psi ( W ) \subset W$ (here we use that $( W ^ { \perp } ) ^ { \perp } = W$ , see Lemma 1.1.3). Now let $\psi ( g ) = \alpha g + \beta f + \gamma y$ . Expanding the equations

$$
\begin{array} { r } { 1 = b ( \psi ( g ) , \psi ( f ) ) } \\ { 0 = b ( \psi ( g ) , \psi ( y ) ) } \\ { b ( g , g ) = b ( \psi ( g ) , \psi ( g ) ) , } \end{array}
$$

yields $\alpha = 1 , \gamma = - 1$ (here we use $q ( y ) \neq 0$ ), and $\beta = - q ( y )$ .

From now on, we again suppose that $L$ is a non-degenerate symmetric lattice and $V = L _ { \mathbb { Q } }$ . Observe that the defining equation (17.6) shows that the Eichler-Siegel transformation $\psi _ { f , y }$ of $V$ preserves $L$ provided $f$ and $y$ belong to $L$ and $q ( y ) \in \mathbb { Z }$ . We can say more:

Lemma 17.3.3. Suppose $f \in L$ is a primitive isotropic vector and suppose $y \in L$ satisfies $b ( y , y )$ even and $b ( f , y ) = 0$ . Then $\psi _ { f , y }$ induces a lattice isometry of $L$ with the following properties.

1. $\psi _ { f , y } \in { 0 } ^ { \in } ( L )$ for $\epsilon = -$ as well as for $\epsilon = +$ .

2. $\psi _ { f , y }$ induces the identity on the discriminant group.

3. One has $\psi _ { f , y } = \psi _ { f , y + f }$ and the map

$$
\begin{array} { r } { L _ { f } = f ^ { \perp } / \mathbb { Z } f \stackrel { \psi _ { f } } { \longrightarrow } 0 ( L ) } \\ { y + \mathbb { Z } f \longmapsto \psi _ { f , y } } \end{array}
$$

is a well-defined injective group homomorphism. In particular $\psi _ { f } ( L _ { f } )$ is an abelian subgroup of $\mathrm { O } ( L )$ whose rank equals $\operatorname { r a n k } ( L _ { f } )$ .

4. $\psi _ { f } ( L _ { f } )$ is a normal subgroup of ${ \sf O } _ { f } ( L )$ , the stabilizer of $f$ .

Proof. 1. The spinor norm is continuous on $\mathsf { O } ( V _ { \mathbb { R } } )$ (see Remark 13.3.6.2) and the path $t \mapsto \psi _ { t f , y }$ belonging to $\mathrm { O } ( V _ { \mathbb { R } } )$ connects $\psi _ { f , y }$ to the identity and so $\Lambda \mathrm { m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ^ { \epsilon } \psi _ { f , y } = 1$ .

2. Let $u \in L ^ { * }$ , then, since $b ( u , y )$ , $b ( u , f )$ and $q ( y )$ are integers, (17.6) shows that $\psi _ { f , y } u \equiv u$ mod $L$ which means precisely that $\psi _ { f , y }$ induces the identity on ${ \mathsf { d g } } _ { L }$ .

3. $q ( y + f ) = q ( y ) + q ( f ) + b ( y, f ) = q ( y )$. Using this, the first assertion and the well-definedness of $\psi _ { f }$ follow from

$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \psi _ { f , y + f } ( x ) = x + b ( x , y + f ) f - b ( x , f ) ( y + f ) - b ( x , f ) q ( y + f ) f } } \\ { { \qquad = x + b ( x , y ) f + b ( x , f ) f - b ( x , f ) y - b ( x , f ) f - b ( x , f ) q ( y ) f } } \\ { { \qquad = x + b ( x , y ) f - b ( x , f ) y - b ( x , f ) q ( y ) f } } \\ { { \qquad = \psi _ { f , y } ( x ) . } } \end{array}
$$

The second assertion follows from

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \psi _ { f , y ^ { \prime \prime } } \psi _ { f , y } ( x ) = \psi _ { f , y ^ { \prime } } ( x + b ( x , y ) f - b ( x , f ) y - b ( x , f ) q ( y ) f ) } \\ & { \qquad = x + b ( x , y ^ { \prime } ) f - b ( x , f ) y ^ { \prime } - b ( x , f ) q ( y ^ { \prime } ) f } \\ & { \qquad + b ( x , y ) f - b ( x , f ) y - \ b ( x , f ) b ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) f } \\ & { \qquad ~ - b ( x , f ) q ( y ) f } \\ & { \qquad = x + b ( x , y + y ^ { \prime } ) f - b ( x , f ) ( y + y ^ { \prime } ) - b ( x , f ) q ( y + y ^ { \prime } ) f } \\ & { \qquad = \psi _ { f , y + y ^ { \prime } } ( x ) , } \end{array}
$$

where we have used

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \psi _ { f , y ^ { \prime } } ( f ) = f , } \\ & { \psi _ { f , y ^ { \prime } } ( y ) = y + b ( y , y ^ { \prime } ) f . } \end{array}
$$

That we get an injection follows since if $\psi _ { f , y } = \mathrm { i d }$ , then either $y$ and $f$ are dependent or $b ( x , f ) y = 0$ for all $x \in L$ in which case $y = 0$ since $^ { b }$ is non-degenerate.

This is because for all $g \in O _ { f } ( L )$ we have $g \circ \psi _ { f , y } \circ g ^ { - 1 } = \psi _ { g f , g y } = \psi _ { f , g y }$

Property 3 shows that a non-degenerate lattice of rank $\geq 3$ containing isotropic vectors and at least one vector $y \in f ^ { \bot } - \mathbb { Z } \cdot f$ with $b ( y , y )$ even has an infinite isometry group. The existence of such a $y$ with $b ( y , y )$ even can be circumvented by replacing $L$ with $L ( 2 )$ which has the same isometry group as $L$ . Hence we have shown:

Proposition 17.3.4. Let $L$ be a non-degenerate lattice of rank $n \geq 3$ containing an isotropic vector. Then $\mathrm { O } ( L )$ contains a free abelian group of rank $n - 2$ . In particular, L has infinitely many isometries.

Corollary 17.3.5. Let $L$ be a non-degenerate indefinite lattice of rank $\geq 5$ , then O(L) is infinite.

Proof. By Meyer's theorem 3.3.4, the rational space $L _ { \mathbb { Q } }$ has an isotropic vector and hence this is also the case for $L$ .

Eichler-Siegel transformations of the form $\boldsymbol { \psi } _ { f , r }$ with $r$ a $\left( - 2 \right)$ -root are compositions of reflections. More is true:

Proposition 17.3.6. Let $L$ be a non-degenerate lattice of rank n containing a primitive isotropic vector $f$ and $a$ $\left( - 2 \right)$ -root $r \in f ^ { \perp }$ . Then

1. $\psi _ { f , r } = \sigma _ { f - r ^ { \circ } } \sigma _ { r }$ .   
2. The image of the $\left( - 2 \right)$ -root lattice of $L _ { f }$ under $\psi _ { f } : L _ { f } \to { \mathsf { O } } ( L )$ is contained in the Weyl group $W ^ { - } ( f ^ { \bot } )$ considered as the subgroup of ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( L )$ generated by reflections in $\left( - 2 \right)$ -roots of $f ^ { \bot }$ (and hence preserving $f$ ).   
3. If $y \in L _ { f }$ is orthogonal to the $\left( - 2 \right)$ -root lattice $L _ { f , \mathrm { r o o t } }$ of $L _ { f }$ , then $\psi _ { f } ( y )$ restricts to the identity on the $\left( - 2 \right)$ -root lattice of $f ^ { \bot }$ . In particular, $W ^ { - } ( f ^ { \bot } ) \cap$ $\psi _ { f } ( L _ { f , \mathrm { r o o t } } ^ { \perp } ) = \{ \mathrm { i d } \}$ .

Proof. 1. Given two $\left( - 2 \right)$ -roots $r , r ^ { \prime }$ in a lattice $( L , b )$ , one has

$$
\sigma _ { r ^ { \prime } } \sigma _ { r } ( x ) = \sigma _ { r } ( x ) + b ( r ^ { \prime } , \sigma _ { r } ( x ) ) r ^ { \prime } = x + b ( x , r ) r + b ( x , r ^ { \prime } ) r ^ { \prime } + b ( r , r ^ { \prime } ) b ( x , r ) r ^ { \prime } , \quad x \in L .
$$

Substituting $r ^ { \prime } = f - r$ , one gets $\sigma _ { r - f ^ { \circ } } \sigma _ { r } ( x ) = x + b ( x , r ) f - b ( x , f ) r + b ( x , f ) f =$ $\psi _ { f , r } ( x )$ .

2. From 1 we infer that if $y = \sum a _ { j } r _ { j }$ ,a $\mathbb { Z }$ -linear combination of roots in $f ^ { \bot }$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { \psi _ { f , y } = \prod _ { j } ( \sigma _ { f - r _ { j } } \circ \sigma _ { r _ { j } } ) ^ { a _ { j } } \in \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( f ^ { \bot } ) } \end{array}$ .

3. In this situation $\psi _ { f , y } ( x ) = x + b ( x , y ) f$ Hence, if thee class of $y$ belongs to $L _ { f , \mathrm { r o o t } } ^ { \perp }$ then $\psi _ { f , y }$ is clearly the identity on the $\left( - 2 \right)$ -root lattice of $f ^ { \bot }$ .

Finally, suppose that $\gamma \in \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( f ^ { \perp } ) \cap \psi _ { f } ( L _ { f , \mathrm { r o o t } } ^ { \perp } )$ . Then  is a composition of reflections in (−2)-roots of $f ^ { \bot }$ incing te nyo he latce $M : = f _ { \mathrm { r o o t } } ^ { \perp }$ spanned by all such $\left( - 2 \right)$ -roots $r$ . But then $\gamma = \mathrm { i d } _ { L }$ since it is the identity on the orthogonal complement of $M$ in $L$ , because this is the intersection of the reflection hyperplanes for the $\sigma _ { r } \in M$ .

17.3.B Application to Lorentzian lattices. The aim is to find a criterion which ensures that a Lorentzian lattice $L$ is not $\left( - 2 \right)$ -reflective, i.e., a lattice for which the reflection group generated by reflections in $( - 2 )$ -roots is not of finite index in $\mathrm { O } ( L )$ . We start with a technical result.

Lemma. Suppose that a Lorentzian lattice $L$ contains a (primitive) isotropic vector $f$ . Then

$$
\mathsf { W } _ { f } ^ { - } L = \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( f ^ { \perp } ) ,
$$

where we recall that $\mathsf { W } _ { f } ^ { - } L$ is the subgroup of the Weyl group of $L$ fixing $f$ , and the right-hand side, $W ^ { - } ( f ^ { \bot } )$ , is identified with the subgroup of ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( L )$ generated by reflections in $\left( - 2 \right)$ -roots of $f ^ { \bot }$ (and hence preserving $f$ ).

Proof. We first construct a partitioning of the $\left( - 2 \right)$ -roots in $L$ using that a root $r$ either is contained in $f ^ { \bot }$ , or else $b ( r , f ) \neq 0$ . Choosing $z \in f ^ { \bot } \otimes \mathbb { R }$ not belonging to the hyperplanes orthogonal to roots in $f ^ { \bot }$ , the former can be partitioned into $\Delta _ { 1 } ^ { + } \cup { - } \Delta _ { 1 } ^ { + }$ where each root $r \in { \Delta } _ { 1 } ^ { + }$ satisfies $b ( r , z ) > 0$ . A root with $b ( r , f ) \neq 0$ either satisfies $b ( r , f ) > 0$ ; such roots form a set $\Delta _ { 2 } ^ { + }$ . Or one has $b ( r , f ) < 0$ and such roots form $- \Delta _ { 2 } ^ { + }$ . Combining the two gives a partition $\Delta ^ { + } \cup - \Delta ^ { + }$ , $\Delta ^ { + } = \Delta _ { 1 } ^ { + } \cup \Delta _ { 2 } ^ { + }$ of the roots in $L$ . This partition is closed under taking sums: a root which is a sum of roots from $\Delta ^ { + }$ belongs to $\Delta ^ { + }$ . Hence, by Proposition 17.2.6 it defines a Weyl chamber and Remark 17.2.8 implies that the Weyl group is generated by reflections in indecomposable roots.

To continue, note first that $\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( f ^ { \perp } ) \subset \mathsf { W } _ { f } ^ { - } L$ . Conversely, assume that $g \in \mathsf { W } _ { f } ^ { - } L$ and write $g$ as a product of reflections from ${ \Delta } _ { 1 } ^ { + }$ and $\Delta _ { 2 } ^ { + }$ . If $g \notin \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( f ^ { \perp } )$ at least one reflection $\sigma _ { r }$ , $r \in \Delta _ { 2 } ^ { + }$ , must appear in the product and then $b ( \sigma _ { r } ( f ) , f ) ~ >$ 0. Products of reflections in roots from ${ \boldsymbol { \Delta } } _ { 1 } ^ { + }$ do not alter this number. So we may assume that $g = \sigma _ { r _ { k } ^ { \circ } } \cdot \cdot \cdot \circ \sigma _ { r _ { 1 } }$ with indecomposable roots $r _ { j } \in \Delta _ { 2 } ^ { + }$ . Since the number $b ( g ( f ) , f )$ does not depend on the order of the roots $r _ { j }$ in the expression for $g$ , we may assume that each root appears at most once. For two different indecomposable roots $r _ { i } , r _ { j }$ we have $b ( r _ { i } , r _ { j } ) \geq 0$ . It then follows inductively that for any finite product $g$ of different indecomposable roots in ${ \boldsymbol { \Delta } } _ { 2 } ^ { + }$ one has $b ( g ( f ) , f ) > 0$ contradicting our assumption that $g ( f ) = f$ .

This result yields the criterion we are after:

Proposition 17.3.7 (compare [172, Prop. 1.3.1]). For a Lorentzian type lattice $L$ of rank $\geq 3$ containing a primitive isotropic vector $f$ and associated negative definite lattice $L _ { f } = f ^ { \perp } / \mathbb { Z } f$ , let $\delta _ { f } = \mathrm { r a n k } ( L _ { f } ) - \mathrm { r a n k } ( L _ { f , \mathrm { r o o t } } )$ . Then $\mathsf { O } ( L ) / \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L )$

contains a normal abelian subgroup of rank $\delta _ { f }$ . In particular, if $L _ { f }$ is not spanned by its roots, the group $\mathsf { O } ( L ) / \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L )$ is infinite.

Proof. By Proposition 17.3.6 and (17.7) we have $\mathsf { W } _ { f } ^ { - } ( L ) \cap \psi _ { f } ( L _ { f , \mathrm { r o o t } } ^ { \perp } ) = \{ \mathrm { i d } \}$ . Since $\mathrm { I m } ( \psi _ { f } ) \subset \mathsf { O } _ { f } ( L )$ , the intersection $\mathsf { W } _ { f } ^ { - } ( L ) \cap \mathrm { I m } ( \psi _ { f } )$ coincides with the intersection $\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L ) \cap \mathrm { I m } ( \psi _ { f } )$ . Consequently, $\psi _ { f } ( L _ { f , \mathrm { r o o t } } ^ { \perp } ) \subset \mathsf { O } ( L ) / \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L )$ By Lemma 17.3.3, the Eichler-Siegel transformations $\psi _ { f , y }$ $y \in \psi _ { f } ( L _ { f } )$ , form an abelian subgroup $\psi _ { f } ( L _ { f } )$ of the stabilizer of $f$ in $0 ^ { - } ( L )$ .Since $\operatorname { r a n k } ( \psi _ { f } L _ { f } ) = \operatorname { r a n k } ( L _ { f } )$ , it follows that $\psi _ { f } ( L _ { f } ) / \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L )$ contains an abelian group of rank $\delta _ { f }$ .

Example 17.3.8. Consider the root lattice of the Lorentz lattices $E ^ { 1 , n }$ of Examples 17.2.10.1. If $n = 2$ , the lattice is spanned by $\alpha _ { 0 } = \left( 1 , - 1 , - 1 \right)$ , $\alpha _ { 1 } = ( 0 , 1 , - 1 )$ and $\alpha _ { 2 } = ( 0 , 0 , 1 )$ . It contains the isotropic vector $f = \alpha _ { 0 } + \alpha _ { 1 } + \alpha _ { 2 }$ and $f ^ { \bot } / \mathbb { Z } f$ has rank 1 and is spanned by the class of $\alpha _ { 0 }$ which is a $( - 1 )$ -root and not a $\left( - 2 \right)$ -root. A similar calculation shows that $E ^ { 1 , 3 }$ is not $\left( - 2 \right)$ -reflective.

For $n = 5 , \ldots , 9$ the computation is slightly different: the vector $f = e _ { 0 } + e _ { n } =$ $\textstyle { \alpha _ { 0 } + \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } i \alpha _ { i } }$ is isotropic and $f ^ { \bot } / f$ has root basis $\alpha _ { 1 } , \ldots , \alpha _ { n - 2 } , \alpha _ { n - 1 } + \alpha _ { n }$ which gives the root system $B _ { n - 1 }$ and so $f ^ { \bot } / f$ is not spanned by $\left( - 2 \right)$ -roots. Hence also for $n = 5 , \ldots , 9$ the root-lattice for $\mathbb { Z } ^ { 1 , n }$ is not $\left( - 2 \right)$ -reflective.

17.3.C Application to lattices splitting off copies of the hyperbolic plane. This situation occurs frequently in the study of singularities as we shall see in Chapter 18. Assume that we are given an even lattice $L = U \oplus L ^ { \prime }$ and we let $\{ e , f \}$ be the standard basis of $U$ . Then for all $y \in L ^ { \prime }$ one has Eichler-Siegel transformations $\psi _ { e , y }$ as well as $\psi _ { f , y }$ . The group generated by those transformations will be denoted by

$$
\psi _ { U } ( L ^ { \prime } ) = \langle \psi _ { e , y } , \psi _ { f , y } \rangle _ { y \in L ^ { \prime } } \subset { \ O } ( L ) .
$$

As indicated by the notation, this group does not depend on the choice of basis for $U$ (see Example 17.1.2.2). The following result shows how one can use Eichler-Siegel transformations to describe certain orbits under the isometry group.

Lemma 17.3.9 ([144, Lemma 2.5]). Let $U$ be a hyperbolic plane with standard basis $\{ e , f \}$ . Consider the lattice $U \odot U ^ { \prime }$ where $U ^ { \prime }$ is another hyperbolic plane. Then $\psi _ { U } U ^ { \prime } = \psi _ { U ^ { \prime } } U \simeq \mathrm { S L } _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { Z } ) \times \mathrm { S L } _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { Z } )$ . Moreover, every vector $x$ is in the $\psi _ { U } ( U ^ { \prime } )$ -orbit of some vector of the form $a e + d f$ with $d | a$ . In particular, if $x$ is primitive with $q ( x ) = a$ , we can take $d = 1$ .

Proof. Let $\{ e ^ { \prime } , f ^ { \prime } \}$ be a standard basis for $U ^ { \prime }$ , then

$$
a e + d f + b e ^ { \prime } + c f ^ { \prime } \mapsto { \left( \begin{array} { l l } { a } & { b } \\ { - c } & { d } \end{array} \right) }
$$

defines an isometry between $U { \textcircled { \perp } } U ^ { \prime }$ and $( \mathsf { M a t } ( 2 { \times } 2 , \mathbb { Z } ) , \mathrm { d e t } )$ . Under this isometry the transformations $\psi _ { e , \pm e ^ { \prime } } , \psi _ { e , \pm f ^ { \prime } } , \psi _ { f , \pm e ^ { \prime } }$ , $\psi _ { f , \pm f ^ { \prime } }$ correspond to row and column additions and subtractions.  Since $\operatorname { S L _ { 2 } } ( \mathbb { Z } )$ is generated by the corresponding elementary matrices, this shows in particular that $\psi _ { U } U ^ { \prime } = \psi _ { U ^ { \prime } } U \simeq \mathrm { S L } _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { Z } ) \times \mathrm { S L } _ { 2 } ( \mathbb { Z } )$ the first copy acting from the left on $2 \times 2$ integral matrices, and the second copy acting from the right. Using these elementary transformations, a given matrix $M \in$ $\mathsf { M a t } ( 2 \times 2 , \mathbb { Z } )$ can be put in diagonal form $\mathrm { d i a g } ( a , d )$ with $d | a$ (use the elementary divisor theorem A.1.2 applied to the submodule of $\mathbb { Z } ^ { 2 }$ generated by the column vectors ${ \binom { a } { - c } } \ \mathrm { a n d } \ { \binom { b } { d } } )$ .In ters primiiveveor $x \in U \mathbb { \textcircled { 1 } } U ^ { \prime }$ this means that we can either take $x = f$ or $x = a e + f$ .

Corollary 17.3.10. Suppose $L = U \oplus L ^ { \prime }$ , with $L ^ { \prime } = U ^ { \prime } \oplus L ^ { \prime \prime }$ , $L ^ { \prime \prime }$ even, and let $x \in L$ . Then

1. there exists an isometry of $L$ belonging to $\psi _ { U } ( U ^ { \prime } )$ which sends $x$ to $\alpha e { + } \beta f { + } x ^ { \prime \prime }$ with $\beta | \alpha$ and $x ^ { \prime \prime } \in L ^ { \prime \prime }$ ;

2. if, moreover, $b ( x , L ) = \mathbb { Z }$ , there is an isometry belonging to $\psi _ { U } ( L ^ { \prime } )$ sending $x$ to $a e + f$ , $a = q ( x )$ .

Proof. Assume $x = x ^ { \prime } + x ^ { \prime \prime }$ with $x ^ { \prime } \in U \circledast U ^ { \prime }$ and $x ^ { \prime \prime } \in L ^ { \prime \prime }$ .

1. This follows by applying Lemma 17.3.9 to $x ^ { \prime }$ . We thus may assume that $x ^ { \prime } = \alpha e + \beta f \in U$ , where the integer $\beta$ divides the integer $\alpha$ . This implies

$$
b ( x , u ) \equiv 0 \bmod \beta , \quad \forall u \in U .
$$

2. Suppose that $y \in L$ satisfies $b ( x , y ) = 1$ and write $y = u + y ^ { \prime }$ , $u \in U , y ^ { \prime } \in L ^ { \prime }$ , and apply $\psi = \psi _ { e , y ^ { \prime } }$ to $x$ . Then we have $\psi ( e ) = e$ and $\psi ( f ) = f - y ^ { \prime } - q ( y ^ { \prime } ) e$ . Since $\psi ^ { - 1 } = \psi _ { e , - y ^ { \prime } }$ we find $\psi ^ { - 1 } ( f ) = f + y ^ { \prime } - q ( y ^ { \prime } ) e$ and so, writing $\psi ( x ) = a ^ { \prime } e + b ^ { \prime } f + z$ , $z \in L ^ { \prime }$ , one finds

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { b ^ { \prime } = b ( \psi x , e ) = b ( \psi x , \psi e ) = b ( x , e ) = \beta } \\ & { a ^ { \prime } = b ( \psi x , f ) = b ( x , \psi ^ { - 1 } f ) = b ( x , f + y ^ { \prime } - q ( y ^ { \prime } ) e ) = \alpha + b ( x , y ^ { \prime } ) - q ( y ^ { \prime } ) \beta } \\ & { \quad \equiv b ( x , y ^ { \prime } ) \bmod \beta \mathrm { ~ s i n c e ~ } \beta | \alpha } \\ & { \quad \equiv b ( x , u + y ^ { \prime } ) \bmod \beta \mathrm { ~ b y ~ } ( 1 7 . 8 ) } \\ & { \quad \equiv b ( x , y ) \bmod \beta } \\ & { \quad \equiv 1 \mathrm { ~ m o d ~ } \beta \mathrm { ~ b y ~ t h e ~ a s s u m p t i o n ~ o n ~ } y . } \end{array}
$$

It follows that $a ^ { \prime } e + b ^ { \prime } f \in U$ is primitive and so, again by Lemma 17.3.9, we may assume that $b ^ { \prime } = 1$ , that is, the $\psi _ { U } L ^ { \prime }$ -orbit of $x$ contains a vector of the form $a ^ { \prime } e + f + z ^ { \prime }$ . Applying $\psi _ { e , z ^ { \prime } }$ to this vector yields a vector of the form $\tilde { x } = a \ e + f$ with $a = q ( { \tilde { x } } ) = q ( x )$ .

In Section 18.1 we shall use some more properties of lattices that split off a hyperbolic plane:

Lemma 17.3.11. Let $L$ be an even lattice. Suppose that $L = U \mathbb { \textcircled { 1 } L ^ { \prime } }$ and let $\{ e , f \}$ be a standard basis for $U$ . Then

1. The group $\mathsf { O } ( U )$ normalizes $\psi _ { U } ( L ^ { \prime } )$ .

2. Suppose that $r \in L ^ { \prime }$ is $a$ (-2)-root. Then

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \psi _ { e , r } = \sigma _ { r ^ { \circ } } \sigma _ { r + e } } \\ & { \sigma _ { r } = \psi _ { f , r ^ { \circ } } \psi _ { e , - r ^ { \circ } } \psi _ { f , r ^ { \circ } } \sigma _ { e - f } } \end{array}
$$

3. Suppose that $L ^ { \prime }$ is a lattice generated by $\left( - 2 \right)$ -roots. Then $\psi _ { U } ( L ^ { \prime } ) \subset \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L )$ .

Proof. 1. By Example 17.1.2 we only have to consider the effect of the reflection $\sigma _ { e - f }$ interchanging $e$ and $f$ . For $y \in L ^ { \prime }$ one finds $\sigma _ { e - f } \circ \psi _ { e , y } \circ \sigma _ { e - f } = \psi _ { f , y }$ and likewise $\sigma _ { e - f } \circ \psi _ { f , y } \circ \sigma _ { e - f } = \psi _ { e , y }$ .

2. By Lemma 17.3.3.3 we have $\psi _ { e , r } = \psi _ { e , r + e }$ which by Proposition 17.3.6.1 equals $\sigma _ { e - ( r + e ) ^ { \circ } } \sigma _ { r + e } = \sigma _ { - r ^ { \circ } } \sigma _ { r + e }$ .

Historical and Bibliographical Notes. Isometries in hyperbolic spaces and for Lorentzian lattices have been studied by many people, especially by $\acute { \mathrm { E } }$ Vinberg [237, 238, 239, 240] and by V. Nikulin [170, 172]. Reflection subgroups of lattices with higher Witt index have been investigated by M. Kneser [121]. M. Eichler remarks in Kap. V.1. of [67] that his transformations $\psi _ { f , y }$ that we introduced in Section 17.3 were for the first time used by C.-L. Siegel, whence the terminology "Eichler-Siegel transformation". The present treatment is heavily influenced by W. Ebeling's book [62] and the articles [60, 61].

# Applications to Singularities

# Introduction

In this chapter we consider quadratic lattices $( L , q )$ generated by roots $r$ with $q ( r ) = - 1$ . If a spanning set $\Delta$ of roots can be found which forms a single orbit under the Weyl group ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( \Delta )$ , we speak of a vanishing lattice. As we shall see in Section 18.2, these occur in the study of monodromy of singularities and of families of hypersurfaces in projective space.

The goal of Section 18.1 is twofold. First we describe tools to recognize vanishing lattices. The second goal is to see when the Weyl group is as large as possible, that is, equal to $\scriptstyle { 0 ^ { - , \# } ( L ) }$ . The idea is first to show that $\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Delta ) = \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L )$ and then to apply M. Kneser's result, Theorem 17.2.11.

In practice $L$ is often the lattice associated to a generalized Dynkin diagram $\Gamma$ . However, in general the roots corresponding to the vertices of $\Gamma$ do not define a vanishing lattice. Theorem 18.1.7 provides a large class of Dynkin diagrams that do not suffer from this defect. As demonstrated in Section 18.2, these can be used to determine the monodromy group of many singularities.

However, in applications we need more, namely a class of vanishing lattices which in a certain sense is stable under inclusions, the so-called complete vanishing lattices (cf. Definition 18.1.4). Many lattices associated to Dynkin diagrams yield complete vanishing lattices and so for those not only $\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L ) = \mathsf { O } ^ { - , \# } ( L )$ , but this equality persists under inclusion into larger vanishing lattices. This is used in Section 18.3 to determine global monodromy groups (cf. Theorem 18.3.2) .

# 18.1 Generalized Dynkin Diagrams and Vanishing Lattices

In this section $( L , q )$ is a quadratic integral lattice with polarization $^ { b }$ . By "root" we shall mean " $\left( - 2 \right)$ -root" and accordingly we set $\epsilon = -$ . With appropriate changes all results are valid for 2-roots and $\epsilon = +$ . The set of roots in $L$ is denoted $\Delta ( L )$ , the lattice generated by these $L _ { \mathrm { r o o t } }$ , and the Weyl group ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( L )$ .

The lattices we consider in this chapter are spanned by roots which form the nodes of a graph. If $r , r ^ { \prime }$ are such roots and $b ( \boldsymbol { r } , \boldsymbol { r } ^ { \prime } ) = 1$ , as usual, we connect the corresponding nodes by an unlabelled edge. In the lattices also pairs $\{ r , r ^ { \prime } \}$ occur for which $b ( r , r ^ { \prime } ) = - 2$ . We connect the corresponding nodes by a doubly dashed edge. The resulting graphs $\Gamma$ are called (generalized) Dynkin diagrams and the corresponding even integral lattice $L _ { \Gamma }$ they give rise to the associated rootlattice. Identifying the vertices of $\Gamma$ with roots in $L _ { \Gamma }$ , the Weyl group ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( { \Gamma } )$ of $\Gamma$ is the group generated by the reflections determined by $\Gamma$ .

Let $\Delta \subset L _ { \Gamma }$ be a set of roots. A 1-connected path within $\Delta$ from $r \in \Delta$ to $r ^ { \prime } \in \Delta$ is a chain $r = r _ { 0 } , r _ { 1 } , \dots , r _ { N } = r ^ { \prime }$ of roots in $\Delta$ such that $b ( r _ { j } , r _ { j + 1 } ) = 1$ , $j = 0 , \ldots , N - 1$ . This defines an equivalence relation on $\Delta$ . The equivalence classes are called the 1-connected components of $\Delta$ . If there is only one component, $\Delta$ is called a 1-connected set. The Dynkin diagrams associated to finite 1-connected sets of roots are connected. Such graphs will be called 1-connected. Similarly, one can speak of the 1-connected components of a Dynkin graph.

We also need a suitable notation to deal with orbits of a possibly infinite set of roots, say $\Lambda \subset L$ . If ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( \Lambda )$ is the group generated by the reflections $\sigma _ { \lambda }$ , $\lambda \in \Lambda$ , we shall denote the orbit of $\Lambda$ by the corresponding bold letter:

$$
\Lambda = \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Lambda ) \Lambda \subset L _ { \mathrm { r o o t } } .
$$

Lemma 18.1.1. Two roots in a 1-connected component of a set of roots $\Delta \subset L = L _ { \Gamma }$ belong to the same ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( \Delta )$ -orbit.

Proof. This follows from the observation that for any two roots $r _ { i }$ , $r _ { j }$ with $b ( r _ { i } , r _ { j } )$ $= 1$ , one has $\sigma _ { r _ { i } } \circ \sigma _ { r _ { j } } r _ { i } = \sigma _ { r _ { i } } ( r _ { i } + r _ { j } ) = r _ { j }$ .

As announced, the specific root lattices coming from singularities are the vanishing lattices, ordered under containment:

Definition 18.1.2. 1. A vanishing lattice consists of a pair $( L , \Delta )$ of a lattice $L$ and a set of roots $\Delta$ spanning $L$ and forming a single orbit under $W ^ { - } ( \Delta ) =$ $\langle \sigma _ { r } \rangle _ { r \in \Delta }$ , that is $\Delta = \Delta$ .

2. A vanishing lattice $( L , \Delta )$ contains the vanishing lattice $( L ^ { \prime } , \Delta ^ { \prime } )$ if $L ^ { \prime }$ is a primitive sublattice of $L$ and $\Delta ^ { \prime } \subset \Delta$ .

Remark 18.1.3. The vertices of a generalized Dynkin diagram $\Gamma$ form a finite set of roots, say $\Delta$ , spanning the lattice $L _ { \Gamma } = \mathbb { Z } \cdot \Delta$ . If $\Delta$ is 1-connected, by Lemma 18.1.1 all roots in $\Delta$ are in the same orbit under the reflection group ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( \Delta )$ , but $\Delta$ need not be an entire orbit. Taking $\Delta = \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Delta )$ instead of $\Delta$ then yields a vanishing lattice. In general, if the subset $\Delta$ of roots of $L$ belongs to a single ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( \Delta )$ -orbit, this procedure yields a vanishing lattice. Clearly, this also shows that such a vanishing lattice is determined by the lattice itself.

For a general vanishing lattice $( L , \Delta )$ , the Weyl group ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( L )$ of course contains the subgroup ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( \Delta )$ , but the entire Weyl group of $L$ might be larger. Our goal is to give a large class of vanishing lattices for which $\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Delta ) = \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L )$ . Since in applications we need a class of vanishing lattices which is stable under containment, we shall look within the class of so-called complete vanishing lattices (see below for their definition). The basic building block for such lattices is the pair $( L _ { \mathrm { m i n } } , \Gamma _ { \mathrm { m i n } } )$

with $L _ { \operatorname* { m i n } } : = U \circledast U ^ { \prime } \circledast A _ { 2 } ( - 1 )$ and, using the standard basis $\{ e , f \}$ of $U$ , $\{ e ^ { \prime } , f ^ { \prime } \}$ of $U ^ { \prime }$ , $\{ \omega _ { 1 } , \omega _ { 2 } \}$ of $A _ { 2 } ( - 1 )$ with

$$
{ \bf T } _ { \mathrm { m i n } } = \{ r _ { 1 } = e - f , r _ { 2 } = \omega _ { 1 } - e , r _ { 3 } = \omega _ { 1 } , r _ { 4 } = \omega _ { 2 } , r _ { 5 } = \omega _ { 1 } - e ^ { \prime } , r _ { 6 } = e ^ { \prime } - f ^ { \prime } \} .
$$

There are of course other choices for a spanning set of roots, e.g., we may replace gives thhe graph with $r _ { 2 } ^ { \prime } = - \omega _ { 1 } - \omega _ { 2 } - e - \left( e ^ { \prime } + f ^ { \prime } \right)$ $\Gamma _ { \mathrm { m i n } } ^ { \prime }$ and $r _ { 5 }$ with $r _ { 5 } ^ { \prime } = - \omega _ { 1 } - \omega _ { 2 } - e ^ { \prime } - ( e + f )$ which are connected and since the transition matrix expressing the roots in the basis is unimodular, the roots give a basis of $L _ { \mathrm { m i n } }$ and so this indeed defines vanishing lattices.1

![](images/e13ccd2cf8ede569c4eaf817c02242c14210fc2bef18905190a29dd4ea35aad0.jpg)  
Figure 18.1.1: $\mathbf { { { T } } _ { \operatorname* { m i n } } }$ and $\Gamma _ { \mathrm { m i n } } ^ { \prime }$

Definition 18.1.4. A vanishing lattice $( L , \Delta )$ is called complete if it contains a copy of $( L _ { \mathrm { m i n } } , \Gamma _ { \mathrm { m i n } } )$ .

This concept is obviously preserved under containment of vanishing lattices; since this plays a central role later on, we set this apart.

Lemma 18.1.5. A vanishing lattice containing a complete vanishing lattice is itself complete.

We shall further make use of some technical concepts which play a central role in the proofs that follow:

Definition 18.1.6. A (possibly infinite) subset $\Lambda$ of roots in $L$ is called a special subset of roots of $L$ if it contains three roots $r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } , r _ { 3 }$ , by definition a socle of $\Lambda$ , which have the following two properties:

1. The intersection behaviour of roots in the socle and with other roots $r \in \Lambda$ is as in the following graph:

![](images/8efac71491350b32349c96ce8640d61d191c7346b7bb81725fec158edf8c8997.jpg)

In other words, $b ( r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } ) = 1$ , $b ( r _ { 2 } , r _ { 3 } ) = - 2$ , $b ( r _ { 1 } , r ) = 0$ for $r \neq r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 }$ and, finally, $b ( r , r _ { 2 } ) = b ( r , r _ { 3 } )$ for $r \neq r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } , r _ { 3 }$ . In particular it follows that $r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } , r _ { 3 }$ are independent (consider the Gram matrix).

2. The set $\Lambda ^ { \prime } = \Lambda - \{ r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } \}$ is 1-connected.

We make some observations and introduce related terminology.

$\bullet$ If the set $\Lambda$ contains at least 4 elements, it is 1-connected since then there exists $r \in \Lambda ^ { \prime }$ , $r \not = r _ { 3 }$ for which $b ( r _ { 3 } , r ) = 1$ and thus $b ( r _ { 2 } , r ) = 1$ . The hyperbolic plane with standard basis $e = - r _ { 2 } + r _ { 3 }$ , $f = - r _ { 1 } - r _ { 2 } + r _ { 3 }$ is called the socle plane, and the resulting decomposition $L = U \oplus L ^ { \prime }$ the socle decomposition. The lattice generated by $\Lambda ^ { \prime }$ belongs to $L ^ { \prime }$ as is easily verified.

The usefulness of these concepts and remarks is illustrated by the next result. Its formulation uses Eichler-Siegel transformations defined in Section 17.3, and the proof makes essential use of the results of $\ S$ 17.3.C.

Theorem 18.1.7 ([60, Thm 3]). Let $( L , q )$ be a quadratic lattice of rank at least 4 containing a special subset Λ of roots which span $L$ . Then $( L , \pmb { \Lambda } )$ is a vanishing lattice. If, moreover, $L$ splits off an extra hyperbolic plane besides the socle plane, then $\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L ) = \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Lambda )$ . More precisely, we have:

1. Let $U$ be the socle plane and $L = U \mathbb { \textcircled { 1 } L ^ { \prime } }$ the corresponding socle decomposition. Then $L ^ { \prime }$ is spanned by $\Lambda ^ { \prime } = \Lambda - \{ r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } \}$ . • Conversely, let $L$ be a quadratic lattice of rank at least 4 with a decomposition $L = U \oplus L ^ { \prime }$ , where $L ^ { \prime }$ is spanned by a 1-connected set of roots $\Lambda ^ { \prime }$ . Let $\{ e , f \}$ be the standard basis of $U$ and $r _ { 3 } \in \Lambda ^ { \prime }$ . Then the set of roots $r _ { 1 } = e - f , r _ { 2 } = - e + r _ { 3 } , r _ { 3 } , r \in \Lambda ^ { \prime }$ forms a special subset of roots.

2. With $\Lambda ^ { \prime }$ as in $\mathit { 1 }$ , the roots $r ^ { \prime } \in \Lambda ^ { \prime }$ belong to the same $\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L ^ { \prime } )$ -orbit.

3. $\psi _ { U } L ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Lambda )$

4. If, moreover, $L ^ { \prime } = U ^ { \prime } \oplus L ^ { \prime \prime }$ for some hyperbolic plane $U ^ { \prime }$ , then $W ^ { - } ( \Lambda ) \ =$ ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( L )$ . In other words, the Weyl group of $L$ is generated by the reflections $\sigma _ { r }$ , where the roots $r$ belong to $\Lambda$ .

Proof. We already observed that we get a vanishing lattice if $\Lambda$ has at least 4 elements, since then $\Lambda$ is 1-connected (cf. Definition 18.1.6 and use Remark 18.1.3). 1. Since $\Lambda$ spans $L$ , $L ^ { \prime }$ is spanned by $\Lambda ^ { \prime }$ . Conversely, the crucial input is $b ( e , r ) =$ $b ( f , r ) = 0$ for $r \neq r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 }$ so that $b ( r _ { 2 } , r _ { 3 } ) = b ( - e + r _ { 3 } , r _ { 3 } ) = b ( r _ { 3 } , r _ { 3 } ) = - 2$ while $b ( r _ { 2 } , r ) = b ( - e + r _ { 3 } , r ) = b ( r _ { 3 } , r )$ if $r \neq r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } , r _ { 3 }$ .

2. By the assumption on the 1-connectedness, Lemma 18.1.1 shows that all roots $r \neq r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 }$ are in the $G$ -orbit of $r _ { 3 }$ , where $G$ is the group generated by the reflections $\sigma _ { r } , r \neq r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 }$ . This group is contained in $\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L ^ { \prime } )$ .

3. The group $\psi _ { U } L ^ { \prime }$ is generated by $\psi _ { e , r }$ and $\boldsymbol { \psi } _ { f , r }$ where $r$ runs through a generating set of $L ^ { \prime }$ . We take for the latter the set of roots $\Lambda ^ { \prime }$ . By equation (17.9), these isometries are products of the reflections $\sigma _ { r }$ and $\sigma _ { r - e }$ or $\sigma _ { r }$ and $\sigma _ { r - f }$ with $r \in \Lambda ^ { \prime }$ . Let us deduce that the above generators for ${ \psi } _ { U } L ^ { \prime }$ belong to ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( \Lambda )$

Since $r _ { 3 } - e = r _ { 2 }$ , the corresponding reflection is in ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( \Lambda )$ . For $r _ { 3 } - f = r _ { 1 } + r _ { 2 } = \sigma _ { r _ { 1 } } r _ { 2 }$ we have $\sigma _ { r _ { 3 } - f } = \sigma _ { r _ { 1 } } \circ \sigma _ { r _ { 2 } } \circ \sigma _ { r _ { 1 } } \in \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Lambda )$ . •Assume that $r \in \Lambda ^ { \prime }$ . Since $\Lambda ^ { \prime }$ is 1-connected, we may write $r = g ( r _ { 3 } )$ for some $g \in \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Lambda ^ { \prime } )$ . But then

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \sigma _ { r - e } = g \circ \sigma _ { r _ { 3 } - e ^ { \circ } } g ^ { - 1 } \in \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Lambda ) , } \\ & { \sigma _ { r - f } = g \circ \sigma _ { r _ { 3 } - f ^ { \circ } } g ^ { - 1 } \in \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Lambda ) . } \end{array}
$$

4. We first show the inclusion $\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L ) \subset \psi _ { U } L ^ { \prime } \cdot \mathsf { O } ( U )$ . By Corollary 17.3.9 any root $r \in L$ can be moved to a root in $L ^ { \prime } = U ^ { \prime } \oplus L ^ { \prime \prime }$ by an Eichler-Siegel transformation $\psi \in \psi _ { U ^ { \prime } } U = \psi _ { U } U ^ { \prime } \subset \psi _ { U } L ^ { \prime }$ . Applying (17.10) it follows that $\sigma _ { \psi ( r ) } = \psi ^ { \prime } \circ u$ with $\psi ^ { \prime } \in \psi _ { U } L ^ { \prime }$ and $u \in \mathsf { O } ( U )$ . By Lemma 17.3.11.1 we find some $\psi ^ { \prime \prime } \in \psi _ { U } L ^ { \prime }$ such that

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \sigma _ { r } = \psi ^ { - 1 } \circ \sigma _ { \psi ( r ) } \circ \psi } \\ & { \quad = \psi ^ { - 1 } \circ \psi ^ { \prime } \circ u \circ \psi } \\ & { \quad = \psi ^ { - 1 } \circ \psi ^ { \prime } \circ \psi ^ { \prime \prime } \circ u , } \end{array}
$$

and hence $\sigma _ { r } \in \psi _ { U } L ^ { \prime } \cdot \mathsf { O } ( U )$ .

Next, since $\ N \mathrm { m } _ { \mathrm { s p i n } } ^ { \epsilon } \psi = \operatorname* { d e t } \psi = 1$ for all $\psi \in \psi _ { U } L ^ { \prime }$ and since by Example 17.1.2 the only isometry in $\mathrm { O } ( U )$ with the same invariants is the identity, we conclude

$$
\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L ) \cap \mathsf { S O } ( L ) \subset \psi _ { U } L ^ { \prime } \subset \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Lambda ) ,
$$

where the rightmost inclusion is assertion 3. If $\sigma \in \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L )$ , equation (18.1) implies that $\sigma \circ \tau \in \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Lambda )$ for all $\tau \in \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Lambda )$ and hence $\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L ) \subset \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Lambda )$ so that these two sets coincide.

If there exists a special subset of roots $\Lambda$ spanning the lattice $L$ then, by Remark 18.1.3, $( L , \pmb { \Lambda } )$ is a vanishing lattice. Now Theorem 18.1.7 comes into play. It states that, if, besides the socle plane, $L$ splits off a second hyperbolic plane, ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( \Lambda )$ is the full Weyl group of the lattice. Let us give an important class of examples which illustrate this and serve to motivate the theorem.

l 8. $T _ { p , q , r } ^ { 1 }$ depicted in Figure 18.1.2. The vertices define a special subset of roots. We shall show that this defines a complete vanishing lattice.

![](images/b90d84de1af3c5a97581be81f68347da7e93a527768a0e15a311d6a8dd2451ff.jpg)  
Figure 18.1.2: Vanishing lattice given by $T _ { p , q , r } ^ { 1 } , p \geq 2 , q \geq 3 , r \geq 7$ .

The graph is 1-connected and defines a vanishing lattice by Remark 18.1.3. The vertices of the graph form a special set of roots with socle $\{ r _ { 1 } , r _ { 2 } , r \}$ . The three legs have lengths $p , q , r$ , respectively. The corresponding quadratic lattice will be denoted by the same symbol. One verifies that

$$
T _ { p , q , r } ^ { 1 } \simeq \widetilde { T } _ { p , q , r } \oplus U ,
$$

where $U$ is the socle plane, i.e., the hyperbolic plane with basis $e ~ = ~ - r _ { 2 } + r$ , $f = - r _ { 1 } - r _ { 2 } + r$ , and $\widetilde { T } _ { p , q , r }$ is the Coxeter diagram depicted in Section 4.1. If $p \geq 2 , q \geq 3 , r \geq 7$ , the diagram of $\ddot { E } _ { 8 }$ is a subgraph of $T _ { p , q , r }$ and a proof similar to the proof of Lemma 4.1.5 shows then that $\widetilde { T } _ { p , q , r } \simeq \widetilde { T } _ { p , q , 4 } \oplus U \oplus A _ { r - 6 } ( - 1 )$ . Since $\widetilde { T } _ { p , q , r }$ $\widetilde { T } _ { p , q , 4 }$ cotains $A _ { 2 } ( - 1 )$ and so $T _ { p , q , r } ^ { 1 }$ contains $L _ { \mathrm { m i n } } = U \oplus U \oplus A _ { 2 } ( - 1 )$ by lattice. Its reflection group is maximal as follows from Theorem 18.1.7, but we shall prove shortly (cf. Theorem 18.1.9) that this also follows from completeness of the vanishing lattice.

We shall show now that the class of complete vanishing lattices has indeed the merit of having maximally possible Weyl groups:

Theorem 18.1.9 ([63, Thm. 5.3.4]). Let $( L , \Delta )$ be a complete vanishing lattice.   
Then $\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( \Delta ) = \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L ) = \mathsf { O } ^ { - , \# } ( L )$ .

Proof. The equality $\mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( L ) \ = \ 0 ^ { - , \# } ( L )$ is a consequence of M. Kneser's result, Corollary 17.2.12, since $L$ contains $L _ { 2 } = U \oplus U ^ { \prime } \oplus A _ { 2 } ( - 1 )$ which has rank 6 and discriminant 3, and $L _ { 1 } = U \oplus U ^ { \prime } \oplus A _ { 1 } ( - 1 )$ which has rank 5 and discriminant $- 2$ .

For the leftmost equality we maneuver us in the situation of Theorem 18.1.7 and search for a special set of roots which generate the lattice. We break up the proof in the following steps.

Connectedness: The graph of $\Delta$ is 1-connected. We postpone the proof, cf.   
Lemma 18.1.10 below.

Characterizing ${ \mathsf { W } } ^ { - } ( \Delta )$ : The Weyl group of $\Delta$ is the group $G$ generated by the reflections in the roots from $\Delta$ having distance $\leq 1$ to $r _ { 3 }$ , that is, the following set of roots

$$
\Delta _ { 0 } = \{ r \in \Delta \mid r = r _ { 3 } \mathrm { o r } b ( r , r _ { 3 } ) = 1 \} .
$$

Moreover, the latter set generates $L$ . Here $r _ { 3 } \in \Lambda _ { \operatorname* { m i n } }$ is as in Figure 18.1.1, a root orthogonal to the sum $U \odot U ^ { \prime }$ of the hyperbolic planes spanned by $\{ e , f , e ^ { \prime } , f ^ { \prime } \}$ .

To show the claim, first notice that by Lemma 18.1.10 we can connect $r \in \Delta$ to $r _ { 3 }$ by a chain $r _ { 3 } , \ldots , r _ { k } = r )$ of minimal length $k - 2$ . Next, we show by induction on the minimal length that $r$ is in the $G$ -orbit of $r _ { 3 }$ . We may assume that $k > 2$ . By the induction hypothesis, there exists $g \in G$ such that $g ( r _ { k - 1 } ) = r _ { 3 }$ and since $b ( r _ { 3 } , g ( r ) ) = b ( g ( r _ { k - 1 } ) , g ( r ) ) = b ( r _ { k - 1 } , r = r _ { k } ) = 1$ , we have $g ( r ) \in \Delta _ { 0 }$ . Hence the reflection $\sigma _ { g ( r ) } = g \sigma _ { r } g ^ { - 1 }$ belongs to $G$ . We infer

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { { \boldsymbol r } = \sigma _ { { \boldsymbol r } _ { k - 1 } } \circ \sigma _ { { \boldsymbol r } _ { k } } ( { \boldsymbol r } _ { k - 1 } ) } \\ & { \quad = \sigma _ { { \boldsymbol r } _ { k - 1 } } \circ g ^ { - 1 } \circ ( g \sigma _ { r } g ^ { - 1 } ) ( { \boldsymbol r } _ { 3 } ) \in { \boldsymbol G } \cdot { \boldsymbol r } _ { 3 } . } \end{array}
$$

# 18.2 Application to the Monodromy of Singularities

In this section $( X , x )$ is a germ of an isolated hypersurface singularity of even dimension (− or −1 if n≡2 mod 4   
$n$ . Furthermore, € = + or 1 if n ≡ 0 mod 4.

18.2.A Introduction to isolated hypersurface singularities. We let $z _ { 1 } , \dots$ $z _ { n + 1 }$ be the standard coordinates on $\mathbb { C } ^ { n + 1 }$ and we shall write $\pmb { z } = ( z _ { 1 } , \dots , z _ { n + 1 } )$ for the vector with coordinates z1, ...,Zn+1

We consider germs $( X , x )$ of $n$ -dimensional hypersurfaces with an isolated singularity at $x$ . Such a singularity will be represented by the zero-set of a holomorphic function $f : \mathbb { C } ^ { n + 1 } \to \mathbb { C }$ restricted to a neighborhood of the origin $0 \in \mathbb { C } ^ { n + 1 }$ , where $0$ corresponds to the singularity at $x$ . To ease the presentation we assume that $0$ is the only critical point of $f$ . So, if $t$ is a coordinate on the target space, the level sets $f ^ { - 1 } ( t )$ for $t \neq 0$ are smooth hypersurfaces while $f ^ { - 1 } ( 0 )$ is smooth away from $0$ . The $t$ -disc of radius $r$ punctured at the origin is denoted $\Delta ^ { * } ( r )$ .

The associated Milnor fibration is obtained by restricting $f$ to

$$
\mathcal { M } = \{ | \boldsymbol { z } | ^ { 2 } < \eta \} \cap f ^ { - 1 } [ \Delta ^ { * } ( r ) ] ,
$$

where $\eta$ and $r$ are sufficiently small so that $f : \mathcal { M }  \Delta ^ { * } ( r )$ is a locally trivial fibration. Its typical fiber, $M _ { * }$ , is the so-called Milnor fiber associated to the singularity. We think of the lower index $^ *$ as the "general point" of the punctured disk $\Delta ^ { * } ( r )$ . The Milnor fiber has the homotopy type of a bouquet of $\mu$ (real) spheres of dimension $n$ , where $\mu$ is the Milnor number and hence $H _ { n } ( M _ { * } , \mathbb { Z } )$ is a free $\mathbb { Z }$ -module of rank $\mu$ . The orientation induced by the complex structure defines the intersection pairing

$$
H _ { n } ( M _ { * } , \mathbb { Z } ) \times H _ { n } ( M _ { * } , \mathbb { Z } ) \to \mathbb { Z } ,
$$

which is symmetric and bilinear, but not necessarily non-degenerate. We denote this pairing with a dot. The resulting lattice

$$
\Lambda _ { X , x } = ( H _ { n } ( M _ { * } , \mathbb { Z } ) , \cdot )
$$

is called the Milnor lattice of $( X , x )$ . It comes equipped with the action of the monodromy operator $T _ { X , x }$ which is induced by moving the Milnor fiber of $f$ once about the origin in anti-clockwise direction.

Examples 18.2.1. 1. The function $f ( z ) = z _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + z _ { n + 1 } ^ { 2 }$ has a single critical point at the origin. The corresponding singularity is an ordinary double point. If $t \neq 0$ , the fiber $f ^ { - 1 } ( t )$ is the smooth hypersurface $\begin{array} { r } { \sum _ { j } z _ { j } ^ { 2 } = t } \end{array}$ . The Milnor number is 1 since $H _ { n } ( M _ { * } , \mathbb { Z } ) = \mathbb { Z }$ is generated by a so-called vanishing cycle $\delta$ given by $\{ x _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + x _ { n + 1 } ^ { 2 } = t _ { * } \} \cap \{ | z | ^ { 2 } < \eta \}$ wwhere $z _ { j } = x _ { j } + i y _ { j }$ , $j = 1 , \ldots , n + 1$ ,and $t _ { * }$ is the $t$ -coordinate of the point $^ *$ . It is well known (cf. e.g. [134, §6]) that $\delta \cdot \delta = 2 \epsilon$ and that the monodromy operator $T _ { X , x }$ is the reflection $s _ { \delta }$ , corresponding to $\delta$ .

2. More generally, consider the du Val singularities of Table 4.5.1. The minimal resolution of these singularities is a connected chain of rational curves of selfintersection $- 2$ whose dual graph is one of the Dynkin diagrams $A _ { k } , D _ { k }$ , $E _ { 6 } , E _ { 7 } , E _ { 8 }$ . The construction on page 102 shows that a tubular neighborhood of such a chain is a disc bundle over a wedge of 2-spheres, and from this it follows that the Milnor fibre has the same homotopy type as the latter wedge of 2-spheres. Du Val-type singularities occur in any dimension and are denoted by the same symbols as for dimension 2. Their Milnor lattices are given in Table 18.2.1. The Milnor number for $A _ { k } , D _ { k }$ and $E _ { k }$ equals $k$ .

18.2.B Deforming hypersurface singularities. For a proper treatment of this topic see e.g. [142, Ch. 8], [5, Ch. 1]. The basic concept is that of a semiuniversal unfolding of the isolated singularity $( X , x )$ . Roughly speaking a semiuniversal unfolding or miniversal deformation of $( X , x )$ is a family of hypersurfaces $\{ X _ { u } \} _ { u \in U }$ , where the base manifold $U$ is a ball centered at $0$ with $X _ { 0 } \simeq X$ and which "contains" all deformations of $( X , x )$ . More precisely, every deformation $\{ X _ { t } \} _ { t \in T }$ of $( X , x )$ is the pull-back of a semi-universal unfolding by a holomorphic map $\phi : T  U$ which is "infinitesimally unique at $0 ^ { \dag }$ in the sense that the derivative of $\phi$ at $0$ is uniquely determined by the family $\{ X _ { t } \}$ . It is well known that there exists a semi-universal unfolding of the shape

$$
F ( \pmb { z } , u _ { 0 } , \ldots , u _ { \tau - 1 } ) = f ( \pmb { z } ) + u _ { 0 } + u _ { 1 } \pmb { z } ^ { B _ { 1 } } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + u _ { \tau - 1 } \pmb { z } ^ { B _ { \tau - 1 } } .
$$

The multi-index notation we use means this: if $B _ { j } = ( b _ { 1 , j } , \dotsc , b _ { n + 1 , j } )$ , one sets

$$
z ^ { B _ { j } } = z _ { 1 } ^ { b _ { 1 , j } } \cdot \cdot \cdot z _ { n + 1 } ^ { b _ { n + 1 , j } } .
$$

The exponents $B _ { j }$ are chosen so that $\{ 1 , z ^ { B _ { 1 } } , \ldots , z ^ { B _ { \tau - 1 } } \}$ is a basis for the algebra $J _ { X , x } / \bar { f }$ , where

$$
J _ { X , x } = \mathbb { C } \big [ [ z ] \big ] / ( \partial f / \partial z _ { 1 } , \ldots , \partial f / \partial z _ { n + 1 } )
$$

is the jacobian algebra and $f \in J _ { X , x }$ is the class of $f$ in the jacobian algebra. Write $\pmb { u } = ( u _ { 1 } , \dots , u _ { \tau - 1 } )$ . The number $\tau$ is the Tjurina number of the singularity. Then the function

$$
F : \mathbb { C } ^ { n + 1 + \tau }  \mathbb { C } ^ { \tau } , \quad ( z , u _ { 0 } , \pmb { u } )  ( F ( z , u _ { 0 } , \pmb { u } ) , \pmb { u } )
$$

restricted to a suitable small neighbourhood $V$ of $0$ is a semi-universal unfolding of $f$ . The critical points of $\pmb { F }$ by definition make up the discriminant locus $\mathrm { D } _ { \mathbf { F } }$ of $\mathbf { F }$ , a hypersurface in $U$ . If $U$ is small enough, the fibers over $\mathrm { D } _ { \mathbf { F } }$ have isolated singularities only and the locus of a given isomorphism type of singularity $( Y , y )$ forms a locally closed subvariety of the discriminant locus. If $( X , x )$ is a singularity in its closure we say that $( Y , y )$ is adjacent to $( X , x )$ . Such a singularity can be viewed as less complicated than $( X , x )$ . The ordinary double point singularities, making up an open dense stratum of the discriminant, give the simplest type of singularity while the stratum $S _ { \mu }$ parametrizes the most complex ones, those with Milnor number $\mu$ . Although the singularities with fixed Milnor number are topologically the same, this need not be the case in the biholomorphic category. To see this, observe that the group of germs of biholomorphic automorphisms of $( X , x )$ acts on $S _ { \mu }$ , and while the points in the orbit of $0$ (corresponding to $( X , x )$ ) are all isomorphic, those in a slice transversal to this orbit are not. The dimension $m$ of such a slice gives the number of moduli of $( X , x )$ and we say that $( X , x )$ is an m-modal singularity. If $m = 1$ we speak of a unimodal singularity.

Examples .1 $z _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + z _ { n + 1 } ^ { 2 } = 0$ of Exaple 18.2.1 has the funcio $z _ { 1 } ^ { 2 } + \dots + z _ { n + 1 } ^ { 2 } - t$ $\tau = \mu = 1$ . The discriminant locus is the origin and the modality is $0$ .

2. The other Du Val singularities have $\mu = \tau$ as well and the modality is $0$ . For instance, for $E _ { 6 }$ the jacobian ring has a basis $\{ 1 , z _ { 2 } , z _ { 3 } , z _ { 3 } ^ { 2 } , z _ { 2 } z _ { 3 } , z _ { 2 } z _ { 3 } ^ { 2 } \}$ consisting of

6 elements and it also contains the defining polynomial.

3. The hyperbolic singularities $T _ { p , q , r }$ . In dimension 2 these singularities are given by:

$$
f = 0 , \quad f = x ^ { p } + y ^ { q } + z ^ { r } + a x y z , \quad a \in \mathbb { C } ^ { \times } , \quad { \frac { 1 } { p } } + { \frac { 1 } { q } } + { \frac { 1 } { r } } < 1 .
$$

With $J _ { f }$ the jacobian ideal, we see that the vector space $\mathbb { C } [ \left\lfloor x , y , z \right\rfloor ] / ( J _ { f } , f )$ is generated by 1 together with the monomials $x ^ { k }$ , $k = 1 , \ldots , p - 1$ , $y ^ { \ell }$ , $\ell = 1 , \ldots , q - 1$ , $z ^ { m }$ , $m = 1 , \ldots , r - 1$ , and so $\tau ( f ) = p + q + r - 2$ . Because of the relation

$$
p ^ { - 1 } x f _ { x } + q ^ { - 1 } y f _ { y } + r ^ { - 1 } z f _ { z } - f = ( p ^ { - 1 } + q ^ { - 1 } + r ^ { - 1 } - 1 ) a x y z ,
$$

we find $\mu = p + q + r - 2$ . For all non-zero $a$ the singularities have the same Milnor number. It turns out (see [5, Ch. I.2.3]) that the isomorphism class of the singularity varies with $a$ , and so it is a unimodal singularity.

4. Milnor lattices can have a non-zero null-space. The simplest are the so-called parabolic singularities. These are also unimodal, again by [5, Ch. I.2.3].

18.2.C Monodromy. Let the base $U \subset \mathbb { C } ^ { \tau }$ of a semi-universal unfolding $\mathbf { F }$ of the singularity $( X , x )$ be a small enough ball about 0 such that $F ^ { - 1 } U \subset V$ away from the discriminant locus $\mathrm { D } _ { \mathbf { F } }$ gives a locally trivial differentiable fiber bundle

$$
\begin{array} { r } { { \cal F } ^ { - 1 } [ U - U \cap \mathsf { D } _ { \bf F } ]  U - U \cap \mathsf { D } _ { \bf F } , } \end{array}
$$

and such that the fiber $\boldsymbol { F } _ { * , 0 }$ of $\pmb { F }$ passing through the point $( * , 0 )$ intersected with the ball $| z | < \eta$ is the Milnor fiber $M _ { * }$ of $( X , x )$ . By definition $H _ { n } ( M _ { * } , \mathbb { Z } ) = \Lambda _ { X , x }$ is free of rank $\mu$ . It is generated by vanishing cycles as follows. A general line $\ell$ intersects the discriminant hypersurface $\mathrm { D } _ { \mathbf { F } }$ transversally. It turns out that $\ell \cap$ $U \cap \mathsf { D } _ { \mathbf { F } }$ consists of precisely $\mu$ points, say $t _ { 1 } , \ldots , t _ { \mu }$ , and the fiber of $\pmb { F }$ over each of these points has exactly one ordinary double point, say $s _ { j }$ , and no other singular points. In Example 18.2.1 we found a vanishing cycle $\delta _ { j } ^ { \prime }$ in the fibre near $s _ { j }$ . We want to transport it to $( * , 0 ) \in U$ along a well-chosen path.

To this end we introduce a distinguished set of generators of the fundamental group $\pi _ { 1 } ( U - U \cap \mathsf { D } _ { \mathbf { F } } , ( * , 0 ) )$ , namely the loops $\gamma _ { j }$ , $j = 1 , \dotsc , \mu$ , which start at $( * , 0 ) \in U \cap \ell$ , follow the straight line segment $\ell _ { j }$ from $( * , 0 )$ to the first point of intersection with a little circle $\sigma _ { j }$ about $t _ { j }$ , traverse this circle in anti-clockwise direction and then go back to $( * , 0 )$ along $\ell _ { j }$ as in Figure 18.2.1. We assume that the loops are numbered consecutively as in the figure and that any two of them only have $( * , 0 )$ in common. These loops generate the fundamental group of $U \cap \ell - \left\{ t _ { 1 } , \ldots , t _ { \mu } \right\}$ (recall that $U \cap \ell$ is a disc containing all of the points $t _ { j }$ ). The vanishing cycle $\delta _ { j }$ in $H _ { n } ( M _ { * } , \mathbb { Z } )$ for $j = 1 , \dotsc , \mu$ , is obtained by transporting $\delta _ { j } ^ { \prime }$ along the path $\ell _ { j }$ to the fiber over $( * , 0 ) \in U$ . The monodromy representation associated to (an unfolding of) the singularity is by definition the representation of the fundamental group $\pi _ { 1 } ( U - U \cap \mathsf { D } _ { \mathbf { F } } , ( * , 0 ) )$ on $\Lambda _ { X , x } = H _ { n } ( F _ { * , 0 } , \mathbb { Z } )$ with image the monodromy group associated to the singularity, denoted

![](images/e30fe4f3ad767e208a3131e0bfb64b400ff0537bcff9a00e534982f02e10db89.jpg)  
Figure 18.2.1: Generators of the fundamental group

$$
\mathsf { M o n } ( \Lambda _ { X , x } ) \subset { \mathsf { O } } ( \Lambda _ { X , x } ) .
$$

Since by [142, Chap. 7] the inclusion $U \cap \ell \hookrightarrow U$ induces a surjection

$$
\pi _ { 1 } ( U \cap \ell - \{ t _ { 1 } , \ldots , t _ { \mu } \} , ( * , 0 ) ) \twoheadrightarrow \pi ( U - \Delta , ( * , 0 ) ) ,
$$

the action of the monodromy group is completely described by the automorphism $T _ { i }$ on $H _ { n } ( M _ { * } )$ resulting from moving vanishing cycles around the loops $\gamma _ { i }$ , $i = 1 , \ldots , \mu$ . From what we have seen in the case of an ordinary double point, $T _ { i }$ is a reflection in the hyperplane $\delta _ { i } ^ { \bot } \subset H _ { n } ( M _ { * } )$ . One can show that the discriminant locus is a connected hypersurface and then, by the arguments in [134, §7], [142, Chap. 7], it follows that all vanishing cycles are in the same orbit under the reflection group they generate:

Theorem 18.2.3. The set $\Delta _ { X , x } = \{ \delta _ { 1 } , . . . , \delta _ { \mu } \}$ of vanishing cycles is a basis for the Milnor lattice $\Lambda _ { X , x }$ . All of these vanishing cycles are in the same orbit under the action of the monodromy group. In particular $( \Lambda _ { X , x } , \Delta _ { X , x } )$ is a vanishing lattice.

For the actual calculation of vanishing lattices such as for the following examples, we refer to [5, Ch.2] and [63].
