Proof. Let $\ell$ be a generator of the second summand of $N _ { k } = E _ { 8 } ( - 2 ) \textcircled { \scriptsize { \oplus } } \langle 2 k \rangle$ . Its orthogonal complement in $N _ { k }$ as well as and in N is the sublattice $E _ { 8 } ( - 2 )$ which does not contain $- 2$ -roots. Hence $\ell \cdot r \neq 0$ for all roots $r$ in either one of these lattices, i.e., $\ell$ belongs to the interior of some Weyl chamber. So, if $X$ is an $N _ { k }$ marked K3 surface or an $N _ { k } ^ { \prime }$ -marked K3 surface, we can adapt the marking in such a way that $\ell$ is an ample class.

Assume for simplicity that we are in the $N _ { k }$ -marked case. Then, since the period point of $X$ is assumed to be general, we may henceforth assume that ${ \mathsf { N S } } ( X )$ corresponds to $N _ { k }$ . If one defines $\iota = -$ id on the first summand $E _ { 8 } ( - 2 )$ of $N _ { k }$ and $\iota = \mathrm { i d }$ on the orthogonal complement of this summand in $\Lambda _ { \mathsf { K 3 } }$ , it extends to an involution $\iota$ on $\Lambda _ { \mathsf { K 3 } }$ by the extension criterion from Theorem 15.1.7 (use that the discriminant group of $E _ { 8 } ( - 2 )$ is 2-torsion). Let $G$ be the order two group generated by t. Under the marking $\operatorname { T r s } ( X ) \subset \Lambda ^ { G }$ , so that $G$ preserves the Hodge decomposition. Moreover, $G$ preserves the ample class $\ell$ . So by Theorem 19.2.2 the involution $\iota$ is induced by a unique (symplectic) involution on $X$ . By Proposition 20.7.1 this implies that $\iota = \iota _ { \mathsf { N i k } }$ , the lattice Nikulin involution. Hence $D ( N _ { k } ^ { \bot } ) \subset D ( \Lambda ^ { G } )$ .

The above argument is essentially the same for $N _ { k } ^ { \prime }$ .

# 20.8 Shioda-Inose structures

In Corollary 5.2.8 we showed that every Kummer surface $\mathsf { K m } ( A )$ (the minimal resolution of the quotient of a complex 2-torus $A$ by the involution $j$ sending $x \in A$ to $- x$ ) admits a double cover $\widetilde { X }$ with 8 exceptional curves which is the blow-up of a K3_surface $X$ . Moreover, the covering involution $\iota$ on $X$ is a Nikulin involution and $\widetilde { Y } = \mathsf { K m } ( A )$ is the minimal resolution of $X / \iota$ . The resulting diagram

$$
\begin{array} { r l } { \overset { \longleftrightarrow } { \longrightarrow } } & { \underset { \underset { \substack { Y = \sum \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots } } { \longrightarrow } } { \longleftrightarrow } } \\ { Y = X / \iota \prec } & { \underset { \substack { \sum \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots \hdots } } { \longleftrightarrow } } \end{array}
$$

is called a Shioda-Inose structure.8

Next we abstract from this specific situation to the one described in the appendix to this chapter. By (20.20) the manifold $X ^ { \prime } = X - \Sigma$ , $\Sigma$ is the fixed point set of $\iota$ ), is shown to have the same 2-cohomology as $X$ . Since $\pi : X ^ { \prime } \to Y ^ { \prime }$ , $Y ^ { \prime } = Y - \iota ( \Sigma )$ is a topological double covering, the transfer homomorphism $\mathrm { t ^ { * } }$ : $H ^ { 2 } ( X ^ { \prime } )  H ^ { 2 } ( Y ^ { \prime } )$ is well defined. Moreover, the inclusion $X ^ { \prime } \hookrightarrow X$ induces an isomorphism $H ^ { 2 } ( X ) \simeq H ^ { 2 } ( X ^ { \prime } )$ and so the transfer homomorphism extends to $H ^ { 2 } ( X )$ and can be identified with the Gysin homomorphism $\pi _ { ! }$ . By Lemma 20.9.3.1 in the appendix to this chapter one has

$$
\pi ^ { * } \circ \pi _ { ! } ( x ) = x + \iota ^ { * } ( x ) , x \in H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } ) .
$$

Let us consider the following lattice theoretic situation involving the abstract Nikulin lattice $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { N i k } }$ , a rank 8 positive definite even lattice of discriminant $2 ^ { 6 }$ (see $\ S$ 5.2.B). It leads to the left-hand half of the above diagram (20.17), without the condition $\widetilde { Y }$ is a Kummer surface:

Theorem 20.8.1 ([158, Th. 5.7]). Let $( X , \varphi )$ be a marked K3 surface such that $\varphi ^ { - 1 } ( \mathbb { O } ^ { 2 } E _ { 8 } ( - 1 ) )$ embeds into ${ \mathsf { N S } } ( X )$ . Then with the notation as above

1. there is a Nikulin involution t on $X$ with $\pi : { \widetilde { X } } \to { \widetilde { Y } }$ ;

2. there exists a primitive embedding $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { N i k } } \oplus E _ { 8 } ( - 1 ) \hookrightarrow \mathsf { N S } ( \widetilde { Y } )$

3. The Gysin morphism $\pi _ { ! }$ induces an isometry $\operatorname { T r s } ( X ) ( 2 ) { \overset { \simeq } { \to } } \operatorname { T r s } ( { \widetilde { Y } } )$ .

Proof. 1. The lattice Nikulin involution $\iota _ { \mathsf { N i k } }$ on $\Lambda _ { \mathsf { K 3 } }$ (see (20.15)) gives an involution on $H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } )$ as follows. Since $\iota _ { \mathsf { N i k } }$ switches the two copies of $E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ inside $\Lambda _ { \mathsf { K 3 } }$ and is the identity on its orthogonal complement, via the marking this gives an involution $\iota ^ { \prime }$ on the embedded copy of $\mathbb { O } ^ { 2 } E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ . We let $G$ be the group generated by $\iota ^ { \prime }$ . Then the anti-invariant lattice $( H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ) _ { G } = ( H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ^ { G } ) ^ { \bot }$ is isometric to $E _ { 8 } ( - 2 )$ and thus does not contain roots. So $H ^ { 2 } ( X ) _ { G } \cap \mathsf { N S } ( X )$ does not contain roots, that is, condition 3 of Criterion 20.2.1 is fulfilled. Condition 1 holds since $H ^ { 2 } ( X ) _ { G } ~ \subset$ $\mathsf { N S } ( X )$ and so $\operatorname { T r s } ( X ) \subset \mathsf { N S } ( X ) ^ { \bot } \subset H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ^ { \cup }$ . Condition 2 holds since $H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ^ { G }$ has signature $( 3 , 1 1 )$ and therefore intersects the positive cone. It follows that for some $w \in \mathsf { W } ^ { - } ( X )$ , $w \prime w ^ { - 1 }$ is induced by an involution $\iota$ on $X$ which by construction is a Nikulin involution. This shows item 1. Note also that upon replacing the embedding $\varphi ^ { - 1 }$ by $w \circ \varphi ^ { - 1 } : E _ { 8 } ( - 1 ) ^ { \oplus 2 } \hookrightarrow H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } )$ , the induced involution $\iota ^ { * }$ on cohomology acts in a similar way as $\iota ^ { \prime }$ .

2. The Nikulin involution on $X$ has eight isolated fixed points, which on $\widetilde { Y }$ give eight $\left( - 2 \right)$ -curves and the primitive_closure of the span of their classes is a copy of $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { N i k } }$ , the Nikulin lattice, in ${ \mathsf { N S } } ( \widetilde { Y } )$ . The second summand comes from the two copies of $E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ in the K3 lattice under the Gysin morphism $\pi _ { ! } : H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } ) \to$ $H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } , \mathbb { Z } )$ , as we now show. By construction, $\iota ^ { * }$ interchanges the two copies of

$E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ in $H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } )$ . So if $x , x ^ { \prime }$ belong to the same copy, and hence $\iota ^ { * } ( x ) \cdot x ^ { \prime } = 0$ , then

$$
x + \iota ^ { * } ( x ) ) \cdot ( x ^ { \prime } + \iota ^ { * } ( x ^ { \prime } ) ) = x \cdot x ^ { \prime } + \iota ^ { * } x \cdot \iota ^ { * } x ^ { \prime } = 2 x \cdot x ^ { \prime }
$$

If $\tau : { \widetilde { X } } \to X$ is the blowing up in the fixed-point set $\Sigma$ , then $\tau ^ { * } : H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } ) \hookrightarrow$ $H ^ { 2 } ( { \widetilde { X } } , \mathbb { Z } )$ by Lemma B.5.2. So we may identify $x$ and $x ^ { \prime }$ with their counterparts in $H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { X } , \mathbb { Z } )$ . By (20.18) one has

$$
y = x + \iota ( x ) = \pi ^ { * } \pi _ { ! } ( x ) , \quad y ^ { \prime } = x ^ { \prime } + \iota ( x ^ { \prime } ) = \pi ^ { * } \pi _ { ! } ( x ^ { \prime } ) ,
$$

an equality of $G$ -invariant elements. Then Lemma 20.9.3.2 implies

$$
\pi _ { ! } ( \pi ^ { * } \pi _ { ! } x ) \cdot \pi _ { ! } ( \pi ^ { * } \pi _ { ! } x ^ { \prime } ) = \pi _ { ! } y \cdot \pi _ { ! } y ^ { \prime } = 2 y \cdot y ^ { \prime } = 4 x \cdot x ^ { \prime } .
$$

Since $\pi$ has degree 2, $\pi _ { ! } \pi ^ { * }$ is multiplication by 2 and the left-hand side equals $4 \pi _ { ! } x \cdot \pi _ { ! } x ^ { \prime }$ . In other words, $\pi _ { ! }$ is an isometry on each of the two copies of $E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ in $H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } )$ and maps these to the same sublattice of $H ^ { 2 } ( { \widetilde { Y } } , \mathbb { Z } )$ . These map into ${ \mathsf { N S } } ( { \widetilde { Y } } )$ since $\pi _ { ! }$ preserves the Hodge structure (see e.g. [186, Lemma 1.19]). Summarizing, ${ \mathsf { N S } } ( { \widetilde { Y } } )$ contains a copy of $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { N i k } } \oplus E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ . Since the first summand, the Nikulin lattice, is primitively embedded and the second summand is unimodular, their direct sum is also primitively embedded as claimed, finishing the proof of 2.

3. We aim to apply Proposition 20.5.5 in the present situation where

$$
\operatorname { T r s } ( X ) \subset L , \quad L = ( \mathbb { \Phi } ^ { 2 } E _ { 8 } ( - 1 ) ) ^ { \perp } \subset H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } ) ^ { G } .
$$

Then $L \simeq V$ . To be able to apply the proposition, we show first that $\widetilde { \pi } . L$ is a primitive sublattice of $H ^ { 2 } ( { \widetilde { Y } } , \mathbb { Z } )$ . So we introduce

$$
M : = ( \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } L ) ^ { \perp } .
$$

Then $M ^ { \perp }$ is the smallest primitive sublattice of $H ^ { 2 } ( { \widetilde { Y } } , \mathbb { Z } )$ containing $\widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } L$ . We wish to show that $M ^ { \bot } = \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } L$ . By the same argument as before, $\pi _ { ! }$ multiplies the intersection form on the invariant part by 2 and so $\widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } L$ is isometric to $V ( 2 )$ and so has discriminant $2 ^ { 6 }$ . On the other hand, by Lemma 1.2.2 we have

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } & { } & { \mathrm { d i s c } ( \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } L ) = [ M ^ { \perp } : \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } L ] ^ { 2 } \cdot \mathrm { d i s c } ( M ^ { \perp } ) } \\ & { } & { \quad \quad = [ M ^ { \perp } : \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } L ] ^ { 2 } \cdot \mathrm { d i s c } ( M ) . } \end{array}
$$

But $\mathrm { d i s c } ( M ) = \mathrm { d i s c } ( \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } L ) = 2 ^ { 6 }$ and so $M ^ { \perp } = \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } L$ , as asserted. By construction $\mathrm { T r s } ( \widetilde { Y } ) \subset \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } L$ and so we can indeed apply Proposition 20.5.5 and conclude that $\pi _ { ! } : \operatorname { T r s } ( X ) ( 2 ) \ { \overset { \sim } { \to } } \operatorname { T r s } ( { \widetilde { Y } } )$ .

Using the previous result, one can characterize the ShiodaInose structures as follows.

Theorem 20.8.2 ([158, Thm. 6.3]). Let $X$ be a K3 surface. Consider the following properties.

1. X admits a Shioda-Inose structure;

2. there is a complex 2-torus $A$ with $\operatorname { T r s } ( X ) \simeq \operatorname { T r s } ( A )$ ;

3. there is a primitive embedding $\operatorname { T r s } ( X ) \subset { \mathbb { O } } ^ { 3 } U$ ;

4. there is an embedding $\oplus ^ { \cdot 2 } E _ { 8 } ( - 1 ) \subset \mathsf { N S } ( X )$

One has the implications $i \implies \mathcal { Z } \implies \mathcal { Z }$ If, moreover, $X$ is algebraic, then 3 $\implies \ : 4 \implies \ : 1$ , and hence in this case all of the above properties are equivalent.

Proof. $1 \implies 2$ : By Theorem 20.8.1, $\operatorname { T r s } ( Y ) \simeq \operatorname { T r s } ( X ) ( 2 )$ , where $Y$ is the Kummer surface of $A$ as in the definition of a ShiodaInose structure. Since also ${ \mathrm { T r s } } ( Y ) \simeq$ $\operatorname { T r s } ( A ) ( 2 )$ we conclude that $\operatorname { T r s } ( X ) \simeq \operatorname { T r s } ( A )$ .

$2 \implies 3$ : Take $A$ as in 2. Then, by 2, the natural embedding $\operatorname { T r s } ( A ) \subset H ^ { 2 } ( A , \mathbb { Z } ) \simeq$ $U ^ { \mathbb { Q } 3 }$ induces $\mathrm { T r s } ( X ) \hookrightarrow U ^ { \oplus 3 }$ .

Now assume that $X$ is algebraic.

$3 \implies 4$ : The given embedding, say $\varphi$ , extends as $\varphi \oplus 0 : \operatorname { T r s } ( X ) \hookrightarrow \Lambda _ { \mathsf { K 3 } }$ . Now $\mathrm { T r s } ( X )$ has signature $( 2 , k )$ , $k \leq 3$ , and thus, by Proposition 19.2.10, it embeds uniquely in $\Lambda _ { \mathsf { K 3 } }$ . This shows that $\varphi \not \in 0$ gives the canonical embedding $\operatorname { T r s } ( X ) \subset$ $H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } ) = \oplus ^ { 3 } U \oplus \oplus ^ { 2 } E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ , which implies that $\mathsf { N S } ( X )$ contains $\mathbb { O } ^ { 2 } E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ .

$4 \Longrightarrow ~ 1$ . By Theorem 20.8.1 there is a Nikulin involution $\iota : X \to X$ such that for the rational quotient map $\pi : X \xrightarrow { \dots } Y$ we have $\pi _ { ! } : \operatorname { T r s } ( X ) ( 2 ) { \overset { \simeq } { \to } } \operatorname { T r s } ( Y )$ . Moreover, $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { N i k } } \oplus E _ { 8 } ( - 1 ) \subset \mathsf { N S } ( Y )$ . The crucial remarks now are:

• $M = \Lambda _ { \mathrm { N i k } } \oplus E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ as well as the Kummer lattice $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { K u m } }$ are negative definite $u _ { 1 } ^ { \mathfrak { Q 3 } }$ and o long. • ${ \mathsf { N S } } ( Y )$ has r ${ \mathrm { a n k } } \geq 1 6 \geq { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } { \mathrm { r a n k } } ( L ) = 1 1$ and so, by Corollary 15.2.7, the isometry class of the lattice ${ \mathsf { N S } } ( Y )$ is unique in its genus.

The lattice $M$ embeds primitively in NS(Y) and hence by Corollary 15.1.4 also $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { K u m } }$ embeds primitively in NS(Y). But then $Y = { \mathsf { K m } } ( A )$ , proving 1.

We come back to the article [211] by T. Shioda and H. Inose where the structure named after them was introduced. In loc. cit. they applied it to the smallest possible transcendental lattices, those of rank 2. These correspond to positive definite integral quadratic forms. Two such forms are isometric if they are equivalent under conjugation by $\operatorname { S L _ { 2 } } ( \mathbb { Z } )$ . Any K3 surface with a transcendental lattice $T$ of rank 2 has no moduli and Theorem 20.8.2 implies that these are obtained from an algebraic torus $A$ via a ShiodaInose structure. It is shown in [211] that in fact $A$ is a product of two elliptic curves. Summarizing:

Corollary 20.8.3. A $K \mathcal { 3 }$ -surface $X$ whose transcendental lattice $T$ has rank 2 is obtained from a product of two elliptic curves by means of a ShiodaInose structure. Such surfaces have no moduli and correspond one-to-one to points of the set of isometry classes of positive definite even lattices of rank 2.

Example 20.8.4 (Non-Kummer Nikulin quotients and non-algebraic K3 surfaces with a ShiodaInose structure). By Theorem 19.2.1, there is a K3-surface $X$ with a marking $\varphi : H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } ) \stackrel { \sim } { \to } \Lambda _ { \mathsf { K 3 } }$ such that $\varphi ( \operatorname { T r s } ( X ) ) = \varnothing ^ { 3 } U \subset \varnothing ^ { 3 } U \oplus \varnothing ^ { 2 } E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ .

Since $\mathsf { N S } ( X )$ is then negative definite, such K3 surfaces (and all of its quotients by an involution) are not algebraic. We next observe that, since ${ \mathsf { N S } } ( X ) \simeq { \mathbb { O } } ^ { 2 } E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ , Theorem 20.8.1 implies that, first of all, $X$ admits a Nikulin involution with quotient $Y$ and with $\operatorname { T r s } ( Y ) \simeq \mathbb { \oplus } ^ { 3 } U ( 2 )$ (so $Y$ is not algebraic), and, secondly, that NS(Y) contains $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { N i k } } \oplus E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ . Note also that $\operatorname { r a n k } ( \mathsf { N S } ( Y ) ) = \operatorname { r a n k } ( \mathsf { N S } ( X ) ) = 1 6$ so that the index $[ \mathsf { N S } ( Y ) : \Lambda _ { \mathrm { N i k } } \oplus E _ { 8 } ( - 1 ) ]$ is finite. Suppose that there exists a torus $A$ with $Y = \mathsf { K m } ( A )$ . Since the two-forms are preserved in a ShiodaInose structure, we would have a Hodge isometry $H ^ { 2 } ( A ) \simeq U ^ { \uplus 3 } \simeq \operatorname { T r s } ( X )$ . Hence for the Kummer quotient $Y$ , by Theorem 20.6.4 one would have ${ \mathrm { T r s } } ( Y ) = \oplus ^ { 3 } U$ and a primitive embedding $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { K u m } } \subset \mathsf { N S } ( Y )$ , which must be an equality since dis $\operatorname { \varepsilon } ( \mathsf { N S } ( Y ) ) =$ $\operatorname { d i s c } ( \operatorname { T r s } ( Y ) ) = 2 ^ { 6 } = \operatorname { d i s c } ( \Lambda _ { \operatorname { K u m } } )$ . Similarly, since $\mathrm { d i s c } ( \Lambda _ { \mathrm { K u m } } ) = 2 ^ { 6 } = \mathrm { d i s c } ( \Lambda _ { \mathrm { N i k } } )$ the inclusion $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { N i k } } \oplus E _ { 8 } ( - 1 ) \subset \mathsf { N S } ( Y )$ becomes an equality. Since $\Lambda _ { \mathrm { K u m } }$ is clearly indecomposable, it cannot be isometric to $E _ { 8 } ( - 1 ) \oplus \Lambda _ { \mathrm { N i k } }$ and there is no Shioda— Inose structure involving $Y$ .

On the other hand, there are non-algebraic surfaces admitting a ShiodaInose structure: just start with a non-algebraic 2-torus. By Corollary 5.2.8 the corresponding Kummer surface is a Nikulin quotient, say of a (necessarily non-algebraic) K3 surface $X$ and so here is no Shioda-Inose structure involving $X$ .

We already observed (see Remark 19.2.12.2) that $T = \mathbb { Q } ^ { 3 } U$ embeds in two ways into the K3 lattice: the standard embedding with $T ^ { \perp } = \oplus ^ { 2 } E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ and another embedding with $T ^ { \perp } = \Gamma _ { 1 6 } ( - 1 )$ . The above argument shows that in order for $X$ to have a ShiodaInose structure, the first embedding is impossible. This implies that $D ( \oplus ^ { 3 } U ) \subset D ( \Lambda )$ is the period domain of K3 surfaces admitting a Shioda-Inose structure, where $T = \oplus ^ { 3 } U \subset \Lambda$ is not the standard embedding. The general point represents non-algebraic surfaces, while the algebraic ones are given by countably many hyperplanes in this 4dimensional period domain.

# 20.9 Appendix: On Surfaces Admitting an Action of a Finite Group

In this section $X$ is any compact (smooth) complex surface with a faithful action of a finite group $G$ , and $\widetilde { Y }$ denotes the minimal resolution of $Y = X / G$ . We write $H ^ { 2 } ( X ) , H ^ { 2 } ( Y ) , \ldots$ to mean integral cohomology while $H _ { 1 } ( X ) , H _ { 2 } ( Y ) , . . .$ stands for integral homology. We relate the intersection lattices of $X$ and $\widetilde { Y }$ . The main result, Theorem 20.9.6, is quite technical, but it is of crucial importance for applications to K3 surfaces in Section 20.2.

20.9.A The set-up. By [35], the action of $g \in G$ on the tangent space at a fixed point can be linearized which implies that the fixed locus of $g$ in $X$ is either empty or a disjoint union of smooth curves and points. The image in $Y$ of an isolated fixed point of $g$ acting on $X$ by definition is a quotient singularity, hence by Proposition 4.5.2, a du Val singularity. We assume that there are only (finitely many) isolated fixed points and we employ the following notation:

$\sigma : \widetilde { Y }  Y$ : the minimal resolution of $Y$

• $\Sigma \subset X$ : the finite set of fixed points of the $G$ -action;   
• $\bar { p } \in { Y }$ : the image of $p \in \Sigma \subset X$ , under $\pi : X \to Y$ ;   
• $\tau : { \widetilde { X } } \to X$ : a minimal the blow-up of $X$ in the points of $\Sigma$ so that $\pi$ extends as $\widetilde { \pi } : \widetilde { X } \to \widetilde { Y }$ ;   
• $E _ { p } \subset { \widetilde { Y } }$ : the exceptional divisor over $\bar { p }$ ;

We gather the information in the following commutative diagram:

![](images/2c73f746750dd2d6be1626c384409ca065ef9f6549ed9571ba2463a5f00ca373.jpg)

Using the Mayer-Vietoris sequence applied to the open sets $X - \Sigma$ and a union of balls around the points of $\Sigma$ , one gets isomorphisms

$$
j ^ { \prime \ast } : H ^ { q } ( X ) \ { \stackrel { \sim } { \to } } \ H ^ { q } ( X ^ { \prime } ) , \quad j ^ { \prime \ast } : H ^ { q } ( X ) ^ { G } \ { \stackrel { \sim } { \to } } \ H ^ { q } ( X ^ { \prime } ) ^ { G } , q = 0 , 1 , 2 .
$$

Since by Lemma B.5.2 the induced map $\tau ^ { * }$ makes $H ^ { 2 } ( X )$ into a direct summand of $H ^ { 2 } ( { \widetilde { X } } )$ , we may and shall consider $H ^ { 2 } ( X )$ as a subgroup of $H ^ { 2 } ( { \tilde { X } } )$ .

Recall that for continuous maps $f : X \to Y$ between connected oriented manifolds $X , Y$ of dimensions $d , d ^ { \prime }$ respectively, the induced maps $f _ { * } : H _ { q } ( X ) \to H _ { q } ( Y )$ , $q = 0 , \ldots , d$ , in homology can be combined with the two Poincaré duality isomorphisms $H _ { c } ^ { q } ( X ) \xrightarrow [ D ] { \simeq } H _ { d - q } ( X )$ and $H _ { c } ^ { d ^ { \prime } - ( d - q ) } ( Y ) \xrightarrow [ D ^ { \prime } ] { \simeq } H _ { d - q } ( Y )$ to give the Gysin homomorphisms in (compactly supported) cohomology 9 $f _ { ! } = ( D ^ { \prime } ) ^ { - 1 } \circ f _ { * } \circ D$ : $H _ { c } ^ { q } ( X ) \to H _ { c } ^ { d ^ { \prime } - d + q } ( Y )$ .See e.g. [50, Ch. VII1 §10].

We shall also make use of extensions of the Gysin homomorphisms in the case of regular topological coverings, such as $\pi : X ^ { \prime } \to Y ^ { \prime }$ , the so-called transfer homomorphisms $\mathfrak { t } ^ { * } : H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } ) \to H ^ { k } ( Y ^ { \prime } )$ and $\mathfrak { t } _ { * } : H _ { k } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) \to H _ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } )$ , $k \in \mathbb { Z }$ . See e.g. [94, §3.2]. If we compose these with the usual induced maps $\pi ^ { * }$ and $\pi _ { * }$ , one obtains similar rather obvious identities which we shall state only for cohomology:

Lemma 20.9.1. Let $\pi : X ^ { \prime }  Y ^ { \prime } = X ^ { \prime } / G$ be as above. Then

1. $\mathfrak { t } ^ { * } \pi ^ { * } : H ^ { k } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) \to H ^ { k } ( Y ^ { \prime } )$ is multiplication by $n = | G |$ . $\pi ^ { * } \mathfrak { t } ^ { * } : H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } ) \to H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } )$ is induced by the action of $\textstyle \sum _ { g \in G } g \in \mathbb { Z } [ G ]$

2. $\pi ^ { * } : H ^ { k } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) \to H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } )$ has its image in $H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } ) ^ { G }$ . The kernel of $\pi ^ { * }$ as well as the kernel of $\mathfrak { t } ^ { * } : H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } ) ^ { G }  H ^ { k } ( Y ^ { \prime } )$ is $n$ -torsion.

3. If $H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } )$ is $a$ free $\mathbb { Z }$ -module, then $H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } ) ^ { G }$ is the primitive closure of $\operatorname { I m } ( \pi ^ { * } )$

Proof. For the proofs of item 1 we refer to [94, §3.2].

2. Since $\pi \circ g = \pi$ for every $g \in G$ , one has $g ^ { * } ( \pi ^ { * } ( y ) ) = \pi ^ { * } ( y )$ , $y \in H ^ { \ast } ( Y ^ { \prime } )$ , and so $\pi ^ { * } ( y )$ is $G$ -invariant. Item 1 shows that $\pi ^ { * }$ and $\mathbf { t } ^ { * } | H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } ) ^ { G }$ are injective modulo $n$ -torsion.

3. By item 2, $\operatorname { I m } ( \pi ^ { * } )$ has the same rank as $H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } ) ^ { G }$ . So it suffices to show that $H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } ) ^ { G }$ is a primitive sublattice of $H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } )$ . To see this, observe that if a $G$ -module $M$ is without torsion, $M ^ { G }$ is a primitive sublattice of $M$ since, if for some $x \in M$ and $g \in G$ one has $m x = m g ( x ) \in M ^ { G }$ , then $x = g ( x )$ .

Remark 20.9.2. If $X ^ { \prime }$ (and hence $Y ^ { \prime }$ ) are oriented compact connected manifolds, the transfer homomorphisms are the same as the Gysin homomorphisms. If $X ^ { \prime }$ and $Y ^ { \prime }$ are oriented but not necessarily compact, the Gysin maps $\pi _ { ! } : H _ { c } ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } ) \to H _ { c } ^ { k } ( Y ^ { \prime } )$ extend the transfer maps, i.e., there is a commutative diagram

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { H ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } ) \xrightarrow { \quad \overbrace { \mathrm {  { ~ \delta ~ } } \mathbf { t } ^ { * } \quad } ^ { \pi ^ { * } } } H ^ { k } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) } \\ & { \quad \quad \bigg | ^ { k } } \\ & { H _ { c } ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } ) \xrightarrow { \pi _ { ! } } H _ { c } ^ { k } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) . } \end{array}
$$

Returning to our setting we have:

Lemma 20.9.3. 1. One has $\begin{array} { r } { \widetilde { \pi } ^ { * } \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } ( u ) = \sum _ { g \in G } g ^ { * } ( u ) } \end{array}$ , $u \in H ^ { 2 } ( X )$ . 2. The Gysin morphism $\tilde { \pi } _ { ! } : H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { X } ) \to H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } )$ restricted to $H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ^ { G }$ is injective and multiplies the intersection form by $| G |$ .

Proof. 1. Let $u \in H ^ { 2 } ( X )$ . Using diagram (20.21) in case $k = 2$ where $H _ { c } ^ { 2 } ( X ^ { \prime } ) \simeq$ $H ^ { 2 } ( X ^ { \prime } ) ~ \simeq ~ H ^ { 2 } ( X )$ , Lemma 20.9.1.2 implies 1. Indeed, in this case the diagram extends as folllows

$$
\begin{array} { r l } & { H _ { c } ^ { k } ( X ^ { \prime } ) \xrightarrow { \pi _ { 1 } } H _ { c } ^ { k } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) } \\ & { ~ \Biggr \downarrow } \\ & { H ^ { 2 } ( X ) \xrightarrow [ \pi ^ { * } ] { } H ^ { 2 } ( Y ) } \\ & { ~ \Biggr \downarrow \overset { \pi ^ { * } } { \underset { \longrightarrow } { \longrightarrow } } \left. \begin{array} { l } { \pi ^ { * } } \\ { \widetilde { \pi } ^ { 2 } } \end{array} \right. } \\ & { H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { X } ) \xrightarrow [ \widetilde { \pi } ^ { * } ] { \widetilde { \pi } _ { 1 } } H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) . } \end{array}
$$

2. If $u , u ^ { \prime } \in H ^ { 2 } ( X )$ , setting $y = \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } ( \tau ^ { * } u ) , y ^ { \prime } = \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } ( \tau ^ { * } u ^ { \prime } )$ , one finds $\widetilde { \pi } ^ { * } y \cdot \widetilde { \pi } ^ { * } y ^ { \prime } = \left| G \right| y \cdot y ^ { \prime }$ , since $\widetilde { \pi }$ has degree $| G |$ . Assume now that $u , u ^ { \prime } \in H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ^ { G }$ . Using item 1 and the (cup-product preserving) injectivity of $\tau ^ { * }$ which allows to drop $\tau ^ { * }$ , we have:

$$
| G | ( \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } u , \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } u ^ { \prime } ) = \widetilde { \pi } ^ { * } \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } u \cdot \widetilde { \pi } ^ { * } \widetilde { \pi } _ { ! } u ^ { \prime } = | G | ^ { 2 } u \cdot u ^ { \prime } .
$$

This implies that $\widetilde { \pi } _ { ! }$ restricts injectively to $H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ^ { G }$ (since this lattice is nondegenerate), and so 2 follows.

Next, we relate the cohomology groups of $X ^ { \prime }$ and its compactification $X$ , as well as those of $Y ^ { \prime }$ and its compactification $\widetilde { Y }$ . To do this, we shall make use of a variant of the so-called Gysin exact sequence which relates the cohomology of an oriented differentiable manifold $M$ and the cohomology of the complement of a smooth submanifold $N \subset M$ :

$$
\cdots \to H ^ { q } ( N ) \to H ^ { q + e } ( M ) \to H ^ { q + e } ( M - N ) \to H ^ { q + 1 } ( N ) \to \cdots \quad e = \mathrm { c o d i m } _ { \mathbb { R } } N .
$$

This is a slightly less known sequence and hence we explain how it arises. One starts with the long exact sequence in cohomology for the pair $( M , M - N )$ . By the excision property, the terms $H ^ { q } ( M , M - N )$ can be replaced with $H ^ { q } ( T , T - N )$ , where $T$ is a suitably small neighborhood of $N$ in $M$ . The so-called tubular neighborhood theorem (cf. [135, Chapter 4.5]) gives a nice choice for $T$ which ensures that $T$ is diffeomorphic to the total space of a 2-disc bundle over $N$ , where we identify $N$ with the zero section $s _ { 0 }$ of this 2-disc bundle of $N$ in $M$ . Finally, by Thom's theorem (cf. [219, Ch. 5.7, Thm 10]) we have a natural identification $H ^ { q } ( T , T -$ $s _ { 0 } ) = H ^ { q - e } ( N )$ . In our case, $N$ is not a submanifold but an $A$ -D $E$ configuration in a complex surface. However, we explained in $\ S$ 4.4.C that a neighborhood of such a configuration is obtained by plumbing the tubular neighborhoods of the components of the configuration. This comes down to identifying the two 2- discs over an intersection point $p$ of two intersecting components. Since $H ^ { q } ( E ) =$ $\bigoplus _ { p \in \Sigma } H ^ { q } ( E _ { p } )$ and $H ^ { 1 } ( E _ { p } ) = 0$ (the curves $E _ { p }$ are unions of smooth rational curves), the Gysin sequence for the pair $( \widetilde { Y } , E )$ leads to

$$
0 \to \bigoplus _ { p \in \Sigma } H ^ { 0 } ( E _ { p } ) \stackrel { i _ { * } } { \to } H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) \stackrel { \widetilde { j ^ { * } } } { \longrightarrow } H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } - E ) = H ^ { 2 } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) \longrightarrow H ^ { 1 } ( E ) = 0 .
$$

20.9.B The case where $\textbf { G }$ is abelian. In this subsection $G$ is an abelian group acting on $X$ with quotient $Y$ . The goal is to relate $H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ^ { G }$ to $H ^ { 2 } ( Y )$ . Over $\mathbb { Q }$ the groups are isomorphic, but the possible torsion in the integral cohomology groups complicates matters. It is easy to impose a condition which implies that the related groups $H ^ { 2 } ( X )$ and $H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } )$ are free of torsion, since the universal coefficient theorem implies that this is equivalent to $H _ { 1 } ( X )$ and $H _ { 1 } ( \widetilde { Y } )$ being free of torsion. The stronger assumption that $X$ be simply connected and that $H _ { 1 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) = 0$ would ensure this. A property of the group action, which holds in the cases of interest to us, makes the last condition superfluous:

Lemma 20.9.4. With $X , G , \Sigma , Y , { \widetilde { Y } }$ as in $\boldsymbol { \xi }$ 20.9.A (with $G$ abelian), let $G _ { p } , p \in$ $\Sigma$ , be the stabilizer of $p$ in $G$ . Suppose that $X$ is simply connected and that the homomorphism $\oplus _ { p \in \Sigma } G _ { p } \to G$ induced by inclusion is surjective. Then $H _ { 1 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) = 0$ .

Proof. Let $U = \widetilde { Y } - E = Y - \pi ( \Sigma )$ , and $V = \textstyle \bigcup _ { p \in \Sigma } T ( E _ { p } )$ , the union of tubular neighbourhoods $T ( E _ { p } )$ of the exceptional sets $E _ { p }$ , $p \in \Sigma$ : Then $\begin{array} { r } { U \cap V = \bigcup _ { p \in \Sigma } T ^ { 0 } ( E _ { p } ) } \end{array}$ , where $T ^ { 0 } ( E _ { p } )$ can be identified with the quotient of a punctured ball by $G _ { p }$ .This quotient has fundamental group $G _ { p }$ since in real dimensions $\geq 3$ a once punctured ball is simply connected. Part of the Mayer-Vietoris sequence for the open cover $\{ U , V \}$ of $\widetilde { Y }$ in homology (cf. [94, §2.2]) reads

$$
H _ { 1 } ( U \cap V ) \to H _ { 1 } ( U ) \oplus H _ { 1 } ( V ) \to H _ { 1 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) \to H _ { 0 } ( U \cap V ) \to \cdots .
$$

Since $X ^ { \prime } = X - \Sigma$ is simply connected and $X ^ { \prime }  Y ^ { \prime } = Y - \pi ( \Sigma ) = U$ is a Galois cover, $\pi _ { 1 } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) = H _ { 1 } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) = G$ and so, by what we just said, the Mayer-Vietoris sequence reads as follows

$$
\oplus _ { p \in \Sigma } G _ { p } \to G \to H _ { 1 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) \stackrel { \delta } \to \oplus _ { p \in \Sigma } \mathbb { Z } \to \mathbb { Z } \oplus \oplus _ { p \in \Sigma } \mathbb { Z } \to \mathbb { Z } \to 0 .
$$

Hence the assumption that $\oplus _ { p \in \Sigma } G _ { p } \to G$ is surjective implies $H _ { 1 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) = 0$ .

Example 20.9.5. If $G$ is a finite abelian group acting symplectically on a K3 surface $X$ , Tables 20.4.1 and 20.4.2 show that the assumption on the stabilizers is satisfied in this case. However, the conclusion that $H _ { 1 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) = 0$ in this case follows also directly since $\widetilde { Y }$ is a K3 surface.

To arrive at the desired comparison stated as Theorem 20.9.6 below, we make use of Proposition A.6.2 which provides an exact sequence

$$
0 \to \operatorname { E x t } ^ { 1 } ( G ) \to H ^ { 2 } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) \overset { \pi ^ { * } } \longrightarrow \mathsf { H } \to 0 , \quad \mathsf { H } : = \ker ( H ^ { 2 } ( X ^ { \prime } ) ^ { G } \overset \delta \to H ^ { 3 } ( G ) ) ,
$$

describing what happens in cohomology under $\pi : X ^ { \prime } \to Y ^ { \prime }$ , the induced unramified $G$ -cover over the smooth part $Y ^ { \prime }$ of $Y$ . Observing that by $\left( 2 0 . 2 0 \right)$ the inclusion $X ^ { \prime } \hookrightarrow X$ induces an isomorphism $H ^ { 2 } ( X ) \simeq H ^ { 2 } ( X ^ { \prime } )$ , we see that in particular the image of $\pi ^ { * }$ in $H ^ { 2 } ( X ^ { \prime } ) ^ { G }$ can be considered as a subgroup of $H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ^ { G }$ of finite index $\leq \ \vert H ^ { 3 } ( G ) ) \vert$ . Note also that $\mathsf { H }$ , as a subgroup of the torsion free group $H ^ { 2 } ( X )$ inherits a lattice structure from the intersection product on $H ^ { 2 } ( X )$ . Introducing the following additional lattices:

$$
\begin{array} { c } { { M _ { Y } ^ { \prime } = \mathrm { s u b l a t t i c e ~ o f ~ } \mathsf { H } _ { \widetilde { Y } } = H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) / \mathrm { T o r s ~ s p a n n e d ~ b y } } } \\ { { \mathrm { t h e ~ c l a s s e s ~ o f ~ t h e ~ c o m p o n e n t s ~ o f } } } \\ { { M _ { Y } = \mathrm { p r i m i t i v e ~ c l o s u r e ~ o f ~ } M _ { Y } ^ { \prime } \mathrm { ~ i n ~ } \mathsf { H } _ { \widetilde { Y } } , } } \end{array}
$$

we can now state the central result of this section:

Theorem 20.9.6. Let $X$ be a compact complex surface admitting an action_by a finite abelian group $G$ of order $n$ , let $\pi : X \to Y = X / G$ be the quotient map, $\widetilde { Y }$ the minimal resolution of singularities of $Y$ , $X ^ { \prime }$ the complement of the fixed points of $G$ , $Y ^ { \prime } = X ^ { \prime } / G$ , and $j ^ { \prime } : X ^ { \prime } \hookrightarrow X$ , ${ \widetilde { j } } : Y ^ { \prime } \hookrightarrow { \widetilde { Y } }$ the inclusions.

Assume that $Y : = X / G$ has at most cyclic quotient singularities, that $X$ is simply connected and that $H _ { 1 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) = 0$ . Then the following assertions hold:

1. Setting $\theta : = ( j ^ { \prime * } ) ^ { - 1 } \circ \pi ^ { * } \circ { \widetilde { j } } ^ { * } : H ^ { 2 } ( { \widetilde { Y } } )  H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ^ { G }$ , the image of $\theta$ belongs to H (cf. (20.23)) and there is an exact sequence

$$
0 \to M _ { Y } / M _ { Y } ^ { \prime } \to H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) / M _ { Y } ^ { \prime } \overset { \theta } { \to } \mathsf { H } \to 0 .
$$

The factor group ${ M _ { Y } } / { M _ { Y } ^ { \prime } }$ is canonically isomorphic to $\operatorname { E x t } ^ { 1 } ( G )$ .

2. $\theta$ induces an isomorphism $H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) / M _ { Y } \stackrel { \simeq } {  } \mathsf { H }$ and an injection $M _ { Y } ^ { \bot } \hookrightarrow \mathsf { H }$ . This is an injection of free $\mathbb { Z }$ -modules of the same rank, but $\theta | _ { M _ { Y } ^ { \perp } }$ multiplies the intersection form with $| G |$ . In case $G$ is cyclic, ${ \mathsf { H } } = H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ^ { G }$ .

3. The elementary divisors $e _ { 1 } | e _ { 2 } | \cdots | e _ { r }$ of the discriminant group of $M _ { Y }$ all divide $n = | G |$ .

4. The length of the discriminant group of the sublattice $\mathsf { H } \subset H ^ { 2 } ( X )$ is at least equal to $\mathrm { r a n k } ( H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ^ { G } ) - r$ . Its elementary divisors are obtained by omitting the integers equal to 1 from the list $( n / e _ { 1 } , \ldots , n / e _ { r } , n , \ldots , n )$ (the size of this list equals $\operatorname { r a n k } ( \mathsf { H } ) = \operatorname { r a n k } ( H ^ { 2 } ( X ) ^ { G } ) = b _ { 2 } ( { \bar { Y } } ) - \operatorname { r a n k } ( M _ { Y } ) )$ .

The discriminant bilinear form of $\mathsf { H }$ assumes values in $n ^ { - 1 }  { \mathbb { Z } } /  { \mathbb { Z } }$ . If the intersection form on $X$ is even, the discriminant quadratic form takes values in $( 2 n ) ^ { - 1 } \mathbb { Z } / \mathbb { Z }$ .

Proof. 1. We first show that

• $\ddot { j }$ induces an isomorphism $\tilde { j } ^ { * } : H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) / M _ { Y } ^ { \prime } \stackrel { \simeq } {  } H ^ { 2 } ( Y ^ { \prime } )$ ;   
there is a canonical identification $\mathrm { T o r s } H ^ { 2 } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) = M _ { Y } / M _ { Y } ^ { \prime } = \mathrm { E x t } ^ { 1 } ( G )$ .

To start, remark that since $H _ { 1 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) = 0$, by the universal coefficient theorem $H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } )$ has no torsion. Next, we invoke the exact sequence (20.22). the image of the map $i _ { * }$ in this sequence is precisely the lattice $M _ { Y } ^ { \prime }$. Since $M _ { Y }$ is its primitive closure, $H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) / M _ { Y }$ is without torsion and under $\tilde { j } ^ { * }$ it is isomorphic to $H ^ { 2 } ( Y ^ { \prime } )$ modulo torsion. Consequently, the sequence implies

$$
H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) / M _ { Y } ^ { \prime } = H ^ { 2 } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) , \quad \mathrm { T o r s } H ^ { 2 } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) = M _ { Y } / M _ { Y } ^ { \prime } .
$$

On the other hand, $\pi$ restricted to $X ^ { \prime }$ gives an unramified Galois cover $\pi : X ^ { \prime } \to$ $Y ^ { \prime }$ and so, since $X ^ { \prime }$ is simply connected, one has $\pi _ { 1 } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) = G$ and so $H _ { 1 } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) =$ $\operatorname { T o r s } H _ { 1 } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) = G$ since $G$ is abelian. By the universal coefficient theorem ([94, Thm. 3.2]), $\operatorname { T o r s } H ^ { 2 } ( Y ^ { \prime } ) = \operatorname { E x t } ^ { 1 } ( G )$ . Using (20.23), the exact sequence (20.24) is then a direct consequence of (20.20) and (20.22).

Proof of $\boldsymbol { \mathscr { z } }$ ._The exact sequence (20.24) shows that $\theta$ induces an isomorphism between $H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) / M _ { Y }$ and $\mathsf { H }$ .Since $M _ { Y } ^ { \prime }$ is non-degenerate, $M _ { Y } ^ { \bot } \cap M _ { Y } ^ { \prime } = \{ 0 \}$ , so the homomorphism $\theta$ restricts injectively to $M _ { Y } ^ { \perp }$ . The morphism $\widetilde { \pi } : \widetilde { X } \to \widetilde { Y }$ induced by $\pi$ is finite of degree $| G |$ and so, using the cup product, $\widetilde { \pi } ^ { * } ( y ) \cup \widetilde { \pi } ^ { * } ( y ^ { \prime } ) = \widetilde { \pi } ^ { * } ( y \cup y ^ { \prime } ) =$ $| G | y \cup y ^ { \prime }$ for all $y , y ^ { \prime } \in H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } )$ . In particular, the restriction of the intersection form on $H ^ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } )$ to $M _ { Y } ^ { \perp }$ gets multiplied by $| G |$ under $\theta$ . For the last statement one makes use of the vanishing of $H ^ { 3 } ( G )$ in case $G$ is cyclic.

oof of $_ { 3 }$ and 4. We are now in the following abstract setting: one has $\bullet$ a primitive non-degenerate sublattice $T : = M _ { Y }$ of a unimodular lattice $( L , b ) : = \mathsf { H } _ { \widetilde { Y } }$ with orthogonal complement $S : = T ^ { \perp }$ (and so $T = S ^ { \perp }$ ); $\bullet$ a lattice $\mathsf { H }$ of rank $N$ ; $\bullet$ an isomorphism $\theta : L / T \xrightarrow { \sim } \mathsf { H }$ of $\mathbb { Z }$ -modules such that for $x , y \in S$ one has $b ^ { \prime } ( \theta ( x ) , \theta ( y ) ) = n \cdot b ( x , y )$ , where $b ^ { \prime }$ is the bilinear form on $\mathsf { H }$ .

Next, recall that by Lemma 1.6.2 the correlation map induces an isomorphism $\overline { { \beta } } _ { S } : L / T \stackrel { \sim } { \to } S ^ { * }$ of free $\mathbb { Z }$ -modules. By what we have said before, on the finite index sublattice $\theta ( S ) \subset { \mathsf { H } }$ the form $b ^ { \prime }$ coincides with $b ( n )$. But then $\theta \circ ( \overline { { \beta } } _ { S } ) ^ { - 1 }$ identifies $( S ^ { * }, b _ { \mathbb { Q } } ( n ) )$ with the (integral) lattice $\mathsf { H }$. since $L$ is unimodular, by Lemma 1.7.6 the sublattices $S$ and $T$ have isomorphic discriminant groups, hence the same length and the same elementary divisors. So we continue with $S$ instead of $T$. Now apply Remark 1.6.10 to the lattice $S$ and its dual and with $\rho = n$. The discriminant group of $\mathsf { H } = S ^ { * } ( n )$ has elementary divisors obtained from $( e _ { 1 } ^ { * }, \ldots, e _ { N } ^ { * } ) = ( n / e _ { 1 }, \ldots, n / e _ { r }, n, \ldots, n )$ by omitting the $e _ { j } ^ { \ast }$ with $e _ { j } ^ { * } = 1$ (recall that $\mathrm { r a n k } ( \mathsf { H } ) = N$ ) and putting them in the right order. This shows in particular that $e _ { j } | n, ~ j = 1, \ldots, r$, and so, if $y \in S ^ { * }$, then $n \cdot y \in S$. From the description of the discriminant form of $S ^ { * } ( n ) ^ { * } / S ^ { * } ( n )$ in Remark 1.6.10 it follows that the discriminant bilinear form $( b ^ { \prime } ) ^ { \# }$ assumes values in $n ^ { - 1 } { \mathbb { Z } } / { \mathbb { Z } }$. A similar reasoning holds for the discriminant quadratic form in case $b ^ { \prime }$ is even. Finally, since ${ \mathsf { d g } } _ { \mathsf { H } }$ has at least $N - r$ elementary divisors equal to $n \neq 1$, its length is at least $N - r$.

Example 20.9.7. For an involution one has $n = 2$ , and all elementary divisors of the discriminant group of $M _ { Y }$ are equal to 2. Hence, in this case the discriminant group of the invariant lattice is isomorphic to $\oplus ^ { \ell } \mathbb { Z } / 2 \mathbb { Z }$ , $\ell = b _ { 2 } ( \widetilde { Y } ) - \ell ( M _ { Y } )$ , and if the intersection form on $X$ is even, then the discriminant quadratic form can be of type I, or of type II (cf. Definition 1.7.2).

Historical and Bibliographical Notes. Proposition 20.1.3, the application to automorphism groups, is due to Pjatecki-Sapiro and Safarevi and expanded in great detail by V. Nikulin in [172]. Proposition 20.1.5 describing the algebraic nature of the automorphism group is due to H. Sterk [220].

S. Mukai [159] discovered that all finite symplectic groups of automorphisms of a K3 surface appear as certain subgroups of $M _ { 2 3 }$ , one of the sporadic simple groups. The sketch of the proof we give of this result (based on Niemeier lattices) is due to S. Kond, c.f. [128]. For other results on special automorphisms on K3 surfaces using lattice theory, see also[6, 7, 76, 77, 80, 82]. That finite abelian groups acting symplecticaly on a K3 surface have an essentially unique action in cohomology is due to V. Nikulin [169] whose proof we have followed in Section 20.2. The uniqueness of a symplectic action in cohomology for (not necessarily abelian) finite groups acting on a K3 surface has been discussed by K. Hashimoto in [93] making use of the embeddings of $G$ in $M _ { 2 3 }$ . He shows that except for four groups one also has uniqueness (up to conjugation).

Our treatment in Section 20.6 is based on Nikulin's article [168]. We also made use of Lemma 20.6.3 which is inspired by Ch. 3.2.4 in D. Huybrechts's book [106]. The lattice theoretic study of the polarized K3 surfaces admitting a Nikulin involution is due to B. van Geemen and A. Sarti [83]. For geometrically constructed K3 surfaces with a Nikulin involution see Section 3 in loc. cit. The lattice theoretic arguments used for Nikulin involutions and for the ShiodaInose structures are largely due to D. Morrison [158]. The term "ShiodaInose structure" refers to the article [211] by T. Shioda and H. Inose.

We finish by mentioning some related developments concerning so-called generalized Kummer surfaces, that is, K3 surfaces which by definition are the minimal resolutions of a quotient of two-dimensional complex tori by some finite group $G$ . If $G$ fixes the origin, apart from the cyclic group $\mathbb { Z } / 2 \mathbb { Z }$ which gives the Kummer surface, only cyclic groups of order $3 , 4 , 6$ , binary dihedral groups $\tilde { D } _ { 4 } , \tilde { D } _ { 6 }$ and the binary tetrahedral groups are possible. See [74]. The analog of the Kummer lattice for the cyclic case has been studied by J. Bertin in [22], and for the remaining groups by K. Wendland [249] and A. Garbagnati [78]. There are also groups $G$ acting in such a way that not all $g \in G$ have the same fixed points. This is only possible if $G$ is the quaternion group or the binary dihedral group $\tilde { D } _ { 1 2 }$ , and these have been studied by X. Roulleau in [197].

The generalized Kummer surfaces also appear in the construction of generalized Shioda-Inose structures $( X , A , G )$ , where $X$ is a K3 surface, $A$ an abelian surface, and the finite group $G$ acts on $A$ and it acts symplectically on $X$ such that $X / G = A / G$ is a generalized Kummer surface. These have been classified in [178] by H. Önsiper and S. Sertöz.

# Applications to Enriques Surfaces

# Introduction

Since an Enriques surface is the quotient of a K3 surface by a fixed point free involution, the moduli space of Enriques surfaces should be a "subspace" of the moduli space of K3 surfaces. We make this precise in Section 21.1. We also consider moduli for those Enriques surfaces that have at least one nodal curve. Like we did for K3 surfaces, once we have a description of the moduli space, we can make use of this to investigate the automorphism groups of Enriques surfaces. This is taken up in Section 21.2. Surprisingly, the automorphism group is generally infinite for instance for Enriques surfaces without nodal curves. In this case, as well as for the case of a general nodal Enriques surface, the automorphism groups can be described explicitly.

# 21.1 Enriques Surfaces: Moduli

In this chapter $( X , j )$ is a pair of a K3 surface together with a fixed point free involution $j$ . As before, the cyclic group of order 2 generated by $j$ is denoted $G$ . The quotient $X / G = Y$ is an Enriques surface. We continue to denote the K3 lattice by $\Lambda$ .

The basic invariants of an Enriques surface $Y$ are as follows (see e.g. Appendix B.3)

$$
b _ { 1 } ( Y ) = 0 , \quad p _ { g } ( Y ) = 0 , \quad H ^ { 2 } ( Y ) / \mathrm { t o r s i o n } \simeq \Lambda _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ,
$$

where $\Lambda _ { \mathsf { E n r } } : = U \oplus E _ { 8 } ( - 1 )$ is the Enriques lattice. Below we shall also encounter $\Lambda _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ( 2 )$ and its discriminant quadratic form given by (see Example 11.2.5.3)

$$
q _ { \Lambda _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ( 2 ) } ^ { \# } \simeq \oplus ^ { 5 } u _ { 1 } .
$$

21.1.A Moduli for Enriques surfaces. The fixed point free involution $j$ on the K3 surface $X$ induces an involution $j ^ { * }$ on $H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } )$ which can be described abstractly, using a properly chosen isometry $H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } ) \ \simeq \Lambda$ . To explain this, we rewrite the K3 lattice as $\Lambda = U \oplus W \oplus W ^ { \prime }$ , where $W , W ^ { \prime }$ are copies of the Enriques lattice. This last decomposition can be used to define the lattice Enriques involution

$$
\iota _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ( u , v , v ^ { \prime } ) = ( - u , v ^ { \prime } , v ) , \quad ( u , v , v ^ { \prime } ) \in U \oplus W \oplus W ^ { \prime } .
$$

The invariant lattice $\Lambda ^ { G }$ consists of the vectors $( 0 , v , v )$ , and so it is isometric to $\Lambda _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ( 2 )$ . Proposition 15.2.10 then implies that there is a marking $\varphi : H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } ) \to \Lambda$ fitting in a commutative diagram1

$$
\begin{array} { r l r } & { } & { H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } ) \xrightarrow [ \varphi ] { \sim } \mathrm {  ~ \beta ~ } \Lambda } \\ & { } & { \quad \quad \quad \quad j ^ { * } \sqrt { \mathrm {  ~ \beta ~ } } } \\ & { } & { \quad \quad H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } ) \xrightarrow [ \varphi ] { \sim } \Lambda . } \end{array}
$$

Such a marking $\varphi$ is called a marking for $( X , j )$ . Since $Y = X / G = X / \langle j \rangle$ has no non-zero holomorphic 2-forms, the involution $j ^ { * }$ acts as -id on $H ^ { 2 , 0 } ( X )$ and hence also on the corresponding period point $[ \omega ] = \varphi [ H ^ { 2 , 0 } ( X ) ]$ . So $[ \omega ]$ belongs to $D ( \Lambda ) \cap \mathbb { P } ( \Lambda _ { G } ) = D ( \Lambda _ { G } )$ where $\Lambda _ { G }$ is the anti-invariant lattice. For later reference, we observe

$$
\Lambda _ { { \cal G } } = \{ ( u , w , - w ) \in { \cal U } \oplus { \cal W } \oplus { \cal W } ^ { \prime } \} \simeq { \cal U } \oplus \Lambda _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ( 2 ) .
$$

We claim that a period point $[ \omega ] \in D ( \Lambda _ { G } )$ such that $[ \omega ]$ is not orthogonal to any root of $\Lambda _ { G }$ corresponds to a K3 surface admitting an Enriques involution. To show this, observe that by Criterion 20.2.1 it suffices to show that a) there is a $G$ -invariant element in the positive cone, and b) $\Lambda _ { G } \cap \mathsf { N S } ( X )$ contains no roots. As to a), by the surjectivity of the period map (Theorem 19.2.1.2), there exists a marked K3 surface $X$ with period point $[ \omega ]$ . We now identify $H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } )$ with $\Lambda$ through this marking. By assumption $\iota _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ( \omega ) = - \omega$ , and so the involution preserves $H ^ { 2 , 0 } ( X )$ . Moreover, $\iota _ { \mathsf { E } \mathsf { n r } }$ acts as −id on the transcendental lattice and so this lattice is contained in $\Lambda _ { G }$ . Hence $\mathsf { N S } ( X )$ and a fortiori $H ^ { 1 , 1 } ( X )$ contain $\Lambda ^ { G }$ , a lattice of signature $( 1 , 9 )$ , and so condition a) holds. A root $r \in \Lambda _ { G }$ cannot be the class of a divisor since by assumption $r \cdot \omega \neq 0$ and so b) holds as well. Consequently, $X$ admits an involution $j$ which under the marking corresponds to $\iota _ { \mathsf { E } \mathsf { n r } }$ . Such an involution $j$ is fixed point free by Lemma 20.5.2, since $\mathrm { T r } ( j ^ { * } ) = \mathrm { T r } ( \iota _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ) = - 2$ . So $X / G$ is an Enriques surfaces and the marking is a marking for $( X , j )$ .

We shall indicate how this implies that Enriques surfaces depend on 10 moduli. We just showed that markings for $( X , j )$ give period points in

$$
D _ { \mathsf { E n r } } = D ( \Lambda _ { G } ) - \bigcup _ { r \in \Lambda _ { G } , r \vdash - 2 } H _ { r } \cap D ( \Lambda _ { G } ) , \quad H _ { r } = r ^ { \perp } ,
$$

and that, conversely, such points correspond to period points for Enriques surfaces coming from marked pairs $( X , j )$ of a K3 surface equipped with an Enriques involution. Such period points will be called period points of Enriques surfaces. The group

$$
\Gamma _ { \mathsf { E n r } } : = \{ \gamma \in \mathsf { O } ( \Lambda ) \mid \gamma \circ l _ { \mathsf { E n r } } = \iota _ { \mathsf { E n r } ^ { \circ } } \gamma \}
$$

acts on $D _ { \mathsf { E n r } }$ in a discrete and proper fashion. If $\varphi$ is a marking for $( X , j )$ , then $\gamma \circ \varphi$ , $\gamma \in \Gamma _ { \mathsf { E n r } }$ , is a marking for a pair $( X ^ { \prime } , j ^ { \prime } )$ with $X ^ { \prime } / j ^ { \prime }$ isomorphic to $X / j$ . The converse holds also and so the (10-dimensional) quotient $\Gamma _ { \mathrm { E n r } } \backslash D _ { \mathrm { E n r } }$ classifies isomorphism classes of Enriques surfaces.

21.1.B Nodal types and the ample cone for Enriques surfaces. In what follows we shall identify $H ^ { 2 } ( X , \mathbb { Z } )$ with the K3 lattice $\Lambda$ through a fixed $( X , j )$ . marking and we let $[ \omega ]$ be the corresponding period point. The sublattice corresponding to the Néron-Severi lattice of $X$ will be denoted by $S$ . Let $\pi ^ { * } : \Lambda _ { \mathsf { E n r } } \to \Lambda ^ { G }$ be the injective map induced by $\pi : X \to Y = X / G$ . This identifies the Enriques lattice with $\Lambda ^ { G } ( \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } )$ .

As is the case for a K3 surface, the ample cone in the Enriques lattice can be described by means of roots. In the present case we need an adapted version which uses pairs of roots on the covering K3 surface.

Definition 21.1.1. For any subset $R$ of a lattice, we let $\langle R \rangle$ be the smallest primitive sublattice containing $R$ .

The collection of all $\iota _ { \mathsf { E } \mathsf { n r } }$ -adapted root pairs of $\Lambda$ is denoted by $\Delta ( \Lambda , \iota _ { \mathsf { E n r } } )$ . If $\{ r , \iota _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ( r ) \} \in \Delta ( \Lambda , \iota _ { \mathsf { E n r } } )$ , we set $r ^ { \pm } : = r \pm \iota _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ( r )$ . The corresponding root $\pmb { r } \in \Lambda _ { \mathsf { E n r } }$ in the Enriques lattice is given by $\pi ^ { * } r = r ^ { + }$ . In particular $\Delta ^ { \pm } ( X ) ) \subset { \mathsf { N S } } ( X )$ .

The above result implies that after a possible change of marking, we may assume that for any given $\iota _ { \mathsf { E } \mathsf { n } \mathsf { r } }$ -adapted root pair $\{ r , \iota _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ( r ) \}$ , the associated root $r ^ { - }$ is of the form $\rho - \iota _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ( \rho )$ where $\rho$ is any root contained in the $W$ -summand. Proposition 21.1.3. Let $( X , j )$ be a pair of a $K \mathcal { 3 }$ surface equipped with an Enriques involution and let $Y = X / G$ be the quotient Enriques surface. Use a marking for $( X , j )$ to identify $H ^ { 2 } ( X )$ with $\Lambda$ and $H ^ { 2 } ( Y ) /$ Tors with $\Lambda _ { \mathsf { E n r } } = \Lambda ^ { G } \big ( \frac { 1 } { 2 } \big )$ . $$
\begin{array} { r l } & { \mathsf { C } _ { X , j } ^ { \mathrm { a m p } } : = \{ x \in \Lambda ^ { G } \otimes \mathbb { R } \mid x \in \mathsf { C } _ { X } , x \cdot r ^ { + } > 0 \ f o r \ a l l \ \{ r , \iota _ { \mathsf { E n r } } ( r ) \} \in \Delta ( X ) \} } \\ & { \quad \quad \quad = \{ y \in \Lambda _ { \mathsf { E n r } } \otimes \mathbb { R } \mid y \in \mathsf { C } _ { Y } , y \cdot r > 0 \ f o r \ a l l \ r \in \Delta ( Y ) \} . } \end{array}

on the positive cone of $\Lambda ^ { G } \otimes \mathbb { R }$ . The latter Weyl group depends only on the set of nodal classes on $Y$ , more precisely, on $\Delta ( Y )$ .

If $x \in \Lambda ^ { G } \otimes \mathbb { R }$ , we have $x = \pi ^ { * } y$ for some $y \in \Lambda _ { \mathsf { E n r } } \otimes \mathbb { R }$ and if $x \in C _ { X }$ , then $y \in { \mathsf { C } } _ { Y }$ .
